## L3c — the engagement loops on a box with no phone: presence, timely delivery, and a prediction that can be graded (prereg; Codex co-prereg answer 09:24Z folded in; no code)

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why | L3b gave the process one delivery door and moved the loops whose lines are informational. Knock, Digest and Ask stayed because each COMMITS an engagement prediction ("recipient engages within 90 min", graded by the next person turn) and E.G1c showed that a prediction about an engagement that cannot happen poisons `judgment_trend`. On a box with no phone the person can still engage — through the cockpit — but only if the line reaches them while they are there, and only if the prediction's clock starts when they could actually see it. |
| Presence (the console's "chat is reachable") | The cockpit is PRESENT iff a machine view registered within the last 90 s (a new `last_view_ms` stamp written by `begin_view_on` only — person console verbs also carry `cli:` labels, so the label alone cannot tell a poll from a person; the instruments and notice polls run every 30 s, so an open tab stamps three times a minute and a closed tab stamps nothing). One atomic in the exclusion, no cookie, no heuristic. `Delivery::has_presence()` = Telegram chat pinned, or console present. |
| Timely delivery | `Delivery::deliver_engaging(kind, text)` — a second entry on the same seam for lines that predict engagement: Telegram when reachable outside quiet hours; else the console queue ONLY when present (the line is leased within 30 s); else `HeldNoPresence` — nothing is queued, because a knock or a digest that sits for hours is a notification, not an interruption that earned itself. One `delivery` record per call as today, with the new outcome. |
| The prediction's clock | On Telegram, unchanged: `note_proactive_sent` / the knock's `judgment_log` at send. On the console, the prediction is committed at the `shown` acknowledgement — the first instant the person could act — with `sent_ms` = the `shown` receipt's time, so the existing resolver (`resolve_proactive`, any surface's person turn within 90 min) grades it unchanged. Queueing commits nothing (L3b's rule stands); if the lease lapses without an acknowledgement the line returns under the same id and still commits nothing. The commit happens inside `ack_notice_shown`'s transaction path for notices carrying an `engagement` marker (kind + subject ref, e.g. `knock:<packet id>`), exactly once per notice (the `shown` uniqueness). |
| The knock's split (found in the source) | `maybe_knock` today evaluates, then COMMITS inside itself (judgment_log with the 90-min due, `knock_last_date`, `knock_pending`, the `sent` disposition) and returns the rendered line — before any send. L3c splits it into `prepare_knock() -> Option<KnockCandidate{pkt_id, band, p, eval_id, trigger, title, receptive}>` (evaluation, escrow hold and blocked dispositions unchanged; no commit) and `commit_knock(candidate, sent_ms)` (the four commits, with the due clock from `sent_ms`). Telegram path: prepare → commit → send, exactly today's order. Console path: prepare → queue with an engagement marker → commit at `shown`. Digest and Ask already commit outside their generators (`note_proactive_sent` after the send), so only the marker and the shown-time commit are new for them. |
| The engagement marker | A bounded column on the notice row (`engagement_json`: kind ∈ {knock, digest, ask}, subject ref, p, band, eval id — never packet text), written with the queue in the same transaction and bound into `verify_notice_row`. `ack_notice_shown` writes the unique `shown` receipt and returns the marker; the engine then commits (`commit_knock` / `note_proactive_sent_at(shown_ms)`). Two phases across two stores, so the guarantee is AT-MOST-ONCE: a crash between the receipt and the commit loses that prediction and never duplicates it (the `shown` uniqueness forbids a second pass). Stated, not hidden. |
| Receptivity | The learned rate against the person's baseline (`proactive_receptivity_ok`) is surface-agnostic and stays the gate; presence replaces "chat != 0"; quiet hours unchanged; the knock's one-per-day cap and `knock_muted` unchanged and checked before delivery, never per surface. |
| Reply grading | `knock_reply` already intercepts show it / later / mute in `handle_turn_as`, which every surface reaches, so a console reply grades the knock as a Telegram reply does. Digest and Ask grade by the next person turn (any surface). |
| Loops that move | Knock, Digest, Ask — bodies moved into the runner with their gates (`timer_chat_quiet` / `idle_gated` with `chat_present := has_presence()`), considered sets, policy lines, ledger recording, `OpportunityGate`s and timer transitions; the ex4 executive shadow stays at the digest's decision moment; the E.G1c paired world-shadow sample records at the knock's decision moment on every box (the sample that could never accrue on the canary). |
| Loops that stay (L3d) | HomeWatch, Family, FollowUp, PriceWatch, MemberBeat, MailSweep, TraditionPrep, Whois — household-facing alerts and asks; each moves after this contract is witnessed, one row, same shape. |
| Gate | (1) Presence fixture: registrations from `cli:*` views within 90 s make the seam present; a person turn does not (it is not a poll); nothing within 90 s makes it absent. (2) Timely-delivery fixture: with no Telegram and no presence, an engaging line records `held-no-presence`, nothing is queued, no prediction exists; with presence it is queued and still no prediction exists until `shown`; the `shown` acknowledgement commits exactly one prediction with `sent_ms` = the receipt's time; a second acknowledgement commits nothing; a lapsed lease commits nothing. (3) Byte-identical Telegram: on a box with a chat, knock/digest/ask sends and their predictions are unchanged over a replayed day. (4) Canary witness: `why loops` shows knock, digest, ask under `process`; with the cockpit open, the first digest lands in the Notices card and its prediction appears in the judgment ledger at the `shown` time; with it closed, the opportunity records `held:no-presence`. |
| Kill | Any engagement prediction committed without a `shown` receipt on the console; a queued engaging line with no presence; a knock's daily cap or mute bypassed by a console copy; a prediction whose clock starts at queue time; the paired world-shadow sample recorded anywhere but the knock's decision moment. |
| Found on the way (goes in the row) | `resolve_proactive(false)` — the tick path that grades STALE sends as ignored — runs only in the Telegram poll loop; on a headless box an unanswered send is never graded until the next person turn. L3c moves that call into the runner's Resolve step (timer-only, no send), so the 90-minute window closes on every box. |
| Codex's answers (09:24Z, adopted) | (a) Presence window 90 s INCLUSIVE: a dedicated `last_view_ms` initialised to 0 and `fetch_max`ed only by `begin_view_on` (the exact machine-view allowlist); recent iff `last_view != 0 && now − last_view <= 90 000`; presence = Telegram pinned OR recent console view; quiet hours remain a separate gate. (b) BOTH, with ONE opportunity: no presence at the runner's precondition is `HeldReason::NoPresence` and is decided BEFORE `proactive_digest` / `proactive_ask` or any other stateful content generation — no delivery call, no delivery row; if presence goes stale between that read and `deliver_engaging`, the seam records `DeliveryOutcome::HeldNoPresence`, queues nothing, and the SAME loop opportunity is rendered held:no-presence (never a second opportunity). `no-chat` is not reused. (c) A SEPARATE console calibration domain (`engagement-console`), cold-started from the existing global receptivity estimate: with zero console grades it emits the global estimate; later it shrinks only against console grades; the surface is stamped on the claim and the marker; the Telegram `engagement` domain stays byte-compatible. Pooling the modalities would make a surface shift look like learning. |
| Amendments required by Codex before ledgering (all adopted) | (1) `resolve_proactive(false)` gets ONE process owner at ≤ 60 s cadence (a runner step ahead of Resolve's hourly gate); the Telegram copy is removed; fixture: an unanswered headless claim resolves no later than deadline + 60 s while an unexpired one stays pending. (2) `proactive_ask` writes `pending_onboard` before delivery today: split into `prepare_ask` / `commit_ask` exactly like the knock; queueing, leasing, expiry or a failed delivery must not arm a question; kill: an ordinary turn swallowed as the answer to a notice that was never shown. (3) One displayed line earns ONE engagement claim: today `maybe_knock` commits `knock:<pkt>` and the caller's `note_proactive_sent` commits a second timestamp claim — that double-booking is not preserved. `proactive_pending` becomes typed, legacy-compatible entries `{sent_ms, ref, surface}`; the knock uses its `knock:<pkt>` ref, digest and ask use deterministic marker refs; the resolver and an explicit reply grade one ref once. Telegram visible behaviour and gates stay byte-identical; the accounting correction is declared. (4) Presence does not guarantee the queued row is leased: engaging notices carry a bound `show_by_ms` and a terminal `expired` receipt; after the short show window they are never leased or shown. At most ONE outstanding (non-terminal) knock per operator per day, enforced in the queue transaction over verified chains — text dedupe is insufficient while `knock_last_date` waits for `shown`. (5) The marker is a canonical typed v1 record, not arbitrary JSON: integer probability units, strict kind-specific fields and ref shapes, bounded ids, no text; its digest and `show_by_ms` are bound into the notice identity and verification; an explicit migration adds the columns to the existing L3b table and pre-marker rows keep validating under the L3b identity formula. (6) The two-store gap is not silently lossy: the `shown` receipt is a durable outbox — a same-lease idempotent ACK returns the original marker and `shown_ms`; `commit_engagement` is idempotent by deterministic ref; a reconciler (each runner beat, and at start) finishes any shown-but-uncommitted marker without duplicating or moving the clock. Gate: no shown marker remains unmatched after a restart; no ref appears twice. |

## E.P3 — CORRECTION (preregistered before the fix): the pace ledger's tick-path resolver marked fresh sends "ignored"

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Finding (source read while moving the stale resolver for L3c amendment 1; confirmed by Codex 09:34Z) | `pace_ledger.rs::ledger_resolve(engaged)` iterates the last 12 pace entries with outcome `pending` and, for each with `age < 90 min`, writes `engaged ? "engaged" : "ignored"`. On the Telegram tick path (`engaged = false`, every ~26 s) that marks a pending pace entry `ignored` seconds after its send — the age predicate is inverted for the tick path. The user-turn path (`engaged = true`) is right. Affected: the pace ledger's `outcome` column only; the judgment ledger and `proactive_pending` were never touched by it. |
| Why it matters now | L3c gives the stale resolver one process-hosted owner at ≤ 60 s cadence on every box. Moving `ledger_resolve(false)` unchanged would widen an immediate false negative from the Telegram box to every headless process. |
| Fix (a prerequisite inside L3c-1, not a silent edit) | The tick pass (`engaged = false`) marks `ignored` only VALID pending rows with `age >= 90 min`; the user-engaged pass marks valid rows with `0 <= age < 90 min` `engaged` and rows with `age >= 90 min` `ignored`; a future or invalid timestamp stays `pending` (fail closed). One process-hosted owner at ≤ 60 s; the Telegram copy is removed only after the fixtures below are green. |
| Fixtures (deterministic, injected clock) | false at 89 m 59.999 s stays pending; false at exactly 90 m becomes ignored; true inside the window becomes engaged; true at/after the boundary becomes ignored; mixed fresh and stale rows resolve independently in one pass; a second pass is idempotent; a future-dated row stays pending under both passes. |
| Not corrected retroactively | Rows already marked `ignored` by the old predicate stay as written (the ledger is append-only in spirit and the true outcomes are not recoverable from the pace ledger alone); the row's `ts` and the transcript remain the evidence. |

## L1d-A — implemented: loop-ledger-v5 and the seven synchronous speakers (commit bb2914c; Codex independent review PASS 12:01Z after two amendment rounds; not yet deployed)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Schema (loop-ledger-v5) | `LoopId` + sixteen ids; `LoopOutcome::Delegated`; `BudgetKind::ModelOneCall`; `LoopPhase {delegated, terminal}` carried in the event's `subject`. The version wall is FAIL-CLOSED: only rows written under v5 aggregate; a v4 row is superseded by version exactly as v3 was under v4, so a v4-labelled row can never carry a new id or a phase into a v5 report. The phase shape is enforced by the reader against the declared schema: a synchronous record carries no phase, no `delegated` outcome and no terminal identity; a `delegated` record is an act of outcome `delegated` without the terminal identity; a `terminal` record carries EXACTLY `loop-<opportunity id>:terminal` and a real outcome; only the nine detached ids (`LoopId::is_detached`) may carry a phase, and a detached id's ACT must carry one (a phase-less detached hold is the synchronous hold its block records, and stands). Reducer: `delegated → terminal` under one opportunity id is ONE opportunity in either input order and never a duplicate; two terminals are a duplicate; a lone `delegated` reduces to an unfinished act, visibly. |
| Gate kinds (code, not ledger schema) | `window_chat_quiet(now, open, presence)` and `window_receptive(now, open, presence, receptive)`: due-ness is an open window read as state; blockers in the legacy order — chat, quiet, then receptivity; no timer to advance. The replay oracle covers both. |
| The seven speakers | briefing and evening keyed by the local day through `briefing_window_open` / `evening_window_open` (the due read without the compose-and-mark side effects; the impure due call stays the act); anticipate, dream, book-ask and event-ask keyed by their persisted stamps through new side-effect-free `*_state()` reads that return the EFFECTIVE period (the domain pace applied) — the `*_due` rules compute through the same reads, and the ledger's cadence line is that period, not the env base; support keyed by the ACTUAL candidate: `support_nudge_prepare` (side-effect-free, every content gate, NO surface blockers — quiet hours and receptivity are the outer gate's, so a quiet-hours candidate is `held:quiet-hours`, not a non-opportunity) → its event key digested to a name-free 64-bit key, never a clock bucket — no candidate, no opportunity; the SAME prepared candidate is committed (`support_nudge_commit`, the audit before the send as before) and sent inside the act, so the ledger is never bound to a candidate that moved. Each records `acted` and holds once per window through its opportunity gate under `LoopHost::Telegram`. Behaviour unchanged: same guards, same generators, same sends, same claims; book-ask's post-accept ordering (arm, stamp, claim, ledger row after the API accepted) verbatim; event-ask recorded as media and not moved. |
| Outcomes | Never collapsed: briefing, evening, anticipate and dream record `nothing-to-say` / `ran` / `found-undelivered` (generated, send failed); book-ask and event-ask record `nothing-to-ask` / `asked` / `found-undelivered`; support records `ran` / `found-undelivered`. Count = sends. Attempt keying (book-ask, event-ask — whose stamps do not move on a failed send; support for a repeat under one key): the first act of a window is keyed by the stamp, every later attempt in the same window is its own opportunity keyed by its instant, so every retry is a separate visible act and the reducer never shows a final result as the only attempt; a no-candidate act is recorded once per window. |
| Pre-existing gap, stated | The support nudge writes its audit BEFORE the send and never undoes it: a failed API send leaves `already_sent` true and the event is suppressed for good. Not changed here; the ledger's `found-undelivered` is what makes it visible. |
| Guards | The seven ids in the poll-loop id table; a per-block guard (not lexical over the body): each tagged block contains `record_loop_tick`, its own id and a window gate. |
| Fixtures | mind-observability (3): the detached lifecycle reduces to one opportunity (spawn + success, + silent, + failure, duplicate terminal, order invariance, phase round-trip, malformed delegated, v4 superseded, v3 superseded, the sixteen ids parse); the version wall (a well-formed v4 act superseded, never aggregated; a v4-labelled delegated row with a new id and a phase never enters) and one refusal per wrong phase shape (delegated without a phase, delegated carrying the terminal identity, terminal without its identity, terminal under another id, terminal of outcome delegated, a phase on a synchronous loop — both phases, a synchronous record carrying a terminal identity, a phase-less detached act; a phase-less detached hold stands), `is_detached` over all 35 ids, the key digest stable and distinct; the window gates' blocker order. |

## L1d-B — behaviour deviation, declared (Codex round 2, 12:41Z; accepted round 3, 12:52Z): the forge gate opens only when the venture the act would consume has itself cooled
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Legacy behaviour | Two reads that could disagree: `forge_due` answered true when ANY active venture had cooled ≥ 15 min; `forge_tick` then advanced the FIRST active venture — which could be a fresh one, re-run only because a later venture was due. |
| Now | ONE read, `forge_due_target()`, returns the venture the act would consume (the first active one) with its stage and pre-act stamp, and only when THAT venture has cooled; the act revalidates all three before the dry-day latch, the treasury draw or any stage work. A fresh first venture is no longer re-run on a later venture's account. |
| Why it is a deviation and not instrumentation | The L1d-B prereg promised no behaviour change. This one changes when forge acts in the multi-active case. It is the same class as the L1b mail-sweep double-spawn fix: the ledger cannot honestly key an opportunity on a target the act does not consume, so the gate was made to name the target it acts on. Recorded here so the change is on the record before it is deployed; a preregistered row only ever claims what its code does. |
| Governance | Both agents agreed; prod deployment of this binary remains Pranab's explicit word. Reversal: return the gate to the legacy pair and key the ledger on the fresh-first case as a known gap. |

## L4-0 — FINDING and co-prereg: the attention budget has no instrument; the spend ledger comes before the budget (Codex co-prereg with amendments 13:11Z; no code)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Finding (staging decision log, 24 h to 13:03:36Z box clock; counts only) | 530 loop acts across 7 loop ids (dmn 62 acts / 218 s wall, lease-sweep 439, ics 17, resolve 5, heartbeat 4, ask 2, knock 1). `model_calls` is `None` on EVERY row — the loop ledger records calls only when a site measures them, and no site does. The inference pool counts privacy lanes and household call-sites in process memory (`record_household_callsite`, `PRIVACY_SERVED`) — no timestamps, no series, lost on restart. The treasury counts PASSES per subsystem per day (default cap 2), file-backed — passes are policy tickets, not calls, wall or tokens. So L4's gate "idle spend within budget" has three partial instruments and no ledger: the mind cannot say how many model calls it made in the last hour, by which loop. |
| Why it matters | L4 proposes a per-hour budget spent by the arbiter. A budget without a meter is a guess wearing a number. The AGI manifest already names cost/latency and model-version stamps as a Phase A schema gap. Measure first (Doctrine 2). |
| L4-0, the instrument (one row, no policy) | ONE terminal `inference_call` decision event per LOGICAL request at the OUTER shared inference-request seam — spanning gate through completion, plain and streaming paths alike (Codex: the post-success serving-link seam loses refusals and failures). Fields: `callsite` (the static `&'static str` the code already passes — never a prompt, never user data); `scope`; the SELECTED route label plus optional `served_by` (the link that answered); `outcome` ∈ refused (zero backend attempts) / failed (accepted, no backend served) / served (a response); `provider_attempt_count` (exact: failover and retry turn one logical request into several outbound attempts — a chain that fails one link then serves another is ONE served row with attempts > 1); `latency_ms`; `model` label as the backend names it; `process_start_ms` (explicit process identity, so the process-lifetime oracle is selectable without timestamp inference); the loop `cycle_id` / opportunity trace when the call runs inside a loop wake, shared with the loop tick's trace id when available — absent otherwise, NEVER timestamp-joined. Evaluator id `inference-ledger-v1`. Recording binds to the engine/pool's actual recorder, not another process-wide first-install observer. |
| Tokens — the provenance wall (Codex, pre-code) | `LLMResponse` token fields carry no provenance today: zero conflates "unavailable", and the Claude CLI backend ESTIMATES completion tokens. L4-0 writes tokens as ABSENT until a typed provenance says provider-reported; availability is never inferred from a nonzero value; an estimate never lands on the ledger. |
| Read side | `ym why spend [window]` — logical requests, attempts, wall (and tokens where present) per callsite per hour, and per loop id through the on-row cycle id; a STATIC callsite→loop table may CLASSIFY an otherwise unattributed row but never invents cycle identity; `unattributed` is counted, never guessed. Treasury passes stay in `ym budget` (linked, not a fourth spend unit). |
| What it is not | No budget, no gate, no refusal, no change to any dispatch. Instrumentation only; a refused or failed request still writes its row (exposure, E.OBS1c's split). |
| Gate | On a box that makes model calls (staging's DMN and resolve do): every logical household request has exactly one row; the oracle the ledger did not write — over one process lifetime, `served + failed` household rows == the household callsite counters (which count authorized household dispatches only), and refusals match their own counter or subset; `ym why spend 1h` names the loops in descending requests with `unattributed` shown. Fixture: a scripted backend under a fake clock — served, refused, failed each write one row with the right outcome and attempt count; a fail-then-serve chain writes one served row with attempts 2; no tokens when the backend reports none; a streaming path writes exactly one terminal row. |
| Kill | A row carrying prompt text or a user datum; a callsite derived from anything but a static string; a token count without provider provenance; a row missing for a refused or failed request; two rows for one logical request; a cycle id inferred from timestamps. |
| Then L4 proper | Only after 24 h of `inference_call` rows on staging: the budget prereg names its numbers from the measured series, not from guesses. |

## L4-0 — correction: a fourth partial instrument exists (docs-only; found reading the seam before any code)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Correction | The finding row counted three partial spend instruments. There is a fourth: the provider CHAIN writes `provider_usage.json` (`YM_STATE_DIR`, best-effort, 14-day window) — per LOCAL DAY, per PROVIDER LINK: served, failed, tokens in, tokens out — from `provider_record_usage` on every link outcome. It is the closest thing to a meter the mind has. |
| Why it still is not the meter | Chain-only: a pool built on a single backend never writes it. Per provider, never per callsite or per loop. Per local day, never per hour. Its token fields inherit the provenance wall (an estimating backend's numbers land beside a provider's, indistinguishable). It records link ATTEMPTS, not logical requests — one request that fails a link and serves on the next writes two entries, which is exactly the attempt/request split L4-0 keys on. `ym why resources` reads `model_calls` off decision rows and therefore reads nothing today. |
| Consequence for L4-0 | The oracle gains a second leg where a chain is configured: over one process lifetime, the sum of L4-0 `provider_attempt_count` across served and failed rows must equal the chain's served + failed link entries for the same day range (the rollup the ledger did not write). Where no chain is configured the first leg (household callsite counters) stands alone. The read side must not import `provider_usage.json`'s tokens. |

## L4-0 — implemented: the spend ledger (inference-ledger-v1) — one terminal row per logical inference request; tokens absent; no budget (commit ca90205; Codex independent review PASS 13:52Z after one amendment round; not yet deployed)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Seam | The outer shared request seam in the pool, plain and streaming alike: a gate refusal writes `refused` with zero attempts (route = the label the gate would have selected); after the blocking call, `served` (served_by per E.OBS1c: the chain's note, else the non-chain label) or `failed` (served_by absent). Exactly one terminal row per logical request. The pool records into a bound `InferenceLedger` — the engine's own recorder, bound at `with_recorder`, shared by every clone, every role pool derived from the default and the named critic pool — never a process-wide observer. |
| Attempts (observable boundary, stated) | A per-request counter installed on the blocking thread and held by the awaiting side, so a backend panic loses the thread but not the count: each provider-chain link invocation (survival tier included) is one attempt; a leaf backend's invocation is counted BEFORE the call (chain-ness read off the backend object, never a label), so a panic inside it is still one attempt. A panic on the blocking thread is a `failed` row with the attempts made — never a missing row. Transport-internal retries a backend hides are NOT counted; the number is invocations the pool can see, never a claim about outbound HTTP attempts. A transient error retried by the pool then served is ONE served row with attempts 2. |
| Tokens — the provenance wall | `TokenUsage {prompt, completion, provenance: ProviderReported}` is the contract; nothing constructs it today (no backend reports counts with provenance; the Claude CLI estimates). Every row carries tokens ABSENT; the reader refuses a v1 row that claims any. `model` deliberately absent: a route or provider is never relabelled as a model. |
| Identity on the row | `process:<start ms>` — the PINNED process start, one identity for every engine and every bind in a process; and the loop opportunity id, carried by a task-local the loop host sets around the act (`within_opportunity`; the process runner wraps dmn, resolve, profile-refresh and patterns with their own `LoopOpportunity::Window` id). Never timestamp-joined. The static callsite table classifies an otherwise unattributed row (today only `:forge-*` → forge); it never invents identity; `unattributed` is counted. |
| Row shape | kind `inference_call`; actor `spend`; trigger `callsite:<static string>` (the 160-char field — the 32-char actor would truncate a module path, and the reader refuses a truncated callsite); lane; model_route = route; chosen = served_by (served only); verdict = outcome; outcome `attempts:<n>`; subject `plain` | `stream`; goal_id `process:<ms>`; object_id = opportunity id; evaluator_id `inference-ledger-v1`. The wall is closed: a row whose trace is not `inference`, whose event id is not `inference-call:<its own process start>:<seq>`, or that carries ANY free-text or grading field the schema does not own (purpose, context fingerprint, goal, predicted, confidence, error, brier, semantic success, tool version, lesson, parent, evidence, candidates, rejected, policy) is refused. Other versions supersede, never read. |
| Read side | `ym why spend` (24 h) and `ym why spend 1h`: per (callsite, loop) rows — requests, served, failed, refused, attempts, wall, streaming — with attribution `opportunity` / `callsite` / `unattributed`; requests and attempts per loop; requests per hour; "Tokens: absent" on every render. Treasury passes stay in `ym budget`. |
| Fixtures | mind-observability (2): strict parse with one refusal per wrong shape (refused with attempts; served or failed without one; served_by on a failure; unknown lane; a token claim; an unparsable opportunity; an empty or truncated callsite; a wrong actor; another version superseded) and the attribution order with totals. mind-conversation `l4_0_tests` (9): one row per path (served, streaming, refused) sharing one process id; attempts (transient-then-serve = one served row, attempts 2; non-transient = failed, attempts 1; three transients = failed, attempts 3); a private-grounded escalation = a refused PRIVATE row and a served HOUSEHOLD row, two intentional logical requests; the opportunity by identity and the reducer's per-loop totals; the oracle the ledger did not write — served + failed household rows for one module-path callsite equal that callsite's household dispatch counter delta over the test; role pools share the ledger and `why spend` renders from the verified log; a backend panic is one failed row with its attempt on both paths; two engines in one process stamp one pinned process start; the named critic joins the house ledger (source-asserted). Two foresight fixtures now expect the log to hold their two trace rows PLUS the grading call's spend rows (asserted ≥ 1). |
| Not a fixture, stated | The provider_usage.json oracle leg is a witness-side before/after DELTA over one process lifetime within one local day; staging has no chain and no such file, so that leg cannot run there. |
| Review round | Round 1 (13:42Z) four blockers: the sink stamped now() at bind instead of the pinned process start; the named critic pool built its own pool outside the ledger family; the reader let free-text fields ride a row; a JoinError returned without a failed row. All closed with fixtures. Codex independently ran the four suites and git diff --check. |

## E.CB2-F — preregistration: the page path gets one critic + repair round (the fix E.CB2's Qwen reading called for)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The observation this answers | E.CB2 leg 1: the Mind's page chain spent 31 s and two model calls, handed `publish_page` 968 characters with no `<html>`/`<body>`, and the tool refused. The refusal is right — publishing a fragment is the worse outcome — but the chain then had nothing left to try. The page recipe's own comment already names this signature: a document step that comes back as ~900 characters of non-document. |
| Prior (stated before the change) | The draft step fails this way on a mid-size local model often enough to matter, and a single repair round, given the specific defect and the draft, recovers most of those attempts. If the prior is wrong, the repair round changes nothing and costs one model call on failing runs only. |
| Change | In `page_recipe` (delegate.rs), between the author step and the publish step: (1) a `JumpIf` on a new deterministic condition `VarIsHtmlDocument` that skips the repair when the draft already is a complete document; (2) a repair `Think` step, same document budget, that receives the draft and the exact defect (not a document / truncated / both) and returns one complete document. Publish and notify are unchanged, and `publish_page` keeps its refusals — the repair round never weakens a check, it only spends one more call before giving up. |
| New primitive | `Condition::VarIsHtmlDocument { var }` in mind-recipes: a pure predicate (starts as a document, ends `</html>`), unit-tested against a fragment, a truncated document, prose that merely mentions `</html>`, and a real page. |
| Cost | At most one extra model call, and only on a run that would otherwise have failed. A run whose draft is already a document is byte-identical to today's. Within the E.CB2 per-leg cap of eight. |
| Measurement | Re-run the same three briefs on the same harness under the same profile, before and after, and put the mechanical table beside the E.CB2 rows. The claim under test is narrow: whether the page leg produces a document at all. Quality remains the viewer's call, unchanged. |
| Kill | The repair step publishing anything `publish_page` would have refused; more than one repair round; a check softened anywhere; the recipe silently succeeding with no URL. |
| Order | This row → the code with its tests → Codex review → staging deploy → the re-run, on whichever profile the reading uses. |

## E.CB2-F — implemented (e22894e, review fixes 6d633d4); E.CB2-N harness second review folded in (de98f1f)

| E.CB2-F code | `Condition::VarIsPublishableDocument` in mind-recipes plus a repair `Think` step in `page_recipe`. The guard is not a predicate of its own: the four publish-path helpers moved into mind-recipes and the conversation crate re-exports them. (Amended after review: at first the tool still repeated the component checks rather than calling the shared predicate, and the opening test accepted any text containing `<html` — so `<htmlish>not a document</html>` would have been published. The tool now calls `is_publishable_document` and reports which half failed only to choose its error message, and the opening test is tag-boundary aware. This makes `publish_page` refuse non-document markup it used to accept: on the page path that draft now gets the repair round instead of becoming a live page.) Codex's review caught the first version being STRICTER than the tool — a fenced document, a preamble, or a page ending `</body>` would have paid for a repair they did not need; all three are now regression tests. The repair prompt also lost the mounted pack rules in the first version and now carries them. |
| Tests | mind-recipes: the predicate against seven cases. mind-conversation: four shape tests plus three that run the branch through the real RecipeEngine — a publishable draft costs one model call and publishes verbatim, a prose draft costs exactly one repair and publishes the repair, two bad drafts publish nothing and the run reports failure. Suites: 95 and 709 green. |

Cap evidence (a refusal, or accepted over cap) is independent too. The Mind driver reports its own reasons split, and the parent promotes only the independent ones, so a transport outage ending at the wall is a void and not also a disqualification. A rerun needs a PURE void. The key's uid and mode are checked before any DNS resolution. A proxy that cannot start writes a pre-invocation void. The egress policy moved into a dedicated `CB2-EGRESS` chain, flushed and rebuilt each run, jumped to from DOCKER-USER position 1 and audited rule for rule. |

| The bug | The stray-rule audit was emitted as `grep -c -- '172\.30\.'` — two backslashes inside single quotes, so grep matched nothing and the check could never fail. ## E.AGI-I1 — preregistration: the two directions E.AGI-I0 could not measure, and the baseline it lacked
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What I.0 left open | I.0 measured one direction (16/152 rows, ~10.5% post-green peer catches, all Codex catching me) and named its own two gaps: the reverse direction returned zero grep hits because the ledger is written by one of the two agents, and there is no baseline for what the same author would have caught alone. Codex's independent sweep of the reverse direction returned REFUSED-INSUFFICIENT-RECORD. |
| The idea | The missing baseline is not a counterfactual solo run, which nobody can stage honestly here. It is the SELF-CATCH: a defect an author finds in their own artifact after declaring it ready but before the peer names it. Self-catches and peer catches are both post-green and both recorded, and their ratio is what "what does the peer add" actually means in this arrangement. |
| Counting rule (fixed before any counting) | An event is in scope when an artifact was declared ready — committed and pushed, or sent to the peer for review — and a defect in it was then named. Classify each by FINDER: `peer` (the other agent named it first), `self` (the author named it first, in a message or a commit message, before the peer's report arrived), `both` (independently, within one exchange). Classify each by CONSEQUENCE, defined before counting: **A** would have produced a wrong measurement, a false claim, or a silent non-check; **B** would have wasted resources only; **C** wording, docs, or naming. A defect found before the artifact was declared ready is OUT of scope, in both columns. |
| Corpus | This session on 2026-09-02 from 15:00Z, both directions: the ledger rows added, the commits on main, and each agent's own message record. Each agent counts its OWN record independently against this rule; the two counts are published side by side without reconciliation, and disagreement is data rather than an error to fix. |
| Prediction (pre-registered, before I count) | My own count will show peer catches outnumbering my self-catches on the harness work, because that is where I am both the author and the only reviewer of my own shell and escaping code. I expect at least one A-class defect in each direction. If my self-catches come out at zero, that is the most important number in the row: it would mean my declaring something ready carries no independent signal at all. |
| Kill criteria | REFUSED-INSUFFICIENT-RECORD if either agent cannot classify finder and consequence for at least 90% of its in-scope events. No lift claim, and no rate comparison against I.0's 10.5% (different corpus, different unit). A defect fixed silently and never recorded is uncountable by construction, and the row must say so rather than assume none exist. |
| AGI feed | Phase I gets its reverse direction and its first self-catch baseline, from persisted evidence, in a form that states plainly what it cannot see. |

## E.AGI-I1 — amendment, agreed with Codex before any counting (their six points, 19:08Z, adopted verbatim in substance)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Corpus cutoff | THIS COMMIT. The corpus is every in-scope event whose first persisted naming lands at or before the commit that adds this row; anything after is out of scope for both halves. "From 15:00Z" without an end was moving while we worked. |

| 3. Consequence | Highest applicable class only, A > B > C, so the classes are exclusive. |
| 4. `both` | Kept, but only when persisted timestamps show each side named the same root defect before receiving or observing the other's report. Otherwise the first persisted naming wins. "Within one exchange" alone was too loose. |
| 5. Same-message disclosures | If a defective commit was already pushed or declared reviewable before the message, naming its defect later is SELF. If the first readiness declaration and the disclosure are atomic in one message with no earlier ready or pushed evidence, the event is OUT OF SCOPE — it was never represented as clean. A later corrective commit naming a defect in an earlier ready commit is SELF. |
| 6. Halves are author-centric | Each agent classifies defects in artifacts IT authored and declared ready — its own self-catches AND the peer's catches on its work — from its own persisted record. Denominators and unclassifiable counts are published independently, with no reconciliation. This removes the finder-centric reading of "own record" and makes the two halves disjoint by construction. |
| Consequence of 6, stated in advance | Today's corpus is lopsided: I authored nearly everything and Codex reviewed it, so my half will be large and theirs small. That asymmetry is a fact about how this session was organised, not a quality signal about either agent, and the row must not be read as one. |

## E.CFG1 — preregistration: a role can name a model its provider does not serve, and nothing says so until a call fails
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The finding that earns this (verified live, 19:20Z) | `Router::from_env` validates a role spec by asking two questions: is the provider in the catalogue, and is its key present. It never asks whether the MODEL exists. A role set to `nim:z-ai/glm-5.2` therefore builds a pool that looks configured, reports itself as configured, and fails only when something calls it. Staging's own `YM_ROLE_RESEARCH` is in exactly that state today, and the same mistake cost E.CB2-N a preflight round: the provider answered 410 Gone eight times for a model that is not in its catalogue of 82. |
| Why it matters beyond a typo | The router's whole purpose is that a function can be pointed at a different brain. A spec that silently resolves to nothing inverts that: the operator believes a role is served by the model they named, the calls fall back or fail, and the evidence names neither the role nor the spec. Every claim about which model did what is unsound while this is possible. |
| Prior (before code) | Both halves of the diagnosis will be true on the current build: the six role variables plus `YM_PRIMARY_BRAIN` are readable and classifiable without a network call, and at least one of the roles configured on the staging box names a model its provider does not serve. |
| Change | A read-only diagnostic, no behaviour change to routing. (1) `provider_catalog(provider)` becomes a public accessor over the one table `backend_from_spec` already uses, so nothing gets a second copy. (2) `role_plan(lookup)` returns, per configured role, the variable, the spec, the provider, the model, and a status that distinguishes UNKNOWN PROVIDER from MISSING KEY — two different fixes the current message conflates. (3) `verify_models(plan, fetch)` takes the catalogue fetcher as a parameter and classifies each spec SERVED, NOT SERVED with the catalogue size, or UNREACHABLE with the reason. (4) `ym why roles` renders the plan and states in its own output that the model half is unverified; `ym why roles verify` performs the live catalogue check against the SAME effective base URL the mind would call, override included. |
| Kill / not claimed | No change to how a call is routed, no startup network call, no automatic correction of anybody's configuration. If the catalogue endpoint is unreachable the diagnostic says UNREACHABLE and never guesses SERVED. A provider that does not expose a catalogue is reported as such rather than as a failure of the role. |
| Measurement | The unit tests carry injected fetchers, so the logic is proven without a network. The live reading is one run of `ym why roles verify` on the staging box, reported as counts and statuses per role — and it must independently reproduce the finding above, naming the research role, or the prior is wrong and the row says so. |
| AGI feed | Phase A: an instrument that makes a configured-but-unserved route visible is a precondition for any claim of the form "model X did Y", which the spend ledger and the route coverage reports both make today. |

## E.PORT1 — preregistration: the mind sends a non-standard field that strict OpenAI-compatible providers reject
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The chain, traced end to end | A recipe step or a role policy asks for thinking OFF (`think: Some(false)` — the page recipe sets exactly this, for good reasons measured earlier). `GenericOpenAIBackend` then adds BOTH `think:false` and `reasoning_effort:"none"` to the request body, for every provider, because on Ollama's OpenAI-compat endpoint `think` is ignored and `reasoning_effort:"none"` is the only thing that suppresses the preamble. `"none"` is not in the OpenAI enum. A provider that validates it answers 400 to every call. Measured: five one-request probes isolate the field, and the provider's text names the three values it accepts. |
| Why this could not have been found here | The gateway on owned hardware accepts the field. Every test the mind has ever run against its own endpoint passes. It took pointing the same binary at a second provider to see it, which is the argument for E.CB2-N existing at all. |
| Constraint that shapes the fix | `yantrik-ml` is a different repository and not mine to edit. The fix must live in this one. |
| Change | A thin adapter in mind-inference around the backends built by `backend_from_spec`: when a per-call config asks for thinking OFF, the adapter passes `None` instead to providers on the strict path, so the backend emits neither `think` nor `reasoning_effort`. The LOCAL Ollama lane is built elsewhere (`local_backend_from_env`, provider preset "ollama") and is deliberately untouched — its behaviour, including the measured 10 s → 0.9 s improvement, is preserved exactly. |
| The trade-off, stated rather than hidden | On a strict provider the mind loses the ability to suppress a reasoning preamble, so those calls may be slower and spend budget on reasoning tokens. That is the honest price of speaking the documented protocol; the alternative is a 400 on every call. If a provider later documents its own suppression field, that belongs in a new row, not in this one. |
| Prior | Every call the mind makes to a strict OpenAI-compatible provider fails today with a 400 naming `reasoning_effort`, and after the change the same call succeeds against the same provider with the same model. |
| Tests | Pure: a config asking for thinking OFF is rewritten to unset on the strict path and left alone on the local lane; the adapter forwards everything else untouched (messages, tools, streaming, token counts, backend name). Live: one call through the contained proxy to the same provider and model that returned 400, which must now return 200 — the direct negation of the measured failure. |
| Not claimed | Nothing about quality, speed or cost on any provider. Nothing about Finding B below, which is a separate row because I do not yet know where it hangs. |
| Kill | Any change to the local Ollama lane's request body. Any provider-specific special case beyond "strict path or local lane". A test that asserts the fix by mocking the provider instead of calling it. |

The job never reported failure, the driver saw no terminal state, and the raw log's last line is the privacy escalation notice — no error, no chain failure, no retry. Only the proxy's client-error counter recorded that anything went wrong. |
| Why it is a separate row | The page chain's author step is configured `on_error: Fail`, so a failing call should have ended the run with an error the delegate reports. It did not, and I cannot yet say whether the call blocked, the error was swallowed between the pool and the recipe, or the job status never propagated. Guessing in a fix is how a silent failure becomes a silent wrong answer. |
| Next step, before any code | One instrumented run against a provider that reliably rejects the request, with the failure path traced from the backend through the pool and the recipe to the job status. Whatever it finds is preregistered as its own change. |
| Standing | E.PORT1 does not close this. A mind that cannot report its own failed call is a worse problem than one that sends a wrong field. |

## E.PORT1-B — preregistration: a delegation must exist on the board before it asks a model anything (Codex diagnosed the mechanism from source, 20:30Z; their acceptance criteria adopted)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The mechanism, now known | `delegate_cmd` awaits `route(task)` BEFORE it mints a job id or writes the ledger row. `route` calls `chat_grounded` with no deadline, and that call runs inside a blocking chain that can traverse multiple long provider attempts. When the provider rejected every request, the routing call never returned, so no row was ever written: the console answered the submission, `ym jobs` and `/api/tasks` listed nothing, and the driver polled a job that did not exist until the 1800 s wall. The delegation was invisible because it had not been born yet. |
| Why the existing error path did not save it | `route` already falls back to a deterministic classifier on `Err`. That handles a call that FAILS. It does nothing for a call that never returns, which is the case that actually happened. |
| Change (Codex's option A, taken deliberately) | **Ledger before routing.** The job id and its row are created from the deterministic floor classification, with the executor-presence check applied to that floor, before any model call. Routing then runs under a bounded deadline and may only REFINE the row's kind; if it exceeds the budget or fails, the floor stands and the job proceeds. |
| The dropped-timeout hazard, named rather than waved at | A timed-out blocking HTTP attempt cannot be cancelled from here — it will finish in its own time. It must therefore not be invisible: the timeout writes an operator-visible line saying routing exceeded its budget and that the model request may still be in flight, and the spend ledger still receives that request's terminal row when it completes, so the attempt is accounted for even though nothing waits on it. |
| Acceptance (Codex's words, adopted as the test list) | Bounded acknowledgement: a delegation submitted while the model blocks forever is acknowledged within the budget rather than never. Truthful job state: the board shows the job, with a kind the floor actually supports, and never claims a state that has not happened. No hidden work: a request abandoned by the timeout is reported, not silently orphaned. |
| Tests | A backend that blocks indefinitely, driven through the real engine: the delegation is acknowledged within the deadline; a ledger row exists for it immediately with the floor kind; the timeout notice is emitted. Plus the bounded-routing helper on its own, with a future that never completes, asserting the floor is returned within the budget and the notice fires exactly once. |
| Not claimed, and the limit of this fix | This does not make a blocked provider call cancellable, and it does not fix the page chain's own behaviour under a failing model — that is E.PORT1's territory. It makes the delegation's EXISTENCE independent of whether a model answers. |
| Kill | A row written for a kind no executor supports (the lie this code already refuses to tell). A budget so long that the acknowledgement is not bounded in practice. Any change that lets routing's result overwrite a row's identity rather than refine its kind. |

## ARRANGEMENT — the review substrate changes: Codex is near its usage limit until 2026-09-06, so a subagent takes the review seat (recorded BEFORE any evidence is produced under it)

You can assign a sonnet or opus subagent to review/assess which codex was doing for the time being." From here until Codex returns, the second pair of eyes is a subagent I spawn, not the peer agent. |
| Why this must be on the ledger rather than done quietly | E.AGI-I1 measured this arrangement's value earlier today: in the classifiable window, 33 defects in my work were found by Codex and 2 by me — my own review caught about 6% of what was wrong with what I had already declared ready. Every "reviewed" claim in this ledger has meant reviewed by an agent with its own context, its own reading of the source, and its own box access. A subagent is not that, and evidence produced under the new arrangement must not be read as if it were. |
| What a subagent reviewer IS | A genuinely independent read: a fresh context that has not watched me build the thing, instructed to look for the specific failure classes today's record shows I produce — a check that cannot fail, a claim that does not match its implementation, a number that measures something other than what it says, an escaping error in generated shell, a test that passes for the wrong reason. It can read the whole repository, run the suites, and refuse. |
| What it is NOT, stated plainly | It shares my model family and my blind spots. It has no independent access to the staging box and cannot reproduce a live receipt. It keeps no record between reviews, so it cannot notice a pattern across days the way a peer with continuity does. It is not a second party in the governance sense: it cannot hold me to a gate I choose not to give it. |
| The rule I am binding myself to | Every artifact reviewed by a subagent is labelled `subagent-reviewed` in its ledger row, never `peer-reviewed`. Anything that would change staging behaviour, spend money, or produce a graded measurement waits for either Codex's return or Pranab's explicit word — a subagent's approval is not a substitute for the gates Codex has been holding. Findings from a subagent are recorded with the same attribution convention as Codex's, so the next E.AGI-I1 sweep can separate the two substrates rather than averaging them. |
| Prediction, registered now | A subagent reviewer will find fewer of my defects than Codex did, and will systematically miss the class Codex is best at: a claim in a comment or a preregistration that the code does not actually implement. If the next sweep shows otherwise I will say so. |

## FINDING — RESOLVED: the L3c flake was the TEST asserting a property the code never promised (diagnosed by review; fixed in 4754b6a)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The mechanism | Two tasks — a resolver invoked by a user turn, and a fresh engagement commit — take the same lock, so they serialise, but the ORDER is the scheduler's. Resolve first: the stale beat grades, the list empties, the commit lands, and the new ref is pending. Commit first: the new ref is pending when the resolver runs, and a user turn answers every beat whose window still contains it — a beat committed microseconds earlier is inside its window, so it grades immediately. Both are correct. The test asserted one of them. |
| Why it is a finding and not a nuisance | A test that fails one run in four teaches the reader to re-run rather than look. This one guards a real property — a resolver must not erase a fresh commit — and it was failing for a reason that had nothing to do with that property, which is exactly how a genuine race would have been dismissed. |
| The fix | It now asserts what the code actually guarantees: the fresh commit is never lost — it is either still pending or already graded — and across the test it is graded exactly once with the right outcome. Six consecutive runs of the test and four consecutive full-suite runs are green. |
| My own error inside the fix, recorded | The first attempt asserted that a row existing meant the beat was graded. The claim row exists from the moment of commit with a null outcome, so that version failed every run instead of one in four. Conflating "a record exists" with "the thing it records happened" is the same mistake as counting a string that measures something else. |
| Reviewer's caveat, kept | The reviewer could not reproduce the flake in 331 executions on their machine and said so plainly; the diagnosis is from source, and the interleaving is genuinely unconstrained, so a different machine flipping it is consistent with the reading. I reproduced it here four times in the same session, which is the other half of the evidence. |

| Why they are written down rather than remembered | Review 4 found five defects that reached only a commit message, and the correction row for that is three rows above this one. A queue item that exists only in my head is the same failure with fewer witnesses. |

## Review 5 — ten findings, and the two worst were inside my own verification fixes
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Standing | CLOSED. All ten fixed; the workspace suite is green (719 mind-conversation, 44 mind-observability, 73 mind-inference, zero failures workspace-wide) and the cb2n tree still re-derives byte-exactly from the frozen cb2 tree plus `scratch/cb2n_patch.py`. |
| The headline | Two of the ten were checks I had just added, in the two commits that were supposed to prove the previous round's fixes. Both were green. Neither could fail. Everything else in this row is less important than that sentence. |
| Finding 1 — a guard blind to the line it excepted | `every_spawn_in_the_delegation_path_carries_its_opportunity` matched lines STARTING with `tokio::spawn(`. The one spawn its own comment names as the exception is written `let handle = tokio::spawn(...)`, so the exception was dead code, the anti-vacuity count was computed the same blind way and reported five while a sixth sat unexamined, and stripping the carry from that spawn left the test green. Now: `contains` anywhere in the line, an exact expected count of six, the exception identified by body content. Proven by stripping that carry and watching the guard name the line. |
| Finding 2 — an immutability check reached through a door that is always shut | `two_concurrent_commits_of_one_ref_write_one_row_and_a_resolver_cannot_erase_a_commit` observed "graded exactly once" after the pending list had emptied. `resolve_proactive` returns at its first line on an empty list, so `judgment_grade` was never re-entered and `outcome_at` could not move for ANY reason, including a deleted immutability guard. |
| What it took to actually fix finding 2 | Three wrong attempts, each of which I believed was right and each of which passed. (a) Re-arm with a bare string: `PendingSend::from_value` accepts a bare i64 or a full object, so a string deserialises as neither and the resolver skipped it. (b) Millisecond timestamps in a test fast enough that two writes land in the same millisecond. (c) A mutation that disabled only half the guard — the outcome half — while the `resolution` half still refused. I found it by instrumenting `judgment_grade` and watching the ref get graded twice, which is what I should have done at the first failure instead of the third. The test now fails when the whole guard is removed and passes when it is restored. |
| Finding 3 | A comment asserting it was "the ONLY place in this file that should mention" the retracted 10 s → 0.9 s measurement, while the figure appeared in two other comments. A claim about the file's contents that had stopped being true of the file. All three are scoped now; none is privileged. |
| Finding 4 — the benchmark was not holding both systems to the same rule | `MANIFEST.json` has always promised, for BOTH systems, that the proxy's accepted count must equal the calls in the agent's own log. Only the Hermes leg implemented it. The Mind's spend ledger went into the receipt and was compared to nothing. The Hermes receipt also demands `1 <= accepted`; the Mind's accepted zero, so a Mind leg that never reached the model could pass a check its opponent could not. |
| Finding 5 | `routed_kind` is in the receipt schema and was absent on the three exit paths that abort before the driver runs (proxy not ready, brain gate failed, driver failed), so a reader indexing the field crashed on exactly the legs whose failure it wanted to read. Present, as null, on every path now. |
| Findings 6–10 | A two-executor test asserting `!= "code"` where the box's answer should be `== "page"` (it passes for "research" too, which is the wrong executor silently chosen); `LOOP_LEDGER_VERSION`'s doc comment orphaned by the v6 insertion and landing on V4, which then carried two eras' documentation and none of its own; `LOOP_LEDGER_V6` documented in the present tense for a writer that does not exist yet; a test asserting a constant equals the literal it is defined as; two residues in `parse_route` (a redundant table lookup guarded by a `?` that could never fire, and an over-general claim that scan order cannot affect the answer — it can, on a tie); and a ten-space run inside an operator-facing failure message. |
| The queued harness defects, now closed | `"proxy_client_disconnects": -1` was a placeholder in the shape of a measurement; the proxy counts disconnects and the receipt now reports what it counted. `spend_rows()` returned `(0, 0, 0)` for a MISSING log, making "the mind cannot account for itself" indistinguishable from "the mind made no calls"; it returns -1 and a missing log is an independent violation, the analogue of Hermes's invalid log. |
| The structural fix, not just the ten | The three receipt defects all lived inside the driver's receipt literal — a rule that decides who wins the benchmark and that no test could reach without running a whole graded leg. It is now `run/verdict.py`, a pure function; the driver imports it, which is what makes the cases a test of the shipped rule and not of a copy; and `selftest/verdict_cases.py` drives it through ten classifications, clean case first. Each of the three new rules was verified by breaking it and watching a named case fail. |
| Where the agreement check could bite | `ledger_attempts`, not `ledger_requests`, is compared to `proxy_accepted`: one attempt is one HTTP request while one `inference_call` row may carry several. If the Mind makes any provider call that does not produce a spend row, this check will fire on the next graded reading. It is DEPENDENT, exactly as on the Hermes side, and the receipt carries `accounting_agrees` beside both numbers — so a disagreement arrives diagnosable rather than mysterious. If it fires, that is a finding about the Mind's self-accounting and will be reported as one. |
| Five rounds, forty-nine findings | Every one real. Five of five rounds found a defect inside a fix for the previous round's finding. My own review of my own work has caught two of the forty-nine. The lesson I am willing to state as a rule: a test I write to prove a fix is not evidence until I have watched it fail. |

## The benchmark no longer requires a production deploy to test a code change
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What was wrong | `mind_leg.sh` mounted `/opt/yantrik-mind/mind-core` — the binary the live companion runs. Testing a code change in the benchmark therefore MEANT replacing production's binary, so a graded reading and a prod deploy were the same act with different authorities. I noticed while about to do exactly that on the wrong box. |
| The fix | `CB2_MIND_BINARY` (default: that same path, so a reading meaning to test the deployed binary still does) and `CB2_MIND_SOURCE` for provenance, which is marked `+dirty` when the named checkout has uncommitted changes. `smoke_mind.sh` takes the same parameter, because a preflight that boots a different file than the leg it clears is not a preflight. |
| Why it is a validity fix and not a convenience | `binary_provenance` used to be read from a deploy clone whose HEAD had no necessary relationship to the binary in `/opt` — on the box I checked, the clone sat 40-odd commits behind the file it had supposedly produced. A receipt that names the wrong commit is worse than one that names none. |

## E.CB2-N — a structural asymmetry in the comparison, recorded BEFORE the Hermes leg finished
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Timing, stated first | Written while the graded Hermes T1 leg was still running. I do not know its score. This is recorded now precisely so it cannot be read later as an excuse assembled after seeing a loss. |
| The finding | Hermes is invoked with `-t file,terminal,code_execution` — it can write files, run a shell and execute code. The Mind runs in containment with NO coder at all, so its available executors are `page` and `research` only. The comparison is not "two systems building the same thing"; it is Hermes-with-tools against the Mind's page recipe. |
| Why the coder is absent, mechanically | `mind-core` builds the coder only when a MiniMax key, a Qwen key or a Claude OAuth token is present, and each of those talks to a HARD-CODED external base URL (`api.minimax.io/anthropic`, the Aliyun token-plan host, Anthropic). Containment forbids every cloud key and routes all egress through the run proxy, which forwards to one OpenAI-compatible upstream. So the coder cannot be configured into the contained box even in principle: no key, and no route it can speak. `self.coder.is_some()` is false, and the classifier's floor is constrained to what exists. |
| What this does to the T1 result | T1 asks for a lead-capture form that appends a record, a dashboard with exact aggregates over fourteen day-bins, and a runnable server (`run_sh_present`). Those are code deliverables. The Mind produced one static HTML page and scored 2/11 — a truthful measurement of the page recipe under containment, and NOT a measurement of what the system builds when its builder is present. |
| What the reading IS still evidence for | Everything it was designed to measure and does measure: containment, cost per task at the same meter, model identity, the accounting agreement, artifact safety, and how the two systems compare WHEN THE MIND HAS ONLY THE PAGE RECIPE. It is a real number about a real configuration. It is not a capability ceiling. |
| The honest headline, whatever the Hermes score turns out to be | On this benchmark we are comparing our page recipe against a full coding agent. Any claim of the form "the Mind scores X and Hermes scores Y at building software" is unsupported by this reading and I will not make it. |
| The fix this implies, not attempted now | The coder speaks the Anthropic protocol against a fixed per-provider base URL. To be testable under containment at all it needs (a) a configurable base URL and (b) an OpenAI-compatible path, or the harness needs a second contained upstream speaking Anthropic. That is a product slice with its own prereg, not an edit to make mid-reading. |
| Why I did not stop the reading | The reading is preregistered, the preflight cleared, and a measured number about a real configuration is worth more than no number. Stopping to re-scope after seeing a bad first leg is how a benchmark becomes a negotiation. |

## E.CODER1 — a coder that can be pointed anywhere (PREREGISTERED, before the code)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The finding that prompted it | Recorded above: the Mind's coder cannot exist in the contained benchmark box. Reading the module showed WHY is narrower than I assumed. `mind_tools::Coder` does not speak HTTP at all — it shells out to the `claude` CLI with `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` and `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`. The base URL is already a constructor argument. The hard-coding is in `mind-core`'s construction, which recognises exactly three providers and pins each one's host in source. |
| The claim | An operator can point the coder at any Anthropic-protocol endpoint with environment variables alone, and doing nothing keeps today's behaviour byte-for-byte. |
| The change | `YM_CODER_PROVIDER=custom` plus `YM_CODER_BASE_URL`, `YM_CODER_KEY_ENV` (the NAME of the variable holding the key, so the key itself never has to be named in source or in a shipped config) and the existing `YM_CODER_MODEL`. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) If any of the three existing provider paths changes behaviour when the new variables are unset, the slice is wrong and is reverted. (2) If `custom` can be selected without a base URL or without a resolvable key and still constructs a coder, it is wrong — a coder pointed nowhere is worse than no coder, because the delegation gets accepted and then fails. (3) If the key can be read from a variable the operator did not name, it is wrong. |
| What this does NOT fix, stated now so the row cannot be read as more than it is | It does not make the contained benchmark fair. Two blockers remain and are not addressed here: the contained upstream speaks the OpenAI protocol and the CLI needs the Anthropic one, and the `claude` CLI is not installed in the `cb2-mind` image. This slice removes the first of three obstacles, and the row for reading 3 must keep saying the comparison is uneven until all three are gone. |
| What I am deliberately NOT doing | Not touching `classify`. A brief that says "dashboard" routes to the page recipe by a keyword rule, which is very likely a real product deficiency — but I have just read the checker's verdict on a brief containing that word, and changing the router now would be tuning to a benchmark I am in the middle of running. It gets its own row, its own prereg, and test cases written from general phrasings rather than from the frozen briefs. |

Eight turns cost at least eight requests, so the cap and the turn budget are equal and any retry or extra round is a guaranteed violation. Observed: 11 requests for 7 logged calls, an overhead of roughly 1.6 requests per logged call. |
| The number, chosen and justified BEFORE the run | **24** — three times the larger agent's configured turn limit. Three, not two, because the observed overhead is about 1.6 requests per logged call and a budget that binds at 1.6× would be the same trap one step further out. The cap's job is to stop runaway spend, not to bind normal operation; an agent that needs more than 3× its own turn limit really is running away. |
| What is NOT changed | Hermes keeps `agent.max_turns 8` — that is its frozen configuration and raising it would change what is being measured. The wall stays 1800 s. The briefs, the checker, the containment, the model and the invocation counts are untouched. The Mind is unaffected in practice: it used two requests. |
| How the number is carried | `CB2_CAP` enters the immutable run state beside profile, upstream and model, so all five consumers (the proxy's 429, the Hermes leg, the Mind driver, the Mind leg's receipt check, the manifest's rule) read ONE number. They are currently five independent literals, which is its own latent defect: they can drift apart and nothing would notice. A run state written for one cap refuses a load asking for another, exactly as it already does for the profile. |

| Kill criteria for the harness change | (1) A run state written at one cap must refuse a load at another. (2) With `CB2_CAP` unset, every consumer must still see 8 — the existing profiles must be unchanged in effect.
