## L2-B step 1 — the signal set and the shadow row, deliberately not wired to anything
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Scope of this step | The collection point and the record, as pure functions: `WakeSignals` (one typed slot per in-scope loop), the frozen urgency arithmetic, `attention_shadow` (signals in, at most one row out) and the row's single `DecisionEvent`. NOTHING is wired into the poll loop. Wiring is step 2. |
| Why split it that way | The shadow's one kill criterion is that the `attention_shadow` append is the ONLY write attributable to it. A step that cannot be called from the running mind cannot violate that, so the arithmetic and the record can be reviewed on their own before anything can act on them. |
| How the required-signal list is enforced | Structurally, not by convention. The preregistration freezes, per loop, exactly which signals its descriptor may read — "no signal outside it, every signal in it". Each gate kind is a struct with exactly those fields, so a site cannot fill a slot without having read every required signal, and a descriptor cannot reach one the slot does not carry. |
| `due` is the site's answer and is never recomputed | Each entry carries the gate's own verdict. Several due predicates are bespoke (Dmn, Knock, Digest, Ask) and reimplementing them here would be a second answer to one question. A test drives a Dmn slot whose every input looks overdue while the site says no, and requires the shadow to record nothing. |
| An ambiguity in the preregistration, resolved and recorded rather than papered over | The prereg says a row exists for any wake with ≥ 1 in-scope due opportunity, "due-but-missing included". A due opportunity whose slot was never filled is by definition invisible to the writer, so the writer cannot honour that as written. The implementable rule is: the writer records a row iff ≥ 1 FILLED slot reported due, and the read side, joining `buildable` against the ledger's own due rows for the same `cycle_id`, treats a wake with ledger-due rows and no shadow row as a build shortfall with buildable 0. The metric's meaning is unchanged — build completeness is still buildable ÷ ledger-due — and no wake is silently dropped from a denominator. |
| A dead tie-break in L2-A, found while testing this and not deleted | `attention_rank`'s THIRD tie-break (the longest wait) is unreachable in the shadow's use. Scope index is unique per loop and the shadow emits at most one candidate per loop, so the scope comparison never returns Equal and `last_ms` never decides anything. The preregistration describes it as the final tie-break; it is really a guard for a caller passing the same loop twice, which the shadow never does. Left in place, documented at the test that proves the second tie-break decides, and recorded here. |
| Fourteen tests, four mutations | Removing the no-due-means-no-row rule, the due filter, or the forced-Whois supersession each fails a named test. |
| The fourth mutation caught a vacuous test of mine, again | Deleting the ranking call entirely left the suite green. The ordering test paired HomeWatch with Resolve, and HomeWatch both scores higher AND comes earlier in the frozen scope — the row was already correct before anything sorted it. It now pairs Ask (scope index 3, score ≈ 5.3e11) with HomeWatch (index 5, ≈ 1.85e12), where collection order and score order point opposite ways, and it asserts the collection order first so the disagreement is visible in the test itself. Deleting the ranking now fails it. |
| The count so far | That is the third check I have written this session that could not fail, and the third found by breaking the thing it was supposed to be watching rather than by reading it. Mutation is not a finishing step for this work; it is how I find out whether a test exists. |

## E.CB2-N reading 4 — RESULT: Hermes finished cleanly and my harness disqualified it anyway
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What happened | Mind T1 completed with a byte-identical artifact to reading 3 (same verdict hash `1842cdcd…`, 2/11). Hermes T1 **finished**: rc 0, not timed out, valid log, 424 s, NINE model requests against a cap of twenty-four, zero refusals, zero upstream errors, three files. It was disqualified anyway and the sequence halted. |
| Defect 1 — mine, and it decided the outcome | In `hermes_leg.sh` the line `CAP=${CB2_CAP:-8}` sits on line 7 and `cb2_profile_load` on line 8. The cap is read BEFORE the loader exports it. The proxy got 24 (its receipt says `cap: 24` and it refused nothing at request 9), and the leg's own check got 8, so 9 accepted > 8 fired the independent over-cap rule. A leg that finished inside its budget was failed by an assignment one line too early. |
| Why I did not catch it | I preflighted the MIND leg and not the Hermes leg, and the `cap_cases` self-test exercises `profile.sh` in isolation rather than the legs' USE of it. Both gaps are the same mistake: I tested the part I had just written instead of the path the graded run takes. |
| Defect 2 — a rule that was never load-bearing | `proxy_receipt_ok` also failed, because `api_calls_from_log` is 8 while the proxy counted 9 `POST /v1/chat/completions`. All nine responses carried the expected model; the other 25 requests were discovery probes (models, tags, props, version) counted separately as `forwarded_other`. So Hermes's own log genuinely undercounts by one — and that is a fact about its self-reporting, not about whether its artifact is valid. |
| The third reading in a row killed by my harness, not by either system | Readings 1 and 2 halted on Mind-leg defects of mine. Reading 3 halted on a cap that made the opponent's configured turn limit unsatisfiable. Reading 4 halted on an assignment ordering. The pattern is not bad luck: every one of these was a harness change whose first execution was inside a graded run. |
| What reading 4 does establish | Hermes CAN complete T1 in this containment on this model: 9 requests, 424 s, 54711 prompt / 3121 completion tokens, three files, 5800 bytes. The Mind's artifact is reproducible byte-for-byte across two independent legs. Cost on the same meter remains roughly 26× in Hermes's favour of spend and against it on economy. |

## E.CB2-N reading 5 — PREREGISTERED: the own-log agreement stops being a disqualifier, for both systems
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Direction of this change, stated first | It RELAXES a rule that was disqualifying the OPPONENT, and it relaxes the matching rule I added for ourselves this same session and described as earning its keep. I would have had to make the identical change if it had disqualified us, and it is written here before reading 5 runs. |
| The change | The agreement between an agent's own call count and the proxy's accepted count becomes a RECORDED METRIC for both systems, not a disqualification. Both receipts already carry both numbers; they will also carry the boolean, and a disagreement is reported as a finding about that system's spend accounting. |
| Why it is right on the merits, independent of whom it was failing | The proxy is the authoritative meter and the cap is enforced there, before the model, for both systems. An agent cannot hide spend from it. The own-log comparison therefore adds nothing to enforcement — it characterises how well a system accounts for itself, which is worth knowing and is not a reason to throw away an artifact. Artifact validity does not depend on an agent's bookkeeping. |
| What stays a disqualifier | Everything else, unchanged: refusals and over-cap at the PROXY, a missing or untyped proxy receipt, downloads or installs, key leaks, symlinks or special nodes, a failed capture or brain gate, model identity, a non-zero exit and the wall. |
| Defect fix, not a rule change | `CAP` is assigned after `cb2_profile_load` in `hermes_leg.sh`, and a self-test case asserts for every leg script that no consumer reads `CB2_CAP` before the loader runs — the class, not the instance. |
| The process change that matters more than either | BOTH legs get a preflight on a throwaway output root before any graded sequence, not just the Mind's. Three readings have been spent discovering that a harness change's first execution was inside a graded run. |
| Kill criteria for reading 5 | Unchanged except as stated above. If a preflight leg for either system is disqualified for any reason, the graded sequence does not start. |

## Why the Mind scores 2/11 on T1 — a structural diagnosis, not a quality judgement
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Read from the source, not inferred from the score | `page_recipe` in `delegate.rs` is a six-step chain: research → think → a publish-shaped repair round → publish_page → notify. Its Think step instructs the model to "Output ONE complete, self-contained HTML document and NOTHING else", everything inline, no network. `publish_page` takes that one document. |
| So the ceiling is structural | The executor emits exactly one HTML file. T1 asks for a lead-capture form whose submission APPENDS a record, a dashboard computing exact aggregates over fourteen day-bins from that data, and a runnable server (`run_sh_present`). No prompt improvement makes a single self-contained document satisfy those. 2/11 is what this executor can score on this brief; it is not the model underperforming. |
| The two checks it does pass are the two it can | `site_up` and `relative_links_resolve` — the page loads and its links resolve. Everything else needs a second file or persisted state. |
| Which means the honest product question is not "why did the model do badly" | It is "why does a brief that says dashboard, form and data reach a single-page generator at all". The classifier routes on artefact nouns — `site`, `page`, `dashboard` are all PAGE_NOUNS — and the comment above the table explicitly warns AWAY from letting those words reach the coder. On the contained box the coder does not exist anyway, so the floor stands regardless. |
| Two candidate slices, neither started, both needing their own prereg | (a) Teach the classifier to separate a static page from an APPLICATION — a form that saves, a dashboard computed from data, a server to run — and route the latter to the coder where one exists. (b) Give the page lane the ability to emit a small SET of files including a runnable server, which is containment-compatible and needs no coder. |
| Why neither is being done now | Both would be written while a benchmark whose briefs contain those exact words is mid-flight. They get preregistered after reading 5 finishes, with test cases written from general phrasings rather than from the frozen briefs, and the comparison is re-run afterwards so the improvement is measured against a number that already exists. |

Both agents wanting one request past the budget: Hermes stops cleanly and is graded, the Mind is disqualified. The manifest said `agent.max_turns 8` in two places and was equally wrong. Both corrected. |
| Resolution of the cap rule | A cap refusal is no longer a violation for either system. Running out of a budget is the budget working; EXCEEDING it would be misconduct and `accepted > cap` still catches that, though only the proxy could cause it. This one favours US, which is the opposite direction from the relaxation earlier today — recorded so the pattern of who each change helps is legible. |
| The rules that could never be tested | `verdict.py` carried a module-level `CAP = 8` that `verdict_cases.py` imported, so the entire disqualification rule was only ever self-tested at eight while `nim-cap24` enforces twenty-four. And the host-side independent rules (capture, symlinks, specials, key leak, untyped receipt) were one long boolean inside a heredoc no test could reach — the same shape that hid three defects before. They are `host_independent` now, with a case per rule fired alone, and every `classify` case runs at both caps. |
| A self-test that reported success for the wrong reason | The cap-wall case observed only `cb2_profile_load`'s exit code, which is 1 for an unknown profile, a bad key file and an unresolved upstream too. The reviewer ran the suite on a host where several other cases were failing and watched this one report "the cap wall works" for a reason that had nothing to do with the cap. It asserts the refusal message now. |
| Three more of my own claims that were not true of the code | The smoke and the leg shared only a variable NAME while a comment claimed a preflight could not smoke a different binary than the leg it cleared (the smoke records the sha now and the leg refuses a mismatch); `run/verdict.py` was the one file matching the "no hard-coded 8" scan's own regex and missing from its file list; and two of that scan's four rows compared a constant with itself and reported "agree". |
| L2-B: a whole branch that cannot be reached | `abstained_empty` is unreachable under `attention-policy-v1`. The floor is `score >= 1` and the lowest score any in-scope loop can take at any urgency is 131. So the shadow proposes something on EVERY due wake, and the preregistered "shadow false negative" metric — legacy acted while the shadow abstained — is degenerate at zero before any evidence is collected. The field stays (the schema is preregistered, and a policy v2 with a real floor would make it live); the test computes the minimum and fails if a constants change ever makes abstention possible, so that change gets a policy version instead of passing unnoticed. |
| L2-B: the module's central claim was false | Its header says a site cannot fill an entry without reading every required signal and a descriptor cannot reach a signal the entry does not carry. But the real gates take `Presence { chat_present, quiet }`, and five of the eleven entry types collapsed it to one `presence: bool` — dropping `quiet`, including from the two types whose names END in "ChatQuiet". `IdleGated` carried a raw `idle_ms` with no threshold beside it while `DmnGate` and `KnockGate` both carried theirs. Every type carries the whole `Presence` now, and `IdleGated` carries the gate's own `IdleInputs`. |
| L2-B: three more | The `readings()` sort was inert (the push sequence was byte-for-byte the scope order, so deleting the sort changed nothing — collection is in FIELD order now and the scope order is derived, which makes its removal observable); the row was stamped with the loop-ledger schema version while `ATTENTION_POLICY` — the thing that decides every number in it — was written into no row anywhere; and the V6 constant's doc said "NOTHING WRITES IT YET" in the same commit as the writer. |
| Four vacuous tests of mine | A recomputability test calling one pure function twice on the same input (replaced by a round trip through the stored row, which can fail); a test asserting `abstained_empty == ranked.is_empty()` one line after the field is assigned from that expression; a test named "an unfilled slot is not the same as a slot that is not due" that ended `assert_eq!(a, b)`; and a constant compared to its own literal in `l2a_tests`, forty lines above the commit that deleted exactly that pattern elsewhere. |
| The l3c probe, third time | The comment claimed deleting the immutability guard had been caught. It had not: the guard is a CONJUNCTION and my probe reached only the `outcome` half, so deleting that clause alone left the test green. There are three probes now — an answered row, an answered row whose resolution is still pending, and a cancelled row whose outcome is still null — and each conjunct is independently observable. Verified by disabling each alone and watching a named assertion fail. |
| Six rounds, sixty-eight findings, every one real | And for the sixth round running, a defect was found inside a fix for the previous round's finding. |

## The reading-5 preflight blocked the graded run — and the reason is the task, not either system
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The preflight worked, for the first time | Mind T1 clean (done, page, 2 requests, accounting agrees, not disqualified). Hermes T1 DISQUALIFIED: rc 137, wall 1810 s, no session log, 8 accepted, 0 refused, ZERO upstream errors, 5 files / 8584 bytes. Under the preregistered criterion the graded sequence does not start, and it did not. Four readings were spent discovering harness defects; this is the first time one was caught before a graded invocation. |
| What actually happened, from the transcript | Hermes wrote a `run.sh` whose last line is `python3 server.py`, and then RAN it. A web server does not return. The agent blocked on its own verification step until the wall killed it. Eight clean model calls, no upstream trouble, the artifact already on disk. |
| Why this is a benchmark design defect and not a Hermes failure | T1 asks for a runnable server (`run_sh_present` is one of the eleven checks). The harness gives an agent no way to verify that deliverable without blocking forever, and the wall then disqualifies the agent that attempted it. The Mind is structurally immune: its page executor runs nothing. So the wall punishes precisely the behaviour the brief asks for, on exactly one side. |
| It is also bimodal, which matters for n=1 | Reading 4's Hermes finished T1 in 424 s with three files and did not run a server. This preflight's Hermes wrote five files, ran the server and hung. Same brief, same model, same cap. With one invocation per system per task, a competitor whose completion is bimodal makes a single reading a coin flip. |
| What I am NOT doing | I am not relaxing the wall. That would be the third preregistered rule relaxed in one session, and unlike the other two — which fixed rules that were unfair or unsatisfiable by construction — this one changes what "completing a task" means. Codex is out until the 6th and there is no second pair of eyes; a change of that kind should wait for one. It is written up as a proposal, below. |
| The proposal, for review rather than for application | A wall timeout becomes a RECORDED outcome (`wall_hit`) and the artifact is graded, for both systems. Argument: the deliverable is the artifact, the checker validates it independently in a network-less container, and model spend is bounded by the cap regardless. Counter-argument, stated because it is the one that would kill it: we cannot distinguish "finished the artifact then blocked verifying it" from "produced nothing useful and spun", and grading the second rewards a system for occupying the wall. |
| What I AM changing, because it is orchestration and not grading | `run_all.sh` halts the whole sequence on a disqualified leg, so one bad leg destroys a reading and T2 and T3 are never run. It will record a disqualified leg and CONTINUE, still halting on a VOID (which needs a human rerun decision) and on any containment or attachment failure. No grading rule moves; a reading simply stops throwing away the tasks it could still measure. |
| And a refinement to the preflight criterion, preregistered before it is used | A preflight blocks the graded run when it fails for a HARNESS reason — a defect in the scripts, a containment failure, a receipt that cannot be built. It does NOT block when it fails for an AGENT reason — the wall, the agent's own log, its own quality — because that is the measurement, and it belongs under grading rather than in a rehearsal. This unblocks me, so: the distinguishing question is "would this failure have happened to any agent, or did this agent do it", and a preflight that fails for an agent reason must still be reported alongside the reading it permitted. |

## Two defects found in reading 5 WHILE IT RAN — one I created hours ago, one that has been wrong all along
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Written before the reading finished | T2 and T3 are still running as this row is written. Recording now so the diagnosis cannot be shaped by the result. |
| Defect A — I created a new asymmetry in the commit that claimed to remove one | `verdict.py` no longer treats a cap refusal as an independent violation for the Mind. `hermes_leg.sh:65` STILL does: `[ "$RC_REF" -gt 0 ] || [ "$RC_ACC" -gt $CAP ]` → `DQ_IND=true`. So a cap refusal disqualifies Hermes and not the Mind — the exact inverse of the asymmetry I had just fixed, now favouring US. My commit message for e370ba4 says "a cap refusal is no longer a violation for either side". That sentence is false of the code it describes. |
| How it showed up | Reading 5's Hermes T1: rc 0, 198 s, valid log, `api_calls_from_log` 24 = `proxy_accepted` 24 (the own-log agreement HELD), one refusal at the cap of 24. Disqualified. |
| Defect B — the download scan disqualifies an agent for verifying its own work | The same leg reports `download_or_install_lines: 1`. The line that matched, exactly: `curl -s http://0.0.0.0:8123/ \| head -n 5`, with the agent reasoning "curl might not be installed. Use wget?". That is Hermes fetching its OWN LOCAL SERVER over loopback to check the page it had just built — the behaviour T1 asks for, since `run_sh_present` is one of the eleven checks. |
| Why the scan is measuring the wrong thing, independent of whom it caught | It is a regex over an entire transcript, so it fires on any MENTION: a curl example in a generated README, an HTTP error page echoing a prompt, a model reasoning aloud about whether wget exists. Meanwhile the act it names is already impossible — internal network, no DNS, the proxy forwards only to the run state's upstream, and the manifest says so in the same sentence that keeps the scan ("impossible by network … any transcript line matching pip/npm/apt/curl/wget disqualifies anyway"). Real evidence of an attempted egress is a BLOCKED CONNECTION, which the network layer and the proxy's counters already record. A word in a log is not that evidence. |
| And I made it symmetric before I understood it | Hours earlier I mirrored this scan onto the Mind because it was a Hermes-only rule. That was the right instinct applied to the wrong rule: I made a bad check apply to both systems instead of asking whether it measured anything. |
| The three distinct Hermes T1 outcomes so far, same brief, same model | Reading 4: finished in 424 s, 9 requests, 3 files. Reading-5 preflight: ran its own server in the foreground and hung to the 1800 s wall, 8 requests, 5 files. Reading 5: finished in 198 s, 24 requests (cap hit), 5 files, and used curl on loopback to verify. The competitor's behaviour on this task is genuinely trimodal, which matters for a benchmark taking one invocation per system per task. |
| What happens to reading 5 | It runs to completion — the invocations are spent and the artifacts are worth having. Its Hermes verdicts are NOT valid, because they were computed under a rule the Mind was exempt from. The receipts carry every raw number (accepted, refused, downloads, calls), so the verdicts can be re-derived once the rules are symmetric; the artifacts and the checker scores stand on their own. |
| Fixes, and why they are not applied yet | A is unambiguous and is a defect, not a rule change: `refused > 0` comes out of the Hermes leg so the code matches the claim already published. B is a rule change in the OPPONENT's favour and is proposed rather than applied — the scan becomes a recorded metric for both systems and attempted egress is evidenced at the network layer. Neither is being edited right now because an adversarial review of the previous round's fixes is running against these exact files. |

## Review 7 — twelve findings on review 6's fixes, and the first one says the headline fix did not fix
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Standing | All twelve addressed, every fix mutation-verified. Workspace suite green, clippy clean, cb2n re-derives byte-exactly, and the harness self-test passes 75 cases on the box. |
| Finding 1, which is the whole story | "A cap refusal is not a violation for either side" removed the rule from the INDEPENDENT class and left `refused == 0` in each leg's receipt-shape check, which feeds the DEPENDENT class. A cap 429 never touches the upstream, so the leg is not void and it was disqualified anyway — through a second path I never looked at. My commit message asserted the opposite. |
| Why no test caught it | The shape rule was computed inside each leg's heredoc, where nothing can reach it — the third rule in this harness to live there and the third to be wrong there. And `classify`'s `refused` parameter was UNUSED, so the `cap_refusal` case passed at both caps while the real leg disqualified the run. A parameter nothing reads is a case that tests nothing. |
| The fix, and its proof | `receipt_shape_ok` is a pure function used by both legs, with ten cases at each cap including `shape_capped_and_refused`. Reintroducing `refused == 0` makes exactly that case fail at both caps. |
| Three more checks that could not fail | (a) The no-hard-coded-cap scan matched only a bare `CAP = 8`, while every literal actually present is a DEFAULT — changing the driver's `else 8` to `else 0` moved nothing. It now flags a cap-context 8 on a line mentioning neither CB2_CAP nor argv, because a default is legitimate and a literal deciding alone is not. (b) The cap-ordering case decided on a COMMENT: the first mention of CB2_CAP in `hermes_leg.sh` is the sentence explaining that the read had moved below the loader. Case 7 was taught to strip comments in the same commit and this one was not. (c) The round-trip test's closing "the stored order must be the ranked order" used Resolve and Family, whose scope order and score order already agree, so it held with the ranking deleted — a vacuous assertion inside the test written to replace a vacuous test. |
| A check that failed OPEN under a comment claiming otherwise | The smoked-binary coupling wrote the sha only when `CB2_OUT` happened to be set, which no caller exports before a smoke; nothing was recorded and the leg treated the absent file as a pass. The path comes from the run state now, the smoke fails if it cannot write it, and the comment states plainly what it still does not do: a leg run with no smoke at all proceeds. |
| A correction that made a true statement false | The V6 constant's doc originally said "NOTHING WRITES IT YET" and was TRUE. Review 6 read `to_event`, concluded the row is written, and replaced it. Review 7 grepped for a caller of `attention_shadow` and found none — L2-B step 1 is wired to nothing, which the module header says three hundred lines above. Both corrections are now recorded at the site, because the second was worse than the first. |
| A claim finally made true | The assertion that the shadow row carries the policy was messaged "a v2 with different constants must not be indistinguishable from v1", and nothing tied the NAME to the TABLE. All seventeen rows are pinned beside `ATTENTION_POLICY` now; changing any constant without renaming the policy fails. It failed on its first run — because I transcribed MailSweep's row from a truncated ledger line and the CODE was right. |
| And the coverage claim | `filled` was added so a hole in coverage is "visible in the row itself", and it reached the ledger as a COUNT — two wakes missing different slots produced byte-identical events. The event carries the filled ids now. |
| Seven rounds, eighty findings, every one real | And for the seventh time, a defect inside a fix for the previous round. The rate is not falling. What has changed is where they are caught: rounds 1–4 found them after a graded reading was spent, rounds 6 and 7 found them before. |

It failed all four dashboard checks and relative links. So the hardest brief in the set defeats both systems — it just defeats us three times as thoroughly. |
| Cost, the one column we win | Mind: 2 model requests and 34–70 s per task, every task. Hermes: 9–24 requests and 139–198 s. Five to ten times cheaper, four times faster. |
| The one-line version | On three briefs of the kind people actually ask for, a pinned competitor on the same model scored more than five times what we did, and the gap is not explained by anything in this harness. |
| What this reading is now good for | It is a baseline with receipts: every leg valid, every artifact tree-hashed, every rule symmetric and tested, the whole harness re-derivable from the frozen tree plus one recorded patch. Improvements get measured against 4/27 and against the per-task splits, not against an impression. |

## The 2/6 was a FILENAME. A diagnostic that corrects my own reading of the baseline
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Status of the recorded result | UNCHANGED. Reading 5 stands at Mind 4/27, Hermes 22/27. What follows is a diagnostic on copies in `/tmp`; no recorded artifact, receipt or verdict was touched, and nothing here is a re-grade. |
| What I did | Copied the Mind's T2 artifact, renamed the single file from `arjun-mehta---software-engineer.html` to `index.html`, and ran the frozen checker on the copy. |
| The result | **The identical bytes score 6/6.** Every check that failed — contact section reachable, four project articles, three writing articles, loading with no console error or external request — passes. Our T2 page already contained `<section id="projects">`, `<section id="writing">`, `<section id="contact">`, a `mailto:` link, seven `<article>` elements and zero external requests. It ties Hermes exactly. |
| The cause | T2's brief says: "Static files only, entry `index.html` in the project root". `publish_page` names the file by slugifying the page TITLE. The checker loads `index.html`, finds nothing, and every structural check fails. We lost four points to a filename. |
| T1 the same way | 2/11 → **4/11** with the rename. `form_cb2_lead_form_present` and `loads_without_console_error_or_external_request` join the two we had. The remaining seven are a real ceiling: a submit that appends a record, a dashboard with exact aggregates over fourteen day-bins, and `run.sh` — none of which one static file can do. |
| T3 is unaffected | A Python CLI routed to the page executor. Naming changes nothing there. |
| I have to correct what I said about the baseline | I wrote "we are fast and cheap and we produce far too little" and called 2/6 a structural ceiling on the task our page executor was designed for. That was WRONG about T2. The content was competition-grade and the packaging threw the score away. It remains right about T1's dashboard and about T3. |
| The ranked fix list this produces, cheapest first | (1) Honour an explicitly requested filename — worth 4 points on T2 and 2 on T1, and it is a small change. (2) Let the page lane emit a SET of files including a runnable server — the rest of T1. (3) Stop routing code briefs to the page executor — all of T3. |
| Why this was worth finding before writing any of them | An hour ago the obvious next slice was "make the page lane produce much more". On T2 that would have been effort spent on content that was already good enough, while the actual defect was one line of naming. Measure, then read the measurement, then build. |

## E.PAGE1 — an explicitly required filename wins over the page's title (PREREGISTERED, before the code)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The defect, with its measurement | A brief that says "entry `index.html` in the project root" gets a file named after the page's `<title>`. Measured cost: T2 scores 2/6 instead of 6/6 on identical bytes, T1 2/11 instead of 4/11. `publish_page` calls `title_from_html` FIRST and only falls back to the caller's `name` argument, so an explicit instruction cannot reach the filename at all. |
| The claim | When a task explicitly requires a filename, the published page uses it. When it does not, nothing changes: the title slug still wins, because a page named after the user's raw request text is the defect that rule was written to fix. |
| The rule, narrow on purpose | A `<name>.html` token in the task counts ONLY when it appears with a requirement phrase — entry / named / must be / call it / save as / in the project root / at the root. Exactly one distinct such filename must be found; zero or several means no explicit requirement and today's behaviour stands. A page is never named from an incidental mention. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) If a task with NO filename requirement produces a different filename than it does today, the slice is wrong and is reverted. (2) If a mention with no requirement phrase ("see index.html for an example", "unlike about.html") captures the name, it is wrong. (3) If two different required names are found and one is picked, it is wrong — ambiguity must fall back, not guess. (4) If the extracted name can escape the web directory (a slash, `..`, an absolute path) it is wrong and is a security defect, not a naming one. |
| Am I tuning to the benchmark? | The tests are written from general phrasings AND include the frozen brief's phrasing, and I am saying so rather than hiding it. The defence is that this is a defect any user hits — asking for a file by name and getting another name — and that the baseline it is measured against is already recorded and frozen at 4/27. The improvement gets a NEW reading with its own row; the old number is not revised. |
| A trade-off I am taking deliberately | Two tasks that both require `index.html` will collide in one web directory. That is what the user asked for in each case, and the alternative (a per-job subdirectory) would break the "project root" requirement that motivated this. Noted here so the first collision is a known consequence rather than a surprise. |
| What this does NOT fix | T1's dashboard, appending submit and `run.sh` (a single static file cannot do them) and T3's routing. Those are slices 2 and 3 of the ranked list and get their own rows. |

## E.PAGE1 — RESULT: an explicitly required filename wins
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Outcome against the criteria set before the code | PASS on all four, each verified by breaking it. Ten tests, workspace suite green, clippy clean. |
| What shipped | `required_filename(task)` — a narrow extractor — plus the publish path preferring it over the page's `<title>`, and `page_recipe` carrying it into the publish call. Nothing is invented: a task with no requirement produces exactly today's arguments. |
| Kill 1 (nothing changes without a requirement) | Four no-requirement briefs find nothing, and a recipe-level test reads the actual publish step's arguments and asserts no filename is carried. |
| Kill 2 (an incidental mention is not a requirement) | "See index.html for an example", "unlike about.html, this one should be playful", "the old site had a broken contact.html". The FIRST version failed on the second of those: the cue list held bare modals, and "this one should be playful" made `about.html` a requirement. Modals are out; a cue now has to be about the NAME. |
| Kill 3 (ambiguity falls back) | Two different required names return nothing rather than picking. The same name twice is one requirement, not ambiguity. Removing the fallback fails that test by name. |
| Kill 4 (a name may never be a path) | Verified, and it produced a finding of its own: the `/` and `\` guards could not fire. The stem walk stops at any byte outside `[A-Za-z0-9-_.]`, so `../../etc/passwd.html` had already become `passwd.html` before those clauses were reached — the test proving the result holds no separator passed with them deleted. They are gone, the walk is documented as the enforcement, and the guard that CAN fire (a dot run, since the walk allows dots) now has an input that makes it observable. |
| Measured expectation, recorded before it is measured | On the frozen T2 artifact the identical bytes went 2/6 → 6/6 under a rename, so I expect T2 at 6/6 and T1 at 4/11 in the next reading. If T2 does not reach 6/6 the diagnosis was incomplete and that is the finding, not a reason to adjust anything. |
| Still open, unchanged | T1's dashboard, appending submit and `run.sh` need a set of files and a server. T3 needs the router to stop turning code briefs into pages. Slices 2 and 3, each with its own row. |

## E.PAGE1 shipped as a NO-OP, and no test I wrote could have told me
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What was wrong | `publish_html` replaces every character outside `[A-Za-z0-9-_]` with a dash — correct for a page TITLE ("Arjun Mehta — Software Engineer"), wrong for a name a task required. `index.html` became the stem `index-html` and the file landed at `index-html.html`. The whole slice changed nothing. |
| How it got past ten tests and four mutations | Every test was of the RULE (`required_filename` extracts the right token) or of the WIRING (the recipe carries it into the publish call). Both were correct. Not one test asked the only question that matters: what is the file on disk called. I verified the parts and never the outcome, having spent the day writing a ledger about exactly that. |
| How it was actually found | By reading `publish_html` while planning a different slice. Not by a test, not by a review, not by the measurement I was two minutes from running — I would have run the leg, seen T2 still at 2/6, and had to work backwards from a result I had publicly predicted would be 6/6. |
| The fix | `published_stem` is the naming decision, and a name already ending in `.html` keeps its stem: `index.html` → `index`, `Index.HTML` → `index`. A title with a dot in it is untouched (`v1.2 release notes` → `v1-2-release-notes`), because only a `.html` tail is a filename. |
| And the duplication that fix introduced, removed | The rule briefly existed twice — once in `publish_html` and once in `published_stem` so a test could reach it. Two copies of one rule is how a tested rule and a shipped rule come to disagree, which IS this slice's defect. `publish_html` calls `published_stem`; deleting the rule from its one home fails the naming test. |
| Three new tests, and what each is for | The required name becomes that exact file; a page title is still slugified exactly as before (so the old behaviour is pinned, not merely believed); a dotted name that is not a page keeps its old treatment. |
| The rule I keep re-learning, stated once more | A test of a component is not a test of the outcome. "The extractor returns `index.html`" and "the recipe passes `index.html`" were both true while the file was called something else. When a slice exists to change an OUTCOME, the outcome is what must be asserted. |

## E.FILES1 — the mind can write a SET of files as a deliverable (PREREGISTERED, before the code)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The gap, measured | After E.PAGE1 the Mind's ceiling on the frozen benchmark is T1 4/11, T2 6/6, T3 0/10. Every remaining point needs more than one file. T1's contract asks for `run.sh` starting a server on `0.0.0.0:8123`, a form posting to it, `data/leads.json` with append semantics, and a `/dashboard` embedding a JSON block. T3 asks for `tracker.py` plus a passing pytest suite. Both are the same missing capability: the mind can publish ONE HTML document and nothing else. |
| Confirmed from the checker's source, not assumed | `check_web.mjs` spawns `bash run.sh` when it exists and otherwise starts its own static server on the directory — which is exactly why renaming one file to `index.html` moved T1 from 2/11 to 4/11 and why the remaining seven cannot be reached without a server. |
| Scope of THIS slice, deliberately small | The capability only: a `publish_files` tool taking a set of `{path, content}` entries and writing them under the web directory, with path safety and caps. It is wired to NO recipe. Same staging as L2-B step 1, which is the one large slice today that came through review clean: build the thing, wire it separately, so this step cannot change what the mind does. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) Any path escaping the web directory — `..`, an absolute path, a symlink target, a drive letter, a NUL — is refused, and refusal is the WHOLE call, not a skipped entry: a partially written deliverable is worse than none. (2) Refusal must be observable: the tool reports which path it refused and why. (3) Caps enforced and tested — a file count, a per-file size, a total size, a directory depth. (4) An empty set, a duplicate path, and a path that is a directory are each refused rather than silently tolerated. (5) Nothing already published may be read, moved or deleted by this tool; it only creates and overwrites within its own destination. |
| What I will NOT accept as evidence it works | That the extractor is right, or that a recipe passes the arguments. E.PAGE1 shipped as a no-op today with both of those true and no test asking what the file on disk was called. The tests here assert the FILES ON DISK — their paths, their bytes, and that a refused set leaves the directory untouched. |
| Open question I am not deciding yet | Whether the file set lands in the web root (matching T1's "project root") or a job-scoped subdirectory (safer for a companion hosting many things). It is a real trade-off, it interacts with E.PAGE1's collision note, and it belongs to the WIRING slice rather than this one. |

## E.FILES1 — RESULT: the mind can write a set of files, wired to nothing
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Outcome against the criteria set before the code | PASS on all five, each verified by breaking it. Ten tests, workspace suite green, clippy clean. |
| What shipped | `crates/mind-conversation/src/fileset.rs`: `plan_file_set` (pure — validation with no filesystem, clock or environment) and `write_file_set` (thin — applies exactly that plan). No tool exposes it and no recipe calls it. |
| Kill 1 (no path escapes; a refusal is the whole call) | Eleven hostile shapes refused, and a set whose THIRD entry is hostile writes none of its first two — asserted by listing the destination and finding it empty. A half-written deliverable is worse than none because it looks finished. |
| Kill 2 (a refusal is observable) | Every refusal names the entry and gives a reason an operator can act on, asserted per variant. |
| Kill 3 (caps) | File count, per-file bytes, total bytes and depth, each tested AT the cap and one past it. Removing the count cap or the total cap fails by name. |
| Kill 4 (empty, duplicate, directory) | Each refused. Writing under a path that is already a file errors and leaves the existing file's bytes intact. |
| Kill 5 (nothing outside the destination) | A file is planted beside the destination, three traversal shapes are attempted, and its contents are asserted unchanged — then a legitimate write is asserted to land. |
| Two more guards that could not fire | Deleting the `..` refusal and deleting the backslash refusal each left the suite green: the leading-dot rule and the component charset rule already refuse the same inputs. That is the third and fourth dead guard found this way today. They are kept — their diagnostics are clearer than the ones that would replace them — and a test now pins each refusal's REASON, so deleting either fails by name. |
| Deliberately not decided here | Where a file set lands (web root versus a job-scoped subdirectory). It is a real trade-off, it interacts with E.PAGE1's collision note, and it belongs to the wiring slice. A test asserts that nothing calls this module yet, so the wiring cannot arrive without its own row. |

## E.FILES2 — a BUILD executor, and no more silent substitution (PREREGISTERED, before the code)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| A correction to my own diagnosis first | I wrote that T3 was "a routing failure" and named the classifier. It is not. Run against the T3 brief, `classify` returns **code** — the brief contains no page noun at all. What turned it into a page is the E.PORT1-B floor I added to stop reading 2 halting: it constrains the classified kind to the executors that EXIST, and the contained box has no coder. The router was right and my floor overruled it. |
| So the fix is a capability, not a rule | Substituting nothing and refusing honestly would keep T3 at 0/10 forever. What the mind actually lacks is an executor that can produce a code-shaped deliverable without an external CLI or a cloud key — which is exactly what E.FILES1 built the writer for. |
| The claim | A `build` executor serves a task whose deliverable is a SET of files: it asks the model for the set, validates it with `plan_file_set`, writes it, and reports the project. `code` routes to the coder when one exists and to `build` otherwise — a real executor for the kind, not a different kind wearing its name. |
| The output format, decided and argued now | NOT JSON. The existing `extract_html_arg` exists precisely because a `publish_page` call that overflowed the token budget produced unparseable JSON, and a set of files is many times larger. The model emits a delimited plain text stream — a line `=== FILE: <path>` then the file's bytes — which needs no escaping, survives truncation, and lets a cut-off final file be identified and dropped rather than corrupting the whole set. |
| Where a deliverable lands | A per-job project directory under the web dir, recorded in the job's ledger row. NOT the web root: two deliverables both writing `index.html` would silently overwrite each other, and a companion hosting many things must not do that. This makes the mind's "project root" the project directory, which is the same relationship Hermes has to `/work`. |
| The consequence for the benchmark, stated before it is measured | The Mind driver captures files under `/state/public`, so a project subdirectory appears in the artifact as `<project>/index.html` and the checker — which looks at the artifact root — would score it ZERO. That is a real mismatch between an honest product decision and the harness, and it gets its OWN preregistered harness row (the driver captures the project directory named in the job row, falling back to the whole web dir), argued on symmetry with Hermes rather than on the score. I will not put the deliverable in the web root to make a number come out. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) A malformed or truncated stream must never produce a partial deliverable — the set is validated whole and written whole or not at all. (2) A file the model names outside the project must be refused by `plan_file_set`, not sanitised into place. (3) `build` must appear in `available_kinds` only when it can actually run, and a task routed to it must never be recorded as another kind. (4) When NO executor can serve the classified kind, the job is recorded FAILED with a reason an operator can read — never silently rebadged, which is the defect this row corrects. (5) The `page` lane is unchanged: a page brief still routes to `page` and still produces one document. |
| What I will not accept as evidence | That the parser returns the right structure. The tests assert the files on disk, and the end-to-end test drives the recipe and reads the project directory. |

## E.FILES2 — RESULT: a build executor, and the floor routes instead of restricting
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Pranab's design intent, which this restores | "The whole idea of coder was to route to model not restrict in case it is not defined." My E.PORT1-B floor did the opposite: with no coder configured it took the first executor that existed, so a `code` brief was silently rebadged as a `page`. Measured consequence — a Python CLI brief answered with one HTML document, scored 0/10, announced as live. |
| Outcome against the criteria set before the code | PASS on all five. Workspace suite green (752 in mind-conversation), clippy clean, each rule verified by breaking it. |
| What shipped | `build_recipe` (one model call emitting a delimited file stream, then an all-or-nothing write), the `write_files` tool, `publish_file_set` (a project directory per job, never the web root), `build` as a kind, and the floor change: `code` falls to `build` when no coder exists. |
| Why `build` is the right fallback and `page` never was | It produces the same KIND of deliverable by a different route. It runs on the mind's own inference path, which is OpenAI-compatible — so it works with the providers we actually have, and inside containment, where the Anthropic-protocol `claude` CLI cannot go at all. That is the distinction Pranab drew: E.CODER1 already removed the provider restriction, and NIM cannot drive the coder because of a PROTOCOL mismatch, not a configuration one. |
| When nothing fits, it says so | The refusal names the kind and lists what the box does have, instead of "no delegation executor is configured" — or, worse, running something else and calling it done. |
| Three existing tests failed, and every one was right to | A recipe-only box is no longer a menu of one, so the "no router for one executor" premise stopped being true — that property moved to a genuinely single-kind fixture (researcher only) which states its premise with an assertion instead of assuming it. And the two-executor test expected `page` for the T1 brief: that expectation IS the 2/11, and it now expects `build`. |
| What I expect to change on the benchmark, before it is measured | T1 and T3 both classify as `code` and will now route to `build`. If the build lane produces valid file sets, T1 gains `run_sh_present` and the submit/append checks, and T3 becomes reachable at all. If it does not, the finding is that a single model call cannot emit a correct multi-file project, which is worth knowing and is not a reason to change anything. |
| Not yet done, and it blocks the measurement | A project directory means the artifact is `<project>/index.html`, and the checker looks at the artifact root. That harness change is preregistered separately and argued on symmetry with Hermes's `/work`, not on the score. |

## E.CB2-N harness — the artifact is the PROJECT, for whichever system produces one (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The mismatch | The Mind driver captures files added under `/state/public`, and E.FILES2 writes a deliverable into a per-job project directory. So the artifact becomes `<project>/index.html` while the checker looks at the artifact ROOT — a build would score zero for a path reason, which is the same class of defect as the filename that cost T2 four checks. |
| The argument, which is symmetry and not the score | Hermes works in `/work` and its artifact IS `/work`: its project root and the artifact root are the same directory by construction. The Mind's project root is its project directory. Making the artifact the project directory gives both systems the same relationship between "where the agent built" and "what is graded". Grading the Mind at the web root would compare Hermes's project against the Mind's whole filesystem. |
| The rule | If the Mind's delegation reports a project (its result carries a project URL), the artifact is that project directory. Otherwise the artifact is the web directory, exactly as today. The rule is written in terms of what the SYSTEM reports, not in terms of which lane ran. |
| Why the project directory exists at all, restated | Not for the benchmark. Two deliverables both writing `index.html` into one directory would silently overwrite each other, and a companion hosting many things must not do that. The harness is being changed to match an honest product decision, not the other way round. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) A leg that produces NO project must capture exactly what it captures today — no behaviour change for the page lane. (2) The captured root must be a directory the mind actually wrote, never a path derived from the brief or guessed. (3) If a project is reported but its directory is missing or empty, the leg reports that rather than falling back silently to the web root — a fallback would hide a build that produced nothing. (4) The receipt must record WHICH root was captured, so a reader can tell the two cases apart without re-running anything. |
| What it cannot do | It cannot make a bad deliverable score. If the build lane emits an incomplete or wrong file set, the checker will say so, and that is the measurement I am running this reading to get. |

## Reading 6 preflight — the routing fix is confirmed on a real leg, and the build call voided
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Written before the rerun's result | The single declared rerun for a void is in flight as this is recorded. |
| The thing that WORKED, and it is the point of two slices | `routed_kind: build`. The T3 brief — "a command-line task tracker in Python", no page noun anywhere — took the build lane instead of being rebadged as a page. In reading 5 the same brief produced one HTML document and scored 0/10. The classifier had always said `code`; my floor had been overruling it. |
| The thing that failed | The build's model call returned an upstream 429-or-5xx (`upstream_http_errors: 1`, `upstream_client_errors: 0`, and the proxy classifies only those two statuses that way). Zero files, `captured_from: "."` since no project was reported. Correctly classified VOID, not disqualified: infrastructure, not the agent. |
| Two requests, and which one succeeded | `usage: prompt 502, completion 12`. Twelve completion tokens is the routing call answering one word — so the successful request was routing and the failed one was the build. |
| My preregistered prediction was WRONG, and that is worth as much as a right one | I named truncation at the 16000-token cap as the failure I expected. It was not that. `max_tokens: 16000` returns 200 from this model, and a build-sized generation reproduced directly — a full Python tracker plus a pytest suite — returned 200 in 91 s with 3797 completion tokens and `finish_reason: stop`. Neither the cap nor the size is the problem. |
| The hypothesis I am holding rather than acting on | The routing call is DETACHED and still in flight when the build call starts, so two requests overlap on a free-tier account. Reading 5 had the same overlap across six legs and never voided, so it is not obviously the cause. If the rerun voids too, that is where I look — and the fix would be to stop spending a routing call whose answer the floor overrides anyway, which is a cost argument as much as a reliability one. |
| Why a void does not block the graded run | The preflight criterion, preregistered before it was ever used, blocks on a HARNESS reason and not on an agent one. A void is neither: it is the upstream having a bad minute, and the void rule already provides exactly one declared rerun. |

## The build lane died on "unknown source 'write_files'" — the same shape, a third time
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The rerun | No upstream error at all this time (`upstream_http_errors: 0`, not void, not disqualified). Two model requests, both answered, 2278 completion tokens generated. Zero files. `I couldn't finish the build: tool 'write_files' failed: unknown source 'write_files'`. |
| What that means | The model DID the work. It produced a project. The chain then threw it away because the tool name did not resolve. |
| The defect | There are TWO tool dispatches. `capabilities.rs` serves the conversation engine's own tool calls; `call_tool` in lib.rs is what a RECIPE reaches. I registered `write_files` in the first and the build recipe reaches the second. |
| Why nothing caught it | Twenty tests across `plan_file_set`, `parse_file_stream`, `write_file_set` and the recipe's ARGUMENTS — all correct, none of them asking whether the tool a recipe names exists where a recipe looks. This is the third time in one day: E.PAGE1 shipped as a no-op because no test asked what the file on disk was called; E.FILES2's guards were verified and its wiring was not. The parts were right and the outcome did not happen. |
| The fix, and the guard that would have caught it | The arm is registered where recipes look. A new test scans the tool names the delegation recipes emit and requires an arm for each IN THE RECIPE-FACING DISPATCH ONLY — isolated deliberately, because an arm in the other dispatch satisfying the test is precisely the mistake being guarded against. Verified by renaming the arm and watching it fail. |
| Why a source scan and not a call | The dispatch is an `async fn` on a type that needs a whole engine to construct. A test that cannot be written without one does not get written — which is how this happened. The scan is exact about what it checks and carries an anti-vacuity assertion that both real tool names are in the list it iterated. |
| What the preflight bought | Two legs, no graded invocation spent, and a defect that would have made T1 and T3 score zero in reading 6 for a reason having nothing to do with the model. This is the first time the preflight has paid for itself on a defect of mine rather than on the upstream. |
| Still unknown | Whether the build lane produces a GOOD project. Nothing has been measured yet: the first attempt voided upstream and the second was thrown away by this. The 2278 tokens it generated are gone. |

## THE BUILD LANE WORKS — and my own parser was deleting its most important file
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The third preflight leg | `status: done`, not void, not disqualified. `routed_kind: build`. `captured_from: cb2-t3-a70722` — the project directory, so the harness capture works. `tracker.py` written, 2146 bytes, ending in a complete `main()`. 100 s, 2 model requests, 1345 completion tokens. The build lane produced a real deliverable end to end for the first time. |
| And it reported this | "1 files: tracker.py — INCOMPLETE: the generation was cut off inside test_tracker.py". That message was WRONG, and the wrongness was mine. |
| What actually happened | 1345 completion tokens against a 16000 cap — nowhere near it. I reproduced the same generation directly against the same model: `finish_reason: stop`, THREE complete files, and no trailing newline on the last one. The model had finished. My parser deleted its last file every time, because I had made "the stream does not end with a newline" mean "this file was cut off". |
| What it cost | In that leg, the entire test suite. T3's checker asks for `test_files_present` and `pytest_passes`; the model wrote `test_tracker.py` and my rule threw it away and blamed the model. |
| Why the rule was wrong in principle, not just in effect | A missing final newline is EQUALLY consistent with a cut-off generation and with a model that simply ended without one, and models routinely end without one. The text cannot distinguish them. Only the API's `finish_reason` can, and the parser does not have it. I had encoded a guess as a verdict and then acted on the verdict by deleting evidence. |
| The fix | The parser reports the OBSERVATION — `unterminated`, the last file's path when the stream did not end with a newline — and keeps the file. Dropping a probably-complete file is the worse error: a checker can judge a file that exists and can do nothing with one that was deleted. The message says the last file "may be incomplete" instead of asserting it was cut off. |
| The test that asserted the wrong thing | It required the last file to be dropped, and passed. It now requires both files present AND the observation reported, and reintroducing the delete fails it by name. |
| My preregistered prediction, finally settled | I predicted truncation at the token cap. Three legs later: the cap was never reached, the model never truncated, and the only truncation in this story was mine. |
| What is now genuinely unknown, again | How T3 scores with its test file intact. Nothing has been graded yet. |

## E.FILES3 — a repair round for the build lane (PREREGISTERED, before the code)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The evidence, not a guess | Reading 6's only Mind failure is `pytest_passes` on T3. Every check that exercises the TOOL passes; the model's own test suite fails against a tracker the checker has independently verified works. It wrote a correct program and incorrect tests for it, in one pass, and never saw them fail. |
| Why the answer is already in the codebase | The PAGE lane has a repair round: a `JumpIf` that skips it when the draft is already publishable, and a second Think that gets the failed draft back and rewrites it. That round exists because a truncated document used to be published as a finished page. The build lane has no equivalent. |
| The claim | A build that RUNS what it wrote and is shown the failure can fix it, and the check that costs us a point today is exactly the kind a run reveals immediately. |
| The shape, decided now | After the write, execute the deliverable's own verification if it declares one — a test command inferable from the files present (`pytest` when a `test_*.py` exists; `run.sh` health for a server). On failure, ONE repair Think that receives the command, its exit code and its output, and re-emits the file set. Then write again, all-or-nothing, exactly as now. At most one repair round, so the cost ceiling is 2 model calls per build rather than an open loop. |
| The containment problem, named before it bites | Running generated code is the one thing this system has never done inside the mind's own process. It must NOT run in the mind's container with its network and its state: the deliverable is untrusted output. The execution has to be sandboxed — no network, a read-only mount of the project copied to a scratch dir, a hard wall-clock kill, and no access to `/state`. If that sandbox cannot be built cheaply and provably, the slice is abandoned rather than weakened; a mind that executes untrusted code carelessly is a worse product than one that ships a failing test. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) Generated code must never execute with network access, with the mind's filesystem, or without a wall-clock kill — each asserted, and the network one demonstrated by a deliverable that tries to reach out and cannot. (2) A repair must be attempted at most ONCE; a second failure is reported, not retried. (3) The repaired set is validated and written by the same all-or-nothing path — a repair may not bypass `plan_file_set`. (4) A build with no inferable verification behaves exactly as today, with no extra model call. (5) The receipt must record whether a repair ran and whether it helped, so the slice can be measured rather than believed. |
| What I will NOT accept as evidence it works | That the repair prompt is well-written, or that a unit test of the runner passes. The measurement is a graded T3 leg where `pytest_passes` flips, and if it does not flip the finding is that one repair round is not enough — which is worth knowing and is not a reason to add a second. |

## E.FILES3 — the kill criterion FIRED, and the slice is re-scoped rather than weakened
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The blocking assumption, tested before a line of the feature was written | The prereg said running generated code must be sandboxed — no network, no `/state`, a hard wall-clock kill — and that if the sandbox could not be built cheaply and provably the slice would be ABANDONED rather than weakened. So the sandbox was tested first. |
| What the test showed | On the host as an unprivileged user, `unshare -rn` works: a network namespace with no DNS, no privileges needed. **Inside the `cb2-mind` container it fails: "unshare failed: Operation not permitted"** — Docker's default seccomp profile and dropped capabilities block it, which is the containment doing exactly its job. |
| Why that is decisive rather than an inconvenience | The only way to get it inside the container is to grant the capability or relax seccomp, and containment is the benchmark's core guarantee. Weakening the thing that makes the measurement trustworthy, in order to measure an improvement, is the worst trade available. |
| And the risk is real, not theoretical | During a leg the run proxy is reachable on the internal network. Generated code executing unsandboxed in the mind's container could POST to it — burning capped model requests and polluting the very reading it was meant to improve. (A direct probe returned ConnectionRefused, but only because the proxy exists solely during a leg: the test was inconclusive and the risk stands.) |
| The decision | The EXECUTION design is abandoned for now, per the criterion I set. A sandbox that runs untrusted output is a real product slice with its own preregistration and its own security review — not something to bolt on to reach one check. |
| The re-scope, and what it can and cannot do | E.FILES3 becomes a REVIEW round rather than an execution round: after the write, one Think that receives the file set back and is asked whether the tests match the program they test, then re-emits the set. It is exactly the shape the page lane already uses, it runs no untrusted code, and it costs at most one extra model call. It may or may not fix `pytest_passes` — a model reviewing its own output is weaker evidence than running it, and that is the honest limit of what can be measured here. |
| Kill criteria for the re-scoped slice | (1) No process is spawned and no generated file is executed — asserted by source scan. (2) At most one review round. (3) The reviewed set goes through the same all-or-nothing `plan_file_set` path. (4) A build whose review changes nothing costs one extra call and no more. (5) The receipt records whether a review ran and whether the file set changed. |
| The measurement, unchanged in kind | A graded T3 leg where `pytest_passes` flips. If it does not flip, the finding is that self-review cannot catch what running the tests would — which is worth knowing, and is an argument for the sandboxed execution slice rather than for a second review round. |

It did fix it, without executing anything. The self-review caught a test/program mismatch I had assumed only a failing test run could surface. |
