## E.FILES3 — the second leg: the score reproduces, the latency reproduces, and it is not the tokens
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Two legs, same brief, throwaway roots | Leg A: 10/10, 440.1 s, 4 requests, 4226 completion tokens, 3 files. Leg B: **10/10**, **420.1 s**, 4 requests, 3046 completion tokens, 2 files. The score reproduces and so does the wall. |
| The diagnostic that matters | Leg B generated a QUARTER FEWER tokens than leg A and finished only 20 s sooner. The wall is not proportional to generation. Against the pre-review baseline it is starker: 1426 tokens in 40 s became 3046 tokens in 420 s — roughly double the tokens for **ten times** the wall. |
| What the receipts show | 4 requests to `/v1/chat/completions`, 3 carrying usage (4016 prompt + 3046 completion). The fourth is the routing call: the log shows `routing exceeded 20s` once, so it was detached and never contributed usage. `accounting_agrees` true, nothing malformed. |
| What I can and cannot conclude | I CAN conclude the review round reliably buys the last check and reliably costs ~430 s. I CANNOT explain where those seconds go: three model calls totalling ~7000 tokens should not take seven minutes on a provider that returned 3797 tokens in 91 s to a direct probe earlier today. The most likely suspects are the review's large prompt (4016 tokens of prefill) and the detached routing call holding one of two inference permits — but that is a hypothesis, and I have been wrong twice today by stating one as a fact. |
| Why this is worth chasing rather than accepting | If ~200 s per call is fixed overhead rather than generation, it is not a cost of the review — it is a cost of every model call the mind makes, and fixing it would speed up everything. Doubling the tokens for ten times the wall is anomalous, and anomalies in a system's own accounting are the thing this line exists to find. |
| The product decision, stated with its trade | Keep the review. A build that is correct and slow is a better deliverable than one that is fast and ships failing tests, and a delegation runs in the background where the user is not watching a clock. But it is a real regression on the axis where we were furthest ahead — Hermes finishes T3 in 108 s — and it should not be presented as a free win. |
| Next, and it is a measurement not a fix | Time each model call individually rather than inferring from wall clock, and establish whether the overhead is per-call, prompt-size-driven, or permit contention. No change ships on the strength of the hypothesis. |

## E.LAT1 — where do the seconds go (PREREGISTERED, before the measurement)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The anomaly | A build with the review round takes ~430 s reproducibly. Three model calls, ~7000 tokens. A direct probe to the same model earlier today returned 3797 completion tokens in 91 s. Doubling the tokens cost ten times the wall, so the cost is not generation. |
| The two hypotheses, named before testing | (a) PROMPT SIZE: the review's prompt carries the whole file set (4016 tokens), and prefill on this provider is expensive. (b) PERMIT CONTENTION: the routing call is detached after its 20 s budget but keeps running, holding one of two inference permits while the build and review calls queue behind it. |
| The test, which isolates (a) with no code change | Two direct requests to the same model and endpoint, identical `max_tokens` and an identical instruction that fixes the output length, differing ONLY in prompt size — one short, one padded to roughly 4000 tokens. Time both. If prompt size explains the gap, the padded request is dramatically slower. |
| Kill criteria for the conclusion | (1) If the padded request is NOT materially slower, hypothesis (a) is dead and I say so rather than keeping it as a maybe. (2) Neither hypothesis may be adopted from a single pair — each condition runs at least twice, because I have twice today turned one observation into a stated property. (3) No code changes on the strength of this: it decides what to MEASURE next inside the mind, not what to fix. |
| Why it is worth doing at all rather than accepting the latency | If the overhead is per-call rather than per-token, it is not a cost of the review — it is a tax on every model call the mind makes, and the same fix would speed up chat, delegation and every loop. That is a much larger prize than one benchmark check. |

## E.LAT1 — RESULT: both hypotheses dead, and my latency claim is WITHDRAWN as confounded
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What the probes showed | Four requests, each asking the model for a SINGLE WORD. Three returned nothing after **302.2 s** — the same figure three times, which is an upstream gateway timeout, not a measurement. The one that answered took **154.3 s to produce 84 completion tokens**, about half a token per second. A confirming probe minutes later returned **HTTP 504 after 303 s** for "say ok". |
| Against the same endpoint earlier today | 3797 completion tokens in 91 s — roughly 42 tokens per second. The provider is currently something like eighty times slower and frequently timing out. |
| Therefore | Both preregistered hypotheses are dead. It is not the review's 4016-token prompt: a 78-token prompt took 154 s for 84 tokens. It is not permit contention: these probes are direct curl calls with no mind, no permits and no routing call. |
| And the claim I have to withdraw | I reported that the review round costs ~430 s against a 40 s baseline, "eleven times slower", and that it makes us "four times slower than Hermes on T3". **That comparison is confounded.** The 40 s baseline leg ran at ~05:51 during reading 6; the 420 s and 440 s review legs ran around 07:00, as the provider was degrading. I compared two arms measured hours apart through an upstream whose speed changed by an order of magnitude between them, and attributed the whole difference to my own change. |
| What survives, and what does not | SURVIVES: T3 scores **10/10, twice**, with the review round — a score is not affected by how slowly the tokens arrive. DOES NOT SURVIVE: any statement about what the review round costs in wall time. I do not currently know. |
| The near miss worth recording | I was one step from "fixing" a latency regression that may not exist — gating the review behind a condition, or chasing per-call overhead inside the mind. The only thing that stopped it was running the measurement before the fix, and the measurement's first surprise was that a one-word reply took two and a half minutes. |
| How it gets measured properly | Both arms, close together, against a provider whose speed is checked immediately before and after. Until then the latency of E.FILES3 is unknown and is written down as unknown rather than as a number I would rather have. |
| One thing this does NOT touch | Reading 6's wall times. All six of its legs ran between 05:51 and 06:26 with the provider in one state, so the within-reading comparison — Mind 35–73 s against Hermes 108–413 s — stands. |

## E.LAT2 — the receipt carries per-call latency, so "where did the seconds go" is answerable (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The gap E.LAT1 hit | I could not say where a leg's 420 s went, and had to run separate probes hours later — which produced a confounded comparison and a withdrawn claim. Meanwhile the mind ALREADY records what I needed: `InferenceCall` carries `latency_ms`, the callsite, attempts and tokens, and `spend.rs` writes both onto every `inference_call` row. The harness deletes the state directory at teardown, so every leg has been throwing that away. |
| The claim | A Mind receipt should be able to answer "how long did each model call take, and which callsite made it" without a second experiment and without a provider that has moved on. |
| The change | Before the teardown removes the state, summarise the spend rows into the receipt: per callsite, the count, the total and maximum `latency_ms`, and the outcome mix. Counts and integers only — no prompts, no replies, which is what the ledger seam was built for. |
| Why this is worth doing rather than accepting | Today's confound was only possible because a leg's timing and the provider's speed were measured hours apart. With per-call latency IN the receipt, a leg carries its own timing evidence alongside its own wall clock, and a provider that degrades between readings shows up as a fact in the row rather than as a wrong conclusion about my code. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) No prompt or reply text may reach the receipt — asserted. (2) A leg whose spend log is missing must record that distinctly, never as zero latency; the difference between "no calls" and "no log" is the same distinction the driver already had to fix once. (3) The summary must be computed BEFORE the trap deletes the state, and a leg that fails to read it must say so rather than silently omitting the field. (4) No behaviour change to the mind itself: this reads what is already written. |
| What it does not do | It does not explain today's numbers. Those legs are gone. It makes the NEXT ones self-explaining. |

## E.LAT2 — RESULT: a leg now carries its own timing, and the summariser hid its own failure first
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Outcome against the criteria set before the code | PASS on all four. The Mind receipt carries `call_latency`: per callsite, the call count, total and maximum `latency_ms`, and how many were served. Counts and integers only. Read BEFORE the trap destroys the state. The mind is unchanged — this reads what it already writes. |
| The defect the tests caught, which is the same shape as the day's others | The summariser returned an EMPTY summary for every input and said nothing was wrong. `verdict.py` has no `import json`, so `json.loads` raised `NameError` — and a bare `except Exception` around the parse swallowed it and skipped the row. A function that silently reports "no calls" for a log full of calls is worse than one that crashes. |
| The fix, and why the narrow except is not another dead guard | `json` imported at module scope, and the except narrowed to `json.JSONDecodeError`: a malformed LINE is expected and skipped, anything else is a defect and must surface. That property is observable — a case passes a non-string and asserts the failure SURFACES rather than emptying the summary — and restoring the broad except fails it by name. |
| The distinction kept, because this harness has lost it before | `None` for "the log could not be read", `{}` for "there were no calls". The driver had to fix exactly this conflation earlier today, in `spend_rows`. Conflating them again fails a named case. |
| What it changes about future readings | E.LAT1's question — where did 420 seconds go — becomes answerable from the receipt of the leg that took them, with no second experiment and no provider that has since moved on. Today's confound was only possible because a leg's timing and the provider's speed were measured hours apart. |
| Honest limit | It explains nothing about the legs already run. Those states are deleted. It makes the next ones self-explaining, which is the most that can be salvaged from a measurement I got wrong. |

## L2-B step 2a — the shadow reaches the poll loop, on four gates, default OFF (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why now | Pranab's order was: beat the competitors, then the AGI work. Reading 6 closed and measured the competitive gap, so this lane opens. L2 is Phase D — the first time the mind's own priority rule is computed on real opportunities, and the first record of what it would have chosen to do with its own time. |
| Where it stands | L2-A froze the arithmetic. L2-B step 1 built `WakeSignals`, the gate types and `attention_shadow` as pure functions wired to nothing, and a review found five defects in it, all fixed. Nothing calls it. |
| Scope of 2a, deliberately four sites out of eighteen | Mint a `CycleId` per poll wake; fill the four `TimerUnconditional` slots (Resolve, ProfileRefresh, Ics, LeaseSweep — the simplest kind, `Timer` only); build the shadow; append ONE row. Behind an environment switch, DEFAULT OFF. The remaining thirteen sites are 2b. |
| Why staged again | Every large slice this session that came through review clean was staged this way, and every one that was not produced a defect that reached a graded run. Four sites is enough to prove the wiring end to end and small enough that the kill criterion can actually be checked by reading the diff. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) With the switch OFF, the poll loop must behave EXACTLY as today — no row, no allocation-visible change, and the loop-tick rows byte-identical. (2) With it ON, the ONLY new write is the `attention_shadow` append: no memory write, no send, no model call, no timer change. (3) Exactly one shadow row per wake that had at least one due in-scope opportunity, and none for a wake with none. (4) A shadow row must never be able to change what a loop DOES — asserted by the switch being read in one place and never consulted by a gate. (5) The row carries the same `cycle_id` as that wake, and two wakes never share one. |
| What I will NOT accept as evidence | That the functions are correct — step 1 already established that and a review still found five defects in it. The evidence is a replayed poll wake: the row appears, its contents match what the gates reported, and with the switch off nothing appears at all. |
| The measurement this unlocks, and it is not in this slice | Build completeness (buildable ÷ the ledger's own due rows) and the agreement metrics between the shadow's ranking and what the timers actually did. Those need days of real wakes on a Telegram-hosted box, which is why the preregistration says the evidence is owner-gated on the prod batch. |

## L2-B step 2a — RESULT: the shadow reaches the poll loop, four gates, default off
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Outcome against the criteria set before the code | PASS on all five, each verified by a mutation that COMPILES. Workspace suite green, clippy clean. |
| What shipped | A `CycleId` per wake (`process_start_ms` + a wake counter), a fresh `WakeSignals` per wake, the four `TimerUnconditional` gates filling their own slots with their OWN verdict, and one `attention_shadow` append behind `YM_ATTENTION_SHADOW` — read in exactly one place, which is the append's condition. |
| Kill 1, default off | Asserted, and the switch accepts only `1`/`on`/`true`. The first version would have taken any value, so `YM_ATTENTION_SHADOW=off` would have ENABLED it; the mutation that restores `Some(_)` fails the test by name. |
| Kill 2, the append is the only new write | The guarded block is scanned for `profile_set`, `deliver(`, `chat(`, `within_opportunity`, `record_loop_tick` and `spawn`. Sneaking a loop-tick write into that block fails it. |
| Kill 4, a shadow row cannot change what a loop does | The switch is read once. The test counts reads APART FROM THE DEFINITION — counting the definition as a read is how the assertion failed on its first run. |
| Kill 5, one identity per wake | The counter advances, the id is process start plus wake number so a restart cannot reuse one, and the signal set is built INSIDE the wake. Hoisting it outside the loop compiles and is wrong, and the test catches exactly that — carrying a signal set across wakes would report last wake's gates as this wake's. |
| Two defects in my own tests, both self-reference | The source scans matched THEIR OWN TEXT, because `include_str!("loops.rs")` includes the test module that contains the strings being searched for. Both failed on their first run for that reason. The scan now excludes its own module. It is the same defect as a self-test whose regex matched its own explanatory comment earlier today, and I wrote the second one four hours after fixing the first. |
| What is deliberately partial | Four of eighteen sites. The row is a partial view of each wake BY CONSTRUCTION, and the read side sees that as a shortfall when it compares `buildable` against the loop ledger's own due rows. A test pins the count at four, so a fifth site arriving without its own row fails. |
| What this does not yet do | Nothing measures anything. Build completeness and the agreement metrics need days of real wakes on a Telegram-hosted box, which the preregistration already says is owner-gated. |

## THE FROZEN MODEL REACHED END OF LIFE AT 08:00Z TODAY — reading 6 is the last one, ever
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The finding, verbatim from the provider | `410 Gone — "The model 'openai/gpt-oss-120b' has reached its end of life on 2026-09-03T08:00:00Z and is no longer available."` The catalogue now lists 81 models and does not include it. |
| What that means for this line | Every E.CB2-N reading — 3, 4, 5 and 6 — ran on that model. It cannot be run again. **Reading 6 is the final reading under those conditions and can never be re-run, extended or repeated.** Any future reading needs a different model, a new profile and a new baseline, and comparisons across the model change are not valid. |
| It also explains this morning's degradation, and I was wrong about the cause | I recorded the ~430 s legs and the 302 s timeouts as "the provider having a bad minute". They were the wind-down of a model reaching end of life three hours later. The failure was not random load; it was scheduled retirement I had no visibility of. |
| And it settles a question permanently in the worst way | E.FILES3's real cost in wall time — the number I withdrew as confounded and said I would measure properly — can now NEVER be measured on the model the readings used. The honest record is: unknown, and unknowable on that model. |
| What survives, and it is most of it | Reading 6's scores stand: Mind 26/27, Hermes 25/27, six valid legs inside a 35-minute window with the model in one state. Scores do not care that the model was later retired. The harness, its symmetry fixes, the self-test and the receipt improvements all carry to whatever model comes next. |
| The lesson I did not have this morning | A frozen benchmark pins the model NAME, the archive, the checker and the containment — and cannot pin the model's EXISTENCE. A provider can retire the thing being measured mid-line, and the first warning was a 410. Any future line should record the model's availability alongside its identity, and treat "the model still exists" as a precondition checked at the start of a reading rather than assumed by the profile. |
| Immediate operational consequence | Staging's configured brain is that model. It needs repointing before its delegations can work at all. |

## E.MODEL1 — "the model still exists" becomes a precondition, not an assumption (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What today cost | The frozen model was retired at 08:00Z. The first warning was a 410, three hours after its wind-down had already been silently corrupting my measurements — I diagnosed 430 s legs and 302 s timeouts as "a provider having a bad minute", withdrew a claim built on them, and only learned the truth from an error body. |
| The gap in the design | The harness pins the model's NAME (`CB2_MODEL`), the Hermes archive by hash, the checker, the briefs, the cap and the resolved upstream addresses. It cannot pin the model's EXISTENCE, and it never checked. A profile naming a retired model looked exactly like a healthy one until a leg failed. |
| The claim | A reading should refuse to start when the model it names does not answer, and its run state should record that it DID answer, when, and how fast. |
| The change | One preflight request at the start of a run, before any leg: the model named in the profile must return a success. The run state records `model_alive_at` and the observed latency of that probe. Every later consumer already refuses a run state written for another profile or cap; this adds the same treatment for a model that has gone. |
| Why the latency of the probe belongs in the run state | Today's confound was comparing legs measured hours apart through an upstream whose speed had changed. A single number at the top of the run — "the model answered a trivial request in N ms at this time" — is the cheapest possible baseline against which a leg's own per-call latency (E.LAT2) can be read. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) A dead model must REFUSE the run, not warn — a reading that proceeds on a retired model produces voids that look like infrastructure noise, which is exactly what happened today. (2) The refusal must name the model and quote the provider's own reason, so the operator learns "end of life" rather than "it failed". (3) A healthy model must add ONE request and no more; the probe may not consume the leg budget. (4) The probe's own failure to be conclusive — a timeout rather than a clean error — must be reported as inconclusive rather than as death. |
| The unusual opportunity today gives | The refusal path is normally the hard half to test, because it needs a broken provider. Right now `openai/gpt-oss-120b` is genuinely, permanently gone and returns a real 410 with a real reason. The refusal can be verified against the actual failure it was written for, which will not be possible again. |

## E.MODEL1 — SHIPPED. All four kill criteria met; one hole found by mutation, not by reading
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Where the check lives | `cb2_profile_load` in `run/profile.sh`, in the branch that WRITES the run state — one probe per reading, not one per leg. It sits BEFORE the write for the reason the key validation is already first: a model that is gone must leave no resolved state pinned behind it, or a later corrected load silently inherits this resolution. Every later loader call reads the verdict back out of the state, so a whole reading costs exactly one extra request however many scripts source the file, and every leg reports the same answer. |
| The classifier | `model_liveness(status, body)` in `run/verdict.py` — a tested function, not an inline `case`, because its two failure directions are opposite and both costly. `gone` (404, 410, or a 400 whose body names the model) REFUSES the run. `inconclusive` (429, 5xx, 401/403, timeout, transport failure) only warns: refusing there would turn a bad minute into a cancelled reading, which is this morning's mistake inverted. |
| Kill criterion 1 — refuse, not warn | MET, and verified against the genuinely retired model before any stub existed: `profile: the model 'openai/gpt-oss-120b' is GONE — HTTP 410: {...has reached its end of life on 2026-09-03T08:00:00Z...}` / `refusing to start a reading on a model that no longer exists`, exit 1, and no `run_state.json` written. |
| Kill criterion 2 — name the model, quote the provider | MET. The provider's own words are carried through to the operator, so the message reads "end of life" and not "it failed". Mutated to a generic "the model check failed": three cases fail. |
| Kill criterion 3 — exactly one request | MET, counted by shadowing `curl` with a counting function: 1 request on the state-writing load, 0 on every load after it. Mutated to re-probe per load: `reload_makes_no_request` fails. |
| Kill criterion 4 — inconclusive is not death | MET. A 429 loads with a warning and records `model_alive: inconclusive`. Mutated so any non-alive verdict refuses: four cases fail. |
| Recorded in the run state | `model_alive`, `model_alive_at`, `model_probe_ms`. A live probe against `openai/gpt-oss-20b` measured **424 ms** — the baseline the withdrawn E.LAT1 claim never had. A declined probe (`CB2_MODEL_PROBE=0`) records `unchecked`, never `alive`. |
| **The hole mutation found and reading did not** | A mutation classifying **every** non-2xx as death **SURVIVED** the first suite — all 19 cases still passed. The suite's only inconclusive case was a transport failure (code 000), which is not `>= 400`, so nothing watched the 429/5xx direction: the harness could have started declaring the model retired every time NVIDIA had a bad minute, cancelling readings that would have been fine. Fixed by enumerating 429/500/502/503/504/401/403 and a request-defect 400 in `verdict_cases.py`. Sixteen liveness cases now run with the rest of the suite. |
| The surviving mutant I am not fixing | `200 <= code < 300` mutated to `< 299` survives. It differs only for HTTP 299, which no provider returns. Benign; padding the suite to kill it would test a value that does not occur. |
| Why the loader test stubs `curl` | Because the day the refusal could be verified against a genuinely dead model was the day it shipped. `selftest/model_cases.sh` shadows `curl` with a canned-status function, so the refusal path stays testable offline forever — 20 cases, no network, wired into `selftest.sh`. Six loader mutations all die: gone-only-warns, inconclusive-refuses, verdict-never-recorded, re-probe-per-leg, declined-probe-claims-health, refusal-drops-the-reason. |
| Scope found while testing | `meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct` and `qwen/qwen3-next-80b-a3b-instruct` also return 410 on the same upstream. This is a retirement sweep, not one model, which makes a liveness precondition worth more than the incident alone suggested. |
| Exactness | `scratch/rederive.sh` still proves `cb2n` = `cb2` + `scratch/cb2n_patch.py` byte-for-byte; the E.MODEL1 edits are recorded there rather than hand-applied. |
| Still with Pranab | Which model the line continues on. `openai/gpt-oss-20b` is alive on the same NIM upstream and preserves the containment story; keeping the 120b via Groq does not. A new model means a new profile and a new baseline — comparisons across the change are not valid. |

## E.MQ5 v3 — the sealed suite KILLS the candidate router, and says exactly why
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Provenance | Commitment `1e4c97bd…` was committed at fe1a050 **before any candidate router existed**; the candidate and its single production/eval seam were frozen at fbeae7f; the thirty rows were disclosed at d8cca43 and re-hashed to the same commitment inside the test. The result below could not have been fitted to the rows. |
| Result | **FAILED all three gates.** recall **5/10** (gate ≥9), abstain **18/20** (gate 20), wrong_claim **2** (gate 0). Identical on two consecutive runs against the owned local `qwen3.8:27b-q4_K_M` — a stable measurement, not sampling noise. This is the **fourth** sealed kill of this router. |
| The five it caught | `real-money`, `self-restart`, `privacy-lanes`, `pack-choice`, `self-edit`. |
| The five it MISSED | `tool-predictions` ("do you write down what you expect will happen?"), `offline-cognition` ("are you doing any background reflection?"), `tamper-evidence` ("will your recent-activity view still display it as trustworthy?"), `tool-learning` ("competent with an unfamiliar command just by reading its manual?"), `ran-vs-worked` ("the difference between an operation returning and the outcome actually happening"). |
| The two it FALSE-FIRED on | v3-25 "Which expertise pack includes Rust ownership?" → `pack-choice`. v3-26 "Could you edit the builder configuration in this file?" → `self-edit`. Both are questions about the WORLD, not about the mind's own capabilities. |
| **The diagnosis, and both error directions say the same thing** | The router matches capability **vocabulary**, not the question's **subject**. Every kind it caught is one whose own words appear literally in the question — "trades / actual funds", "cycle your own service", "personal-only memory", "knowledge bundle", "rewrite the configuration". Every kind it missed is phrased in ordinary English with none of the system's vocabulary. And the only two negatives it fired on are the only two negatives carrying a claim kind's literal vocabulary — "expertise pack", "edit the … configuration". A keyword detector wearing a router's interface. |
| Why the null majority earned its keep | Twenty of thirty rows expect no claim. A positives-only suite would have scored this candidate 5/10 and read as "needs better recall"; the negatives are what turned it into a diagnosis, because the false fires and the misses are the same defect seen from opposite sides. |
| What I am NOT doing | Not tuning the router against these rows. They are disclosed and therefore burned for evaluation; anything fitted to them measures nothing. A fifth attempt needs a new sealed suite, committed before the next candidate exists. |
| Change made to the test | Per-row output (`EMQ5_V3_ROW … verdict=hit\|MISSED\|MISROUTED\|abstained\|FALSE-FIRE`). The counts alone said it failed but not where, which wastes the one thing a disclosure buys. The gates are untouched. |

## Correction: the live mind DID have the check. Nothing ran it — which is a different, worse bug
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What I claimed one row ago | "the live mind still does not [check that a configured model exists] — only the benchmark does, and that is the next thing worth building." |
| Why that is wrong | **E.CFG1 already built it.** `ym why roles verify` asks each distinct provider whether it serves the model each route names, and the code comment beside it says, in as many words, that it is "the one that would have caught a live role pointing at a model its provider does not carry". Run on staging just now it prints all three routes and their verdicts, and `render_role_plan` even closes with: *"A route naming a model its provider does not serve looks configured here and in every other report; only the verified read can tell you otherwise."* |
| So what actually failed | Not the instrument. **Nothing ever runs it.** `z-ai/glm-5.2` is absent from NVIDIA's 81-model catalogue, so the verified read would have said NOT SERVED on the first day — thirteen days ago. The check existed, was correct, was documented, and was never invoked. |
| Why this is the worse bug | A missing check is a gap you can find by reading the code. A check nobody runs looks *exactly like* a check that passes: every other report says "configured", the operator sees green, and the defect is invisible until a role mysteriously does not work. I had written the instrument and then failed to build the thing that makes an instrument matter — a reader. |
| Building a second checker would have been the wrong fix | Which is what I was about to do, and would have shipped as a duplicate of E.CFG1 with a different name. ## E.CFG2 — a check nobody runs is not a check (PREREGISTERED, before any code)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The claim | A configured route whose provider does not serve its model should announce itself without anyone thinking to ask. |
| The change | The mind runs the E.CFG1 verified read itself — once at startup after the pools are built, and on a slow recurring cadence — and turns a NOT-SERVED route into a durable, visible signal rather than a line in a report nobody opened. It reuses `role_plan` + `verify_models`; **no second checker is written.** |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) A route naming an unserved model must produce a signal that survives the process and is visible without running a command — a log line alone repeats exactly the failure being fixed. (2) A provider that cannot be REACHED must never be reported as "model missing": unreachable is inconclusive, and calling it death is the E.MODEL1 mistake inverted. (3) It must not block startup, delay the first turn, or take part in cognition. (4) It must not repeat the same finding on every cadence — a signal that fires forever is noise, and noise is how the next real one gets missed. (5) Cost is bounded to one catalogue fetch per DISTINCT base URL, not one per route. |
| The honest risk | The failure being fixed is "nobody read the output". A durable signal nobody reads either is the same bug wearing a different coat, so criterion 1 is the one that actually matters and the one to judge this by. |

## E.CFG2 — SHIPPED. The check now runs itself, and the end-to-end test found the flaw a scan would have missed
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What was built | `run_config_check` in the process loop runner calls E.CFG1's **existing** `role_plan` + `verify_models` — no second checker — and hands the results to `ConversationEngine::announce_config_checks`, which writes one durable `config_check` row per route and queues an operator notice for each defect. |
| Kill criterion 1 (the one that matters) — durable AND visible | MET, and tested **end to end** against a real `DecisionLog` and a real notice queue rather than by source scan: three routes in, three rows on the ledger, exactly one notice queued, and the notice names the variable and the dead model. A scan proving the code "says the right words" is how E.PAGE1 shipped as a no-op behind ten green tests, so the load-bearing half is not tested that way. |
| Kill criterion 2 — unreachable is not missing | MET. Only `not_served` is a defect; `served`, `unreachable` and `not_applicable` are recorded and never announced. This is E.MODEL1's lesson inverted: there, calling a bad minute "death" would cancel a good reading; here it would send an operator hunting a config bug that does not exist — and the notice is the only part of this feature that works, so it must not cry wolf. |
| Kill criterion 3 — takes no part in cognition | MET. `fetch_model_catalogue` is blocking ureq with a 20 s timeout **per provider**, so it runs inside `spawn_blocking`; on the runner's thread a slow provider would freeze every loop behind it. The gate's result feeds nothing but its own clock, asserted by scanning for `if`/`match` on the call. |
| Kill criterion 4 — must not repeat every cadence | MET by construction: the notice queue keys on kind + text digest + **UTC day**, so a defect that persists re-announces once a day rather than once every six hours (noise) or once ever (silence). A configuration that is still wrong tomorrow should still be asking. |
| Kill criterion 5 — bounded cost | MET, and free: `verify_models` already caches one catalogue fetch per distinct provider/base-URL pair. Asserted by requiring exactly one `fetch_model_catalogue` mention — a second call site is a second cache. |
| **What the end-to-end test caught that a scan could not** | The operator-facing decisions feed projects a **fixed subset of fields and drops `object_id`**. The row therefore named the dead model but not the variable to edit — correct-looking on the struct, useless in the surface a human reads. Fixed by leading `outcome` with the variable. I only found it because the test read the row back out of the feed instead of asserting on what was put in. |
| Cadence | Six hours, `YM_CONFIG_CHECK_SECS` to override. The clock starts at **zero, not the boot stamp**, so the first wake checks — a defect present at startup is the case that actually happened, and a six-hour wait would have missed it. Mutating it to boot-stamped fails the test. |
| Mutation results | Seven mutations, all die: announce-everything, unreachable-counts-as-defect, nothing-recorded, row-drops-the-variable, fetch-on-the-runner-thread, gate-steers-the-runner, clock-boot-stamped. |
| The risk I wrote down first, restated honestly | The failure being fixed is "nobody read the output". A durable row nobody reads is the same bug in a different coat, which is why the notice — not the row — is the load-bearing half, and why the row was made self-sufficient once the feed turned out to drop a field. Whether an operator actually meets the notice is not yet witnessed; that is the next evidence, not a claim. |

## A preregistered freeze guard caught E.CFG2, and refusing to dodge it made the guard stronger
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What happened | `the_runner_is_frozen_as_preregistered` failed with *"no model call from the runner itself"*. It banned the **substring** `inference` anywhere in the runner, and `run_config_check` calls `mind_inference::role_plan` / `verify_models`. |
| Why the failure was a false positive in substance | Reading a provider's model **catalogue** is a plain `GET /models`. It lists names; it infers nothing, spends no tokens and calls no model. The rule was right; its mechanism could not tell a catalogue read from an inference. |
| The tempting fix, and why it was refused | Re-export the two functions under a name without the string `inference` in it, and the scan goes quiet. That satisfies the *string* while leaving the *rule* unenforced — and a guard you have learned to step around protects nothing afterwards. Dodging a tripwire is worse than never having set it, because it leaves the reassurance behind. |
| What was done instead | The rule is stated properly: an **allowlist** of the exact `mind_inference::` paths the runner may touch (`role_plan`, `verify_models`, `fetch_model_catalogue`, `ModelCheck` — each with a one-line justification), plus a ban on the things that actually perform inference (`InferencePool`, `LLMBackend`). Any new reach into that crate now has to be added deliberately and argued for. |
| The guard is stronger than before, not weaker | Mutation-checked three ways, all caught: constructing an `InferencePool`, holding an `LLMBackend`, and reaching a NEW `mind_inference` path (`local_backend_from_env`). The old blanket ban caught the third only incidentally and could not have distinguished it from a catalogue read; the allowlist catches it *because* it is unlisted. |
| The general point | A preregistered guard firing is evidence, and the first question is whether the rule or the mechanism is wrong — never how to make the message go away. This one had a correct rule and a blunt mechanism, so the mechanism was sharpened in the open and recorded here rather than quietly edited. |

| Deploy | Built on the staging checkout at `748c7a9` (sources touched first, so cargo could not judge a stale artifact current — the 2026-08-31 incident), binary verified to CONTAIN the new code before the swap (`config_check` ×30, the notice text ×1, `attention_shadow` still ×5), sha `ac6aed27a00ee0d6` matched after install. |
| Healthy path | Three `config_check` rows, all `served`, **zero** notices. The check runs and correctly finds nothing to say. |
| The defect path, witnessed properly | A healthy reading proves nothing about the half that matters, so `YM_ROLE_RESEARCH` was set back to the genuinely retired `nim:z-ai/glm-5.2` on staging and the service restarted. Result: durable row `YM_ROLE_RESEARCH = nim:z-ai/glm-5.2 absent from a catalogue of 81`, a real queued row in `mind_notices`, and the operator log line. Restored to the live model immediately after; exactly **one** `not_served` row exists in the whole ledger, the injected one. |
| A false alarm I raised on myself | The `notices` verb returned empty and I took it as evidence the notice had been silently dropped — then found `recipes.db` 0 bytes and root-owned and nearly wrote up a staging environment defect. Both wrong: the recipe store opens `YM_DB` (`mind.db`), that stray file is unused, and `notices` is simply not a command. The notice was in `mind_notices` the whole time. Checking the store directly instead of trusting the absence of output is what settled it. |
| A real defect the witness DID find | The operator-facing line shipped with a run of eighteen spaces mid-sentence (`That route⎵⎵…⎵will fail`) — a Rust string continuation that did not collapse as intended. Harmless to a parser, and exactly the sloppiness that makes a human stop reading the channel this whole feature depends on. Fixed, and guarded: the test now asserts the line contains no run of whitespace, and a re-introduced double space fails it. |
| What is now true, stated exactly | The check runs on its own, a defect produces a durable row AND a queued notice on a real box, and the row names the variable to edit in the surface a human reads. What is still NOT witnessed: an operator actually meeting the notice. That remains the open evidence, and the reason criterion 1 was written as the one to judge this by. |

## E.L2B-R — the attention shadow has no reader. I shipped the same bug I spent today diagnosing (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| How it was found | Sweeping for other rows with E.CFG2's defect — identity living only in a field the operator-facing feed drops. Six event kinds lose fields. Five are fine: `inference_call` and the loop ledger have dedicated renderers (`ym why spend`, `ym why loops`) that show their ids, and `config_check` was fixed this morning. The sixth is **`attention_shadow`, which has no renderer at all.** |
| The finding, stated plainly | There are 22 `ym why` verbs. None reads the attention shadow. Its only operator surface is `web_recent_decisions`, whose projection keeps nine fields and drops `object_id`, `candidates` and `policy` — which are the cycle identity, the buildable loops, and the ranked scores. That is the row's entire content. It is accumulating on staging right now and **cannot be read by anyone.** |
| Why this is worth its own entry rather than a quiet fix | It is the SAME defect as E.CFG2, committed by me, in my own slice, on the same day I wrote "a check nobody runs is indistinguishable from a check that passes" into this ledger. E.G1c's rule was "before calling a shadow live, COUNT its events on the box it is supposed to fire on". I counted them — 29 rows, verified field by field. Counting is not reading. The rule was satisfied and the shadow is still mute, so the rule was too weak: an instrument needs a reader, not a row count. |
| The claim | The attention shadow's rows can be read, and the preregistered L2-B measurement can be computed from them. |
| The change | `ym why attention` — per cycle: the identity, which loops were buildable, which slots were filled, the ranked candidates with their scores, what the policy would have chosen, and the **shortfall** between the shadow's `buildable` set and the loop ledger's own due rows for that same cycle id. Read-only, like every other `ym why`. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) It must show WHICH loops, not counts — a reader that says "buildable: 3" without naming them is the feed's defect with extra steps. (2) It must compute the buildable-vs-due shortfall against the loop ledger for the SAME cycle id; that number is the entire reason the shadow was allowed to ship partial (4 of 18 gates wired), and without it the shadow still has no instrument. (3) With no rows it must say the shadow is off or has not fired — never render an empty table, which reads as "nothing was due". (4) It must decide nothing and write nothing. (5) It must be verified against the REAL rows on staging, not synthetic ones — they exist now, and a reader tested only on fixtures is how the last three defects shipped. |
| The generalisation I am adding to the doctrine | "Preregister the row" is not enough. A shadow is not live when it writes; it is live when someone can read what it wrote. Every future instrument slice names its reader in the same prereg, or it is not done. |

## E.L2B-R AMENDMENT — kill criterion 2 fired before a line of the reader was written
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What fired | Criterion 2 required the reader to compute the shadow's buildable-vs-due shortfall against the loop ledger **for the same cycle id**. Checked against the box first, per criterion 5: **zero of 2308 `loop_tick` rows on staging carry a cycle id.** The pairing is not merely unimplemented in the reader — it is impossible from the data. |
| The code already knew | `LOOP_LEDGER_V6` is a constant with **no writer**; its own doc says so, records that review 6 wrongly claimed the row was written and review 7 caught it by grepping for a caller and finding none, and states the rule: *"a v5 row is never paired with a v6 row, because only a v6 row knows which wake it belongs to."* Staging's rows declare `loop-ledger-v5`; the shadow's declare `loop-ledger-v6`. Two eras that by construction cannot be joined. |
| The uncomfortable part | L2-B step 2a — which I shipped and deployed this morning — was allowed to ship wired to only 4 of 18 gates **on the grounds that** "the read side compares `buildable` against the loop ledger's own due rows and sees the shortfall". That justification was never true of the data. The shadow has been writing rows all day whose central measurement nothing could compute. |
| Consequence for E.L2B-R | Its criterion 2 cannot be met until loop rows carry a wake identity. Rather than quietly widen E.L2B-R or weaken the criterion, the prerequisite gets its own preregistration below. Pairing by TIMESTAMP is explicitly refused: the design note says a wake identity exists precisely because "two loops that acted a millisecond apart are indistinguishable from two loops that acted on different wakes". |

## E.L2B-2b — the loop tick learns which wake it belongs to (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The claim | A loop row and the shadow row of the same wake can be paired by identity. |
| The change | A `loop_tick` written under the process runner carries `cycle:<process_start_ms>:<wake_no>` and declares `LOOP_LEDGER_V6`. The label rides in `context_fingerprint` — NOT `policy`, because `parse_tick` parses policy into typed entries and a stray one is either a parse break or a silently malformed row. `context_fingerprint` is documented as the opaque fingerprint of the decision context, and a wake *is* that context. |
| The scoping tension, named before coding rather than discovered mid-way | Only the process runner has a wake identity. The eight proactive loops in `telegram.rs` (L1d's sixteen speakers) run in a different host with no wake counter, so **their rows stay v5**. A mixed log is therefore the expected steady state, not a migration failure. |
| What that forces the reader to be honest about | The shortfall report must say how many due rows in a window carried a wake id and could be paired, and how many could not because they came from a v5 host. A report that silently omitted the unpairable rows would understate the denominator — which is the exact censoring pattern E.D2 and E.G1c already cost us twice. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code | (1) A v6 row whose cycle label does not parse is MALFORMED and never read as v5 — the code's own stated rule. (2) A v5 row is never paired with a v6 row; the version wall must keep the eras apart while letting both aggregate into counts. (3) The label must not enter `policy`. (4) Every loop site within one wake must carry the SAME cycle as that wake's shadow row — a row whose cycle disagrees with the shadow's is worse than a row with none, because it manufactures a false pairing. (5) Demonstrated on REAL staging rows: at least one wake where a shadow row and its loop rows pair by identity. |
| Kill criterion 4 is the one to watch | It is the only one that can fail silently. A site that takes its cycle from a second `now_ms()` rather than the wake's own would produce plausible, wrong pairings — and every count downstream would still look reasonable. |

## E.L2B-2b — the loop tick carries its wake. Code complete; criterion 5 still owed
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The shape that decides criterion 4 | Every loop row in `loops.rs` is now written through ONE helper, `wake_tick(conv, cycle, tick)`. Eighteen call sites route through it; exactly one direct `conv.record_loop_tick(` remains and it is the helper's own body, asserted by test. "Every row in a wake carries that wake's cycle" is therefore a property of the plumbing rather than a rule eighteen sites must remember — which matters because that criterion is the only one that can fail SILENTLY: a site stamping from a second clock yields a plausible, wrong pairing while every downstream count still looks reasonable. Designed out, not tested for. |
| Where the label rides | `context_fingerprint`, never `policy`. Mutating it into `policy` fails not only the new tests but two existing L1d tests, because `parse_tick` parses policy into typed entries — the prereg predicted this and the mutation confirmed it. |
| The version is derived, not declared | `to_event` emits `LOOP_LEDGER_V6` when a cycle is present and v5 when it is not, so a row cannot claim to know its wake while carrying none. One fact, one source. |
| Kill criterion 1 — malformed, never downgraded | MET. A row claiming v6 with no label, or with an unparseable one, counts as **malformed** and never as a v5 row. Mutating the parser to accept it fails. |
| Kill criterion 2 — the eras stay apart | MET, and a conflation was corrected on the way. The old L2-A test required a v6 row to be **superseded** by the reader; that mixed up "a v5 row is never PAIRED with a v6 row" (the real rule, written on the constant) with "a v6 row is never AGGREGATED beside a v5 row" (which nothing required). v6 is v5 plus a label: both count, and the label alone decides what can pair. Excluding a whole host from the ledger to enforce a pairing rule would have been a larger error than the one it prevented. |
| Kill criterion 3 — not in policy | MET, above. |
| Kill criterion 4 — one wake, one identity | MET structurally, plus a guard: exactly one `CycleId::new` in the wake body, and all seven gates receive it. Minting a second identity in the same wake fails the test. |
| Kill criterion 5 — real staging rows | **NOT YET MET.** The rows on the box are still v5; nothing is proved until a deployed binary writes a wake and a shadow row pairs with its loop rows by identity. Recorded as owed, not as done. |
| Mutations | Four, all die: helper forgets to stamp, second identity minted in a wake, v6-without-a-label read as fine, label moved into policy. Workspace 1736/1736. |

## E.L2B-2b WITNESSED — and the shortfall exists for the first time, after I computed it wrong twice
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Deploy | Built on the staging checkout at `480345e` (sources touched first), `loop-ledger-v6` verified present in the binary before the swap, service restarted, active. |
| Kill criterion 5 — MET | Real rows pair by identity on a real box. Six wakes carry v6 loop rows; all six also carry a shadow row; the pairing is exact. Historical rows stay v5 and are reported as unpairable rather than dropped. |
| **The measurement, for the first time** | `cycle:…:1` — shadow buildable `[ics, lease-sweep, resolve]`; due that wake `[ask held:no-presence, dmn held:idle-gate, ics acted, lease-sweep acted, resolve acted]`. **UNSEEN = [ask, dmn].** One wake in six carried a due loop the shadow never considered. That is the shortfall L2-B step 2a's partial wiring was justified by, and until this deploy nothing could compute it. |
| **I computed it wrong twice first, and both wrong answers said "0"** | (1) First I used only wakes that HAVE a shadow row as the denominator — the exact censoring pattern this slice's own prereg warned about, and one that hides the strongest case: a wake where only unwired loops act writes no shadow row at all. (2) Then, with the denominator fixed, I compared `buildable` against **acted** rows. A **held** row is still a DUE row — `ask` was due and blocked on presence, `dmn` due and blocked by the idle gate — and the shadow claims to rank everything due. Both mistakes reported a clean zero, i.e. "the shadow sees everything", which is false. |
| Why that matters more than the number | The shortfall is easy to compute in a way that FLATTERS the instrument, and both flattering forms look like reasonable code. I only caught it because the loop counts showed `ask` and `dmn` writing v6 rows that appeared in no wake's comparison. The number was not wrong because of a bug; it was wrong because of a definition, twice. |
| What E.L2B-R's reader must therefore do | Denominator = every wake that wrote a loop row, not every wake with a shadow row. Due = acted ∪ held, never acted alone. Both are now written down before the reader exists, which is the only reason they will not be rediscovered the hard way. |
| Honest limit on today's number | Six wakes on an idle staging box is not a measurement of anything but the plumbing. The 1-in-6 is a demonstration that the instrument reads, not a finding about attention. |

## INCIDENT — I broke staging's decision chain, and it exposes a real single-writer assumption
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Symptom | `ym why attention` returned *"DECISION ANALYTICS UNAVAILABLE — the decision log failed integrity after 22086 valid event(s)"*. Not just my new reader: **every** verified report on staging — `loops`, `spend`, `calibration`, `evaluators` — reads through `read_all_verified` and all of them were dead. |
| Diagnosis | The chain breaks at line 22087, `2026-09-03T08:35:32Z`. That line's hash chains from **line 22078, skipping 8 lines** — the signature of a concurrent writer, not a tampered event. Two processes were appending, each tracking its own head. |
| Cause, and it was mine | At ~08:35 I ran `./mind-core ym why roles verify` directly on the box to read the role plan. `mind-core` has no read-only mode: it booted a **second full daemon**, which failed to bind :8077/:8088/:8090 (the "Address already in use" lines I saw and dismissed as harmless) but still started its own loop runner and appended `loop_tick` and `attention_shadow` rows to the same file as the live service. I noticed the bind errors, judged them cosmetic, and moved on. |
| The finding that outlives my mistake | The hash chain's integrity assumes **one writer per file, and nothing enforces it.** `DecisionLog::record` takes an in-process lock (Codex's P.4f review) which is exactly the wrong scope: it serialises threads and does nothing about a second process. Any hand-run of the binary on a box — the most ordinary operator act there is, and one I nearly performed on PRODUCTION while looking for the source tree — permanently and irreversibly disables every integrity-checked report on that box. |
| Why irreversible | The chain is a hash of (previous chain, event bytes). Once two writers interleave, no later writer can repair the prefix; the only recovery is to rotate the file and start a new chain from genesis, abandoning verification of everything before it. |
| What I did | Rotated staging's log (the corrupt file is retained as evidence, not deleted) so the reports work again. Recorded here rather than quietly fixed, because the near-miss on production is the more important half. |
| Preregistered follow-up (E.OBS2) | A second writer must be REFUSED, not tolerated: an OS-level advisory lock on the decision log taken for the process's life, so the second `mind-core` on a box fails loudly at startup instead of silently corrupting the record. Kill criteria: (1) two processes on one log — the second must refuse to write and say why; (2) a stale lock from a killed process must not brick the survivor; (3) a single writer's behaviour and performance must be unchanged; (4) demonstrated by actually running two processes, not by a unit test with a mocked lock. |
| The lesson, stated for the next session | `mind-core` has exactly two modes, daemon and REPL — there is no "just run one command" invocation. To read a `ym` surface on a box, go through the ctl endpoint (`POST 127.0.0.1:8077/cli`, raw line as body); never execute the binary. And when a command prints "Address already in use", that is not cosmetic — it means a second instance of the whole mind just started. |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |

Summary: 2 wakes, 1 carried a due loop the shadow never considered; gates missed — ask 1, dmn 1. |

Guarding the one string had taught me nothing; the habit was the problem. The guard now travels with the habit: it checks every rendered line of this report, allows padded label columns (`scores     :` is deliberate alignment) and catches prose runs. Mutation confirmed. |

## E.OBS2 — the second writer is refused, not tolerated
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The mechanism | `DecisionLog` takes an exclusive `flock` on a sidecar `<log>.lock` the first time it writes, held for the process's life beside the per-file chain state. A process that cannot take it **records nothing** and says so once. Cognition is unaffected — the recorder already had a "write nothing, never fail the caller" path, so a locked-out writer is an extension of an existing state rather than a new failure mode. |
| Why an flock and not a pid file | The kernel releases an flock when the holder dies for ANY reason, `kill -9` included, so a crashed writer cannot leave a stale claim that bricks its successor. A pid file needs a liveness check and that check is itself racy. This is the rare case where the operating system already has the answer. |
| Why a sidecar file | The log is opened and closed on every append, and on some platforms closing any descriptor for a file drops that process's locks on it. The lock file is held open and never otherwise touched. |
| Kill criterion 1 — the second process refuses and says why | MET, with two REAL processes: the test re-executes its own binary, the child writes five events, and the log stays at three. The child prints `CHILD_ATTEMPTED` so a test that silently failed to spawn cannot pass as a success. |
| Kill criterion 2 — a dead holder does not brick the survivor | MET, with a real kill: the child writes (proving it holds the claim), is killed mid-hold, and the successor writes normally. |
| Kill criterion 3 — one writer unchanged | MET: fifty rows land and verify; a second HANDLE in the same process still writes, since that is not a second writer and the engine opens several. |
| Kill criterion 4 — real processes, not a mocked lock | MET, and demonstrated by mutation: replacing `try_lock()` with an always-succeeding stub **fails** the test. That mutation is precisely what a unit test with a mocked lock would have been, and it would have passed against the broken code. |
| Mutations | Three, all die: claim taken but not enforced; lock always succeeds (the mocked-lock case); refusal stops saying why. |
| What this does not do | It does not repair a chain already broken, and nothing can — the corruption is a hash prefix. It prevents the next one. Staging's chain was rotated; production's was verified intact (1333 events, read-only, without executing the binary). |
| Honest limit | The guard binds only processes that go through `DecisionLog`. Anything appending to the file by other means is still unguarded, and no lock can defend a file from `cat >>`. |

## E.OBS2 WITNESSED — the incident was reproduced deliberately and the guard held
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The witness | On staging I started a **second `mind-core` by hand** — the exact act that broke the chain this morning. It printed `REFUSING TO WRITE /var/lib/yantrik-mind/mind.db.decisions.jsonl: another process holds this decision log`, wrote nothing, and the chain verified intact afterwards (83 events). The row count moved 82 → 83 during the window, which is the LIVE service's own writing, not the intruder's. |
| The dependency I added and then removed | I added `fs4` for the advisory lock. The compiler then warned that its trait import was unused — because Rust's std now provides `File::try_lock` inherently, and the inherent method wins. Removing the crate entirely leaves all four two-process tests passing, so the lock was std's the whole time. **No new third-party dependency ships.** Worth noticing rather than leaving: a dependency that is never called is one more thing to audit, update and trust, in exchange for nothing. |
| Third time in one day for the same defect | The refusal message ALSO shipped with a run of spaces mid-sentence. Same as E.CFG2's notice this morning and E.L2B-R's report this afternoon. Each time I fixed the one string and put a guard beside it, and each time the next string I wrote had it again — because the habit was the defect and I was guarding symptoms. |
| The guard that should have existed after the first time | A crate-wide scan: no string literal in `mind-observability` may carry a run of spaces mid-sentence. An aligned label column (`scores     :`, a run followed by a colon) is deliberate and allowed; everything else is prose a person reads. It found 24 offenders on its first run, all repaired. Reintroducing a double space anywhere in the crate now fails it — which no per-string guard would have caught. |
| A bug in the guard itself, caught by running it | It indexed `bytes[i - 2]` from `i = 1` and panicked on underflow. Found because the test ran and crashed, not because the code looked right. |
| Standing rule, now that it is proven | To read a `ym` surface on a box: `POST` the raw command line to `127.0.0.1:8077/cli` with the console token. Never execute `mind-core` on a box running the service. The guard makes that mistake survivable; it does not make it correct — the second instance still boots an entire mind, binds nothing, and does other work. |

## Sweep closed — no other row kind is mute, and two of my own static scans said otherwise
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The open worry | After E.CFG2 I told Codex that other `DecisionEvent` kinds might share its defect — content living only in fields the operator feed drops — and that I had not swept for them. This closes it. |
| Two static scans, two false findings | The first regex matched only `DecisionEvent::new(` and missed `DecisionEvent::span(`, reporting 16 kinds as invisible. The second caught both constructors and STILL reported `cognitive_run` as mute — a claim I could refute by reading forty lines of `cognitive.rs`, which sets goal, goal_id, chosen, confidence and verdict. Neither scan was trustworthy, and both produced dramatic-looking findings. |
| What settled it | The empirical check, on **22,451 real rows** from staging (live log plus the retained corrupt one), pushed through the projection verbatim as `web_recent_decisions` writes it. **No kind is mute.** Every kind that actually occurs carries content into the feed. One single row — an `operator_restart` — carried nothing but its kind. |
| The nuance that keeps this honest | "Not mute" is a FLOOR, not a bar. `attention_shadow` passes this audit — it sets actor, chosen, verdict and outcome — and was still unreadable in substance, because *which* loops and *what* scores lived in `candidates` and `policy`, which the feed drops. E.L2B-R was needed anyway. So the sweep answers "is anything showing literally nothing", not "is everything intelligible", and I am not claiming the second. |
| Why record a null result at all | Because I raised the alarm publicly and a worry left hanging becomes folklore. And because the way I nearly got it wrong is the more useful half: a static scan over a large codebase produced a confident, specific, wrong answer twice, and only checking one case against the source — then all of them against real data — caught it. |
| Method note for next time | For "does this instrument actually show anything", read real rows through the real projection. The source can only tell you what a writer intended; the log tells you what a reader gets. |

## E.G2 READ — 9,889 world-shadow rows nobody had opened, and what they say
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why now | The mute-row audit showed `world_shadow` is the LARGEST population in the log — 9,889 rows — and nothing has ever read them. Under today's doctrine (a shadow is live when someone can read what it wrote) that is an instrument holding 37 hours of unexamined evidence. |
| Finding 1 — the world model is reachable and almost always uninformative | Across every consult, split by sample and never pooled (the code forbids pooling): **`headless-cadence`** (251 rows, 37.4 h) — unknown **70.9%**, stale 25.5%, known **3.6%**. **`knock-receptivity`** (9,638 rows, 15.0 h) — unknown **58.8%**, stale 39.7%, known **1.5%**. E.G1 made the world model reachable; this is the first measurement of what it actually knows when reached, and the answer is that it knows the user's presence in one or two consults per hundred. |
| Finding 2 — the pairing machinery is perfect and measures nothing | Every `knock_disposition` joins its shadow row: **9,638 / 9,638, 100%, zero orphans.** The offline join E.G2 was built for works exactly as designed. And it is vacuous: **all 9,638 dispositions are `before-gate` with `chosen = no_packets`.** The receptivity gate has never run on this box, so `receptive` is null in every row, and the agreement between the world model's verdict and the legacy gate's verdict — the entire purpose of the paired sample — is **uncomputable here.** |
| This is E.G1c one level deeper | E.G1c found the shadow never fired because it lived inside a gate the canary could never open, and moved it. It now fires 9,638 times. But the DECISION it is paired against still never happens: the knock evaluation finds the candidate first and exits at `no_packets` every time, because a canary with no work has nothing to say. The instrument was moved to where it can run; the thing it measures was not. |
| Stated plainly, because it constrains the roadmap | The E.G2 agreement measurement **cannot be produced on staging at all**, and no amount of waiting changes that — 15 hours at ~10.7 evaluations a minute produced zero gate evaluations. It needs a box with real prepared packets, i.e. the Telegram host, which is Pranab's call. Until then `headless-cadence` is the only live signal, and it only says the ingestion → gate → verdict pipeline is alive, not that anything agrees with anything. |
| What is NOT claimed | That the world model is broken. "Unknown" for user presence on a headless canary with no phone channel and no household traffic is the correct answer, not a defect. What is measured is that a decision depending on this model would today be deciding on `unknown` roughly 98% of the time — which is a fact about the evidence available, and an argument about what may be allowed to consult it. |

## E.G2-R — the world shadow gets a reader (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The claim | The world shadow's evidence can be read in the product, and the report cannot be mistaken for a measurement it did not make. |
| The change | `ym why world` — per sample: rows, window, and the known/stale/unknown split; the disposition breakdown of the paired evaluations; the join health; and an explicit statement of whether the agreement measurement is computable at all. Read-only, like every other `ym why`. |
| Kill criteria, set before the code and taken from getting this wrong by hand first | (1) The two samples are NEVER pooled — the code's own rule, because one measures agreement with a decision and the other only that the pipeline is alive. (2) It must print the disposition breakdown beside the known/stale/unknown split: "known 1.5%" without "the gate never ran, 9,638 × no_packets" is a number that invites exactly the wrong conclusion. (3) It must report join health — dispositions with and without a matching shadow row — because a silently broken join would make any agreement number meaningless while looking fine. (4) When no evaluation reached the gate it must SAY the agreement is uncomputable, never print an empty agreement table or a zero, which would read as "no disagreement". (5) Verified on the real 9,889 staging rows, not fixtures. |
| Criterion 4 is the one that matters | Every other failure here is visible. A zero standing where "uncomputable" belongs looks like a healthy result and is the single most likely way this report misleads someone — including me, in three months, having forgotten. |
| Why a reader at all, given the finding is already recorded | Because the finding was produced by an ad-hoc script on my machine, which nobody else can run and which will not exist next week. An instrument whose measurement lives in a scratch file is the same defect this whole day has been about. |

## E.G2-R — SHIPPED, and my own crate-wide guard caught my fourth repeat of the same defect
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |

The crate-wide guard added in E.OBS2 caught it, naming the file and line. Three earlier occurrences each got a fix and a local guard and taught me nothing; the first guard written at the right scope caught the next instance immediately, in code I wrote hours later. |

| Field | Value |

It asserts something security-relevant and it failed once; an unexplained flake in that assertion is worth more attention than I could give it here without stalling the lane. ## The whitespace guard, third attempt — and why the first two were worse than nothing
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What the staging deploy showed | `ym why world` rendered with a run of spaces mid-sentence **and** the crate-wide guard reported green. The guard had passed over a defect I could find with `grep`. |
| Attempt 1 — per-line scan | It looked at one line at a time, requiring an opening AND closing quote on that line. A literal opened on one line and continued on the next has a single quote on each, so the scan skipped it entirely — and that continued-literal form is EXACTLY the construct that produces the defect. A guard blind to the shape of its own bug is worse than none, because it is believed. |
| Attempt 2 — a hand-rolled Rust lexer in a test | Tracking string state across lines desynchronised on quote characters and flagged a dozen innocent format strings. It also carried a logic bug — it compared the character *before the run* against the *previous* character, which is itself a space by then, so the condition could never fire. That version passed over the known defect too. |
| Attempt 3 — deliberately dumb, and it works | No parsing: a run of **three or more** spaces, on a non-comment line, directly after a letter, digit, comma or full stop, and not followed by a colon (which is deliberate column alignment). One finding on the whole crate — the real defect — and no false positives. |
| The stated limit, rather than a hidden one | A run of exactly TWO spaces is not caught. That is a deliberate threshold to keep false positives at zero, verified by mutation: a two-space run survives, a three-space run is caught. Every real defect today had a run of many. |
| Two mutations survived the first pass and both taught something | (1) The two-space case, above — now a documented limit rather than an unknown. (2) The `before == 0` branch was UNTESTED: the deploy printed *"0 evaluation(s) exited before the receptivity gate"* over zero evaluations, which implies evaluations happened and none passed — a different and more damning claim than "nothing ran". Separate wording added, and the mutation that made the branch unreachable now fails. |
| The lesson I keep re-learning in different clothes | Three scanners today produced confident wrong answers: two static audits of event kinds, and two versions of this guard. Every one was corrected either by reading the source directly or by running against real data. Clever static analysis of one's own codebase is the least reliable instrument in this repository, and I reach for it first every time. |

## Why the knock stopped, and why the world model knows presence 1.5% of the time — one answer, two notions of "present"
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The diagnosis, from the loop ledger rather than the source | Knock evaluation runs only when `idle_ok = present && !quiet_now && idle_stretch`, and when `present` is false the knock records NO row at all — which is exactly what the current log shows (zero knock rows, while `ask` sits at `held:no-presence`). `has_presence()` is `telegram_reachable() \|\| console_present()`, and staging has no Telegram. So the 9,638 evaluations ran while **someone had a cockpit open**, and they stopped at 02:59:56Z when it closed. Not a code defect, and not my deploys — the loop ledger answered it in one query, which is what it was built for. |
| **The finding that matters more** | There are TWO independent notions of presence, and they do not talk to each other. **Delivery presence** — `console_present()`, a cockpit polling within 90 s — gates the knock. **World-model presence** — `user/presence` — is asserted in exactly one place: `handle_turn_as`, when the PRIMARY sends a conversational turn. A cockpit poll never reaches the world model. |
| So the 1.5% is explained, not mysterious | During the entire 15-hour window a cockpit was demonstrably open — that is *why* 9,638 evaluations ran at all — and the world model still answered `unknown` 58.8% and `stale` 39.7% about whether the user was present. It was not wrong. It had never been told. Its only input is someone talking, and after that the assertion decays to stale and then to unknown. |
| Deliberate, not accidental | The code says so: *"presence means the primary's presence, by construction, never by inference"*. A polling browser tab is weaker evidence than a sentence — it could be a window left open on a machine nobody is at. The conservatism is a choice, and reading it as a bug would be the wrong correction. |
| The question this raises, which is NOT mine to answer alone | Should a live cockpit be a typed, weaker observation into the world model — `console-polling` rather than `active` — or should the model keep knowing only what it was told? Feeding a new signal changes what the model BELIEVES, and this model is being groomed toward decision authority. Widening its inputs quietly, to make a measurement look better, is precisely the move that would make every later number untrustworthy. Left for Pranab and Codex; nothing changed. |
| What I did not do | Ingest console presence. It would have lifted the "known" rate immediately and made E.G2's numbers prettier, and that is the reason to be suspicious of it. |

## The redaction flake — one hypothesis tested and REFUTED, search narrowed, cause still unknown
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The hypothesis | The assertion reads the RAW file text, which includes the SHA-256 chain value on every line. A 64-character hex string contains the substring `4471` with probability ~0.00098, and over six lines that is ~0.59% per run — the right order of magnitude for one failure in eleven runs (P ≈ 6.3%). It looked like a clean explanation and it was the kind I like: the test, not the code, at fault. |
| Refuted, by measurement and then by thinking | **400 direct runs of the compiled test binary: zero failures.** At the predicted rate ~2.4 were expected. And the reason is decisive rather than statistical: the chain is a deterministic hash over FIXED content from a fresh file, so every run produces the SAME chain values. A chance collision would therefore be permanent, not intermittent. The hypothesis was not merely unsupported; it was structurally impossible, and I should have seen that before measuring. |
| What is now ruled out | Chance collision in the chain hash (above). Path collision (`scratch::unique` carries pid, nanos and an atomic sequence). Env interference (no `set_var` in `mind-evals`). Detector nondeterminism (`first_sensitive` is a pure ASCII scan). A lock-out from E.OBS2 (that yields an EMPTY file and a different panic). The test's own deterministic content path (400 clean runs). |
| What that leaves | Something that differs ONLY under a full workspace run — where many test binaries execute concurrently — and not under 400 single-test runs, 6 crate runs, or 3 concurrent crate runs. I do not have it. |
| Recorded as open, deliberately | It asserts that a card number never reaches a log. One failure in eleven is exactly the rate at which a real defect is dismissed as noise, and I have now spent two rounds on it without an answer. Better to leave a precise account of what was excluded than a comfortable story. |
| The part worth keeping | I built an explanation that fit the observed frequency, and it was wrong for a reason visible without any experiment at all — determinism. Measuring first was still right, because it settled it in one command; but the order should have been "is this even possible" before "how often would it happen". |

That is the solo baseline, and it will not be available on demand later: it exists because of an outage, not a decision. |

| The counting rule, fixed BEFORE counting | A **defect** is anything wrong that required a corrective change or blocked a push. Each is assigned to the EARLIEST filter that caught it: **(A)** my own targeted tests or a mutation, before push; **(B)** the full workspace suite, before push; **(C)** deploying to staging and looking at the result; **(D)** still open. A defect is counted once, at the earliest filter, never at the one I noticed it in. |
| What I may conclude, and what I may not | I may report the DISTRIBUTION — how many defects each filter caught, and how many reached staging. I may NOT claim what Codex would have caught: that is unfalsifiable and self-serving in either direction. The paired arrangement inserts one additional filter between (B) and (C); whether it would have caught any given item is exactly what a future paired measurement decides, not this one. |
| The number that matters | **(C) + (D)** — defects that survived every filter I own. Under the paired arrangement those are the ones peer review exists to catch, so that count is what a later paired period should be compared against. |
| Kill criteria | (1) The rule above is fixed now and not adjusted after seeing the totals. (2) Every defect counted must point at a commit or a ledger row, so the count is auditable rather than remembered. (3) Defects I found in OTHER people's code, or pre-existing ones I merely discovered (the dead role, the chain hole, the knock stoppage), are NOT solo-cost defects and are excluded — counting them would inflate the baseline with work that had nothing to do with review. (4) If the honest count is embarrassing, it is reported unchanged. |
