## E.PROC1 — the procedure-learning gap is WRONGLY STATED, and one banking path loses the creation date
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The gap, verbatim | procedure learning, rung TESTED, IMPLEMENTED-UNWITNESSED: *"no evidence a banked procedure was ever reused to a better outcome"*. |
| The evidence already existed, unread, on the family's box | Ten banked skills on PRODUCTION, with **40 recorded runs and 20 successes**: `web-monitor` 11 runs / 5, `csv-sum` 10 / 7, `headroom-check` 6 / 2, `test-market` 6 / 6, `deal-tracker-page` 4 / 0, `deploycheck.greet` 2 / 0, `github-monitor` 1 / 0, and three never run. Read-only, without executing the binary. |
| So the gap is half wrong and should be split | Reuse is **evidenced**: six distinct procedures were reused, 40 times, at a 50% success rate. What is absent is the **comparison** — nothing measures whether reuse produced a BETTER outcome than not reusing, because nothing records the counterfactual. "No evidence it was ever reused" and "no evidence reuse helped" are different claims, and only the second is true. |
| A second finding, same shape as `LOOP_LEDGER_V6` | The `skill_outcomes` table (`accepted \| succeeded \| failed \| rejected`, with a dedup key) is **empty on both boxes and has NO writer anywhere in the codebase**. Forty runs were counted in `mind_skills.runs` while the richer outcome ledger that would support the comparison above never received a row. A table with no writer is the third instance today of infrastructure that exists and does nothing. |
| A third finding — a real defect, correlated perfectly | **All six `capability`-lang skills on production have `created_ms = 0`** and display as **1970-01-01**; the three `python`/`md` ones carry real timestamps. Cause: `build_capability` in `lib.rs` constructs `Skill { … created_ms: 0 }` while every other banking path (`import_skill.rs`, `pack.rs`, `skills.rs`) sets `now`. It is a lone omission, not a convention, and `created_ms` is exposed to the cockpit through `surface.rs`, so this is visible in an operator surface. |
| Why the defect matters beyond cosmetics | The procedure module's own ordering key is *"proven beats plausible, and a longer record breaks ties"*. A creation date of zero makes every capability skill appear fifty-six years old — the OLDEST records in the store — which is exactly backwards for anything that breaks ties by age or reasons about staleness. |
| What I will do | Fix the omission (kill criteria below), and correct the manifest's gap wording to distinguish reuse from benefit. I will NOT backfill the six zero timestamps on production: inventing creation dates for records whose real dates are unrecoverable would put fiction in the store to make a column look tidy. They stay zero and the ledger says why. |

Ruled out: chance collision in the chain hash (the chain is deterministic over fixed content, so a collision would be permanent), path collision, env interference, detector nondeterminism, an E.OBS2 lock-out. **Cause unknown.** |

Passes 3/3 in isolation. A file deletion failing is a Windows sharing violation: something still holds the handle when the test tries to remove it. Environmental, and clearly so — unlike flake 1. |
| The shared shape, which is the useful part | Neither reproduces at crate scope. Both appear only when many test binaries run CONCURRENTLY, and both involve temp-file operations. The rule found two real defects today that nothing else would have (the runner freeze guard, and a whitespace defect the crate-wide guard caught). ## E.PROC2 — nothing ever judges a skill, so certification is permanently inert (found, not fixed)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The question this answers | E.PROC1 left "reuse happened but did reuse HELP?" unmeasurable and named `skill_outcomes` as an orphan. That was the symptom. This is the cause. |
| The production evidence | Ten banked skills, **40 runs**, and `graded = 0` and `judged_ok = 0` for **every one of them**. Not one execution in the store has ever been judged. |
| The code, counted precisely rather than grepped | `SkillOutcome::judged(ok)` — the constructor that produces a graded outcome — has **ZERO production call sites**. `from_exit` has exactly one (`skills.rs:705`, the sandboxed code path). Three sites record `ungraded()` deliberately: `delegate.rs` ×2 and `pack.rs`, with the comment *"anything useful is unjudged, so it stays out of the success denominator"*. Counted with an inline-test-module cut after two crude greps misled me earlier today. |
| The consequence, which is larger than a missing number | `Skill::reliability()` is `Reliability::new(graded, judged_ok)` — for every skill that is `(0, 0)`. So `skill_reliable(s, min_runs, min_rate)` is FALSE for any `min_runs >= 1`: **pack certification cannot certify anything, ever, on the real box.** And `rank_score()` derives from the same empty record, so the procedure module's stated ordering — *"proven beats plausible, and a longer record breaks ties"* — has no "proven" to work with. Every banked procedure ranks on a prior. |
| This is NOT a bug, and saying so matters | The design is deliberately honest: `task_success: Option<bool>`, *"None when nothing competent has judged it"*, and a run nobody judged is correctly excluded from the denominator rather than counted as a win. The sec6 certification test even asserts that ten unassessed runs must NOT certify. Every piece behaves as designed. **What was never built is the judge**, and `SkillOutcome::judged()` is the seam left waiting for it — the fourth thing today that exists with no caller, after `LOOP_LEDGER_V6`, `ym why roles verify`, and `skill_outcomes`. |
| What I am NOT doing | Building the judge. "What competently judges whether a skill achieved its task" is a design decision with real consequences — an LLM grader introduces a model call and a bias per run; the user grading introduces friction; an exit code is what the sandboxed path already uses and does not generalise to capabilities. Choosing one to make a certification gate light up would be the same move as ingesting console presence to lift a percentage. It belongs to Pranab and Codex, preregistered, with the grading basis decided before any number moves. |
| The pattern, now four for four | Every gap I have chased today ended at working machinery whose input never arrives: a check nobody ran, a shadow nobody read, a constant nobody wrote, a judge nobody built. The code is not the weak part of this system. |

## E.CAL1 — the first calibration reading: well calibrated everywhere EXCEPT certainty
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Provenance, stated first because it constrains everything | Computed over the **chain-verified prefix** of the archived log — 22,086 events whose hash chain I re-derived from genesis and which verify line by line. Nothing past the break I caused is used. The 15 pairs that lived after it are unreadable by the product forever, which is a cost of that incident I had not previously quantified. |
| The dataset | **96 tool predictions, 96 observations, 96 joined pairs, zero orphans.** Each prediction states a confidence before the call; each observation carries a Brier score and a typed outcome. |
| Headline | **Mean Brier 0.0520** — against 0.25 for a system that always says 50%. Observed success **87.5%**, mean stated confidence **83.0%**: slightly UNDER-confident overall. |
| **The finding that matters** | Calibration by stated confidence: said 50% → **91.7%** right (n=12); said 70% → 87.5% (n=8); said 80% → 88.2% (n=17); said 90% → 94.4% (n=36); **said 100% → 73.9% right (n=23).** Every bucket is under-confident except the last, which is badly over-confident. **Certainty is the one place the mind's self-assessment breaks**, and it is not a small miss: one in four "certain" predictions was wrong. |
| A second, smaller finding | The 50% bucket is the low-N default prior (`empirical prior n=0`), and those calls succeed 91.7% of the time. The default is far more pessimistic than reality. |
| Scope, so the number is not read as more than it is | `semantic_success` is a MECHANICAL classifier — `Ok` ⇒ true, `Empty` ⇒ false — not a judge. So this measures *"will this tool return usable output"*, **not** *"will this help the task"*. The tool mix is narrow (recall 33, discover_tools 26 of 96). Buckets are 8–36. This is a real reading of a narrow question, not a general statement about the mind's judgement. |
| The contrast with E.PROC2 worth noticing | Tool prediction HAS a grader and therefore has calibration evidence; skills have none and therefore have nothing. The difference between these two subsystems is not sophistication — it is whether somebody wired a cheap, mechanical outcome classifier. That is an argument about what the skill judge could be: not necessarily an LLM. |
| What I am NOT doing | Capping stated confidence at 0.95, which is the obvious response to a 100%-bucket that is right 74% of the time. n=23 on a narrow tool mix is thin evidence for changing what the system predicts, and a behaviour change to fix a number I just measured needs its own preregistration. Proposed, not done. |

## E.CAL1 CORRECTED — two errors in my own published measurement, both caught by an external model
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| How this was caught | Pranab suggested putting the open design questions to other models. `gpt-5.6-sol`, red-teaming an unrelated proposal, did arithmetic on the calibration table I had published and reported that it implies a Brier of ~0.145, not the 0.052 I had stated. It was right. I checked, and found **two** independent errors. |
| **Error 1 — I invented a confidence bucket that does not exist** | My table reported *"said 100% → 73.9% right (n=23)"* and I built the headline finding on it: *"certainty is the one place the self-assessment breaks."* **The mind never states 100%. Zero predictions in 96 have confidence 1.0.** Confidence is continuous — 33 distinct values, median 0.90 — and my `round(c*10)/10` bucketing silently promoted every 0.95–0.99 into a "100%" bin. The finding was an artefact of my own rounding. |
| **Error 2 — I put two different questions in one row** | The stored `brier` is computed against **execution success**, where `Ok` OR `Empty` counts as 1.0 — *"did the tool run without breaking"*. My table was computed against **semantic success**, where only `Ok` counts — *"did it return something usable"*. The code keeps these apart deliberately (the three-success design; the lesson text even says *"ran fine, found nothing — execution held, semantics did not"*). I reported one and tabulated the other, as though they were the same measurement. **Not a product defect — a conflation in my analysis.** |
| Corrected numbers | Brier against EXECUTION success: **0.0520**. Brier against SEMANTIC success: **0.1413**. Baseline for always-saying-50% is 0.25. Overall stated confidence 83.0%, actual semantic success 87.5%. |
| Corrected calibration, exact confidences in fixed bands | `0.50` default prior (n=12) → **91.7%**; `0.51–0.79` mean 70% (n=14) → **85.7%**; `0.80–0.89` mean 84% (n=21) → **95.2%**; `0.90–0.94` mean 93% (n=26) → **92.3%**; `0.95–0.99` mean 96% (n=23) → **73.9%**. |
| **The finding survives, and is sharper than the wrong version** | The mind predicts *whether a tool will run* very well (0.0520) and *whether it will return anything useful* much less well (0.1413) — and the two diverge most exactly where it is most confident. The top band states 96% and is right 74% of the time. That is a real over-confidence, correctly located in the 0.95–0.99 band rather than at a non-existent certainty. |
| What I should have done | Reconciled the stored metric against a recomputation from its own inputs before publishing either, and never binned a continuous variable by rounding without printing the raw values. Both are one command. I did neither, and published a headline finding that a rounding rule had manufactured. |
| The method point, which is the durable part | Every guard I wrote today was aimed at the CODE. This error was in my ANALYSIS, where I had no guard at all — and no amount of mutation testing would have caught it, because the code was right and the arithmetic about it was wrong. A model with no stake in my conclusion found it in one pass. That is an argument for putting measurements in front of an adversarial reader before they reach a ledger, not only code in front of a reviewer. |

## E.PROC3 — the skill-judge question, put to two independent models, and what the debate got wrong
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why | Pranab: *"you can discuss among different models and see what is the best option."* I ran a two-round adversarial debate against `openai:gpt-5.6-sol` and `deepseek-chat` — different families, deliberately, because same-family models correlate with my own judgement and defeat the purpose. Cost **$0.03 and 334 s**. I argued FOR the mechanical judge so the proposal I favoured would be attacked rather than agreed with. |
| **It caught a published error of mine within one round** | Red-teaming the proposal, `gpt-5.6-sol` did arithmetic on E.CAL1's table and reported that it implies Brier ≈ 0.145, not the 0.052 I had published. It was right, and there were two errors — a confidence bucket manufactured by my own rounding, and a headline computed against a different success notion than the table beside it. Corrected at 6184b89. **No guard I wrote today could have caught this: the code was right and my arithmetic about it was wrong.** |
| The unanimous conclusion | Do NOT populate `task_success` from `Ok/Empty`. It measures output production, stores it as task achievement, and `Reliability::new(graded, judged_ok)` discards `TaskBasis` — so every basis is laundered into one integer before certification sees it. Record the mechanical signal as its own field; make reliability basis-aware FIRST; reserve certification for task-specific postconditions or sampled verification. |
| What I contributed that neither model had | I checked what `skill_reliable` actually gates. It has two production consumers, both in the pack subsystem: drafting a skill INTO a pack, and evaluating a pack's declared invariant. **It does not gate execution anywhere.** So the risk of a bad judge is not "unsafe skills start running" — they already run, 40 times, uncertified. It is that the system starts PACKAGING them and EXPORTING claims. A pack asserting `skill_reliable(x, 4, 0.5)` leaves this machine and outlives the box that produced the number. Less dangerous per execution; far less recoverable. |
| **And the debate's own conclusion is wrong, which I found by checking its premise** | All three of us — both models and me — said "fix the READER; `Reliability` discards `basis`". I went to check. **`basis` is never persisted at all.** The word appears nowhere in the persistence layer; `mind_skills` has no basis column; `record_skill_outcome` writes only `runs`, `executor_ok`, `graded`, `judged_ok`. `TaskBasis` lives on the in-memory `SkillOutcome` and dies at the SQL boundary. The reader cannot be made basis-aware because the writer never gave it a basis. |
| Which makes the orphan table legible | `skill_outcomes` — `dedup_key`, `outcome` (`accepted \| succeeded \| failed \| rejected`), `created_at`, no writer, empty on both boxes — is evidently the per-outcome ledger that was meant to retain exactly this provenance. The design intended per-outcome rows AND aggregate counters; only the aggregates were ever wired. |
| Where that leaves the decision, sharper than it started | Not *"should we wire a cheap judge?"* but: **the evidence path needs a write side before any judge is worth choosing** — persist per-outcome rows with their basis (the orphan table is the intended home), then certification can require a basis rather than a count. That is a schema change, not a one-line reader fix, and it is still a design decision I am not taking alone. |
| The methodological finding, which I think outlives all of this | Everything I built today guarded the CODE — mutation tests, crate-wide scans, source guards. This error was in my ANALYSIS, and I had no guard there at all. An adversarial reader with no stake in my conclusion found it in one pass for three cents. The unguarded surface in this project is not the code. |

## E.AUDIT1 — I re-verified every number I published today. Two of four held; two did not
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why | An external model found two errors in E.CAL1 within one round. If one published measurement was wrong, the others deserved the same check, and it is not honest to correct only the one somebody caught. |
| **E.PROC1 — CONFIRMED exactly** | Production re-read: 10 skills, 40 runs, 20 successes, 0 graded, 0 judged_ok. Identical to what was published. Read from SQLite, so no chain provenance was involved. |
| **E.L2B-2b — HOLDS** | Published "1 of 6 wakes carried a due loop the shadow never considered", labelled at the time as a plumbing demonstration rather than a finding. The larger sample now reads **28 of 181 — the same ~15%**. The snapshot was correct and correctly caveated. |
| **E.G2 — TWO PROBLEMS** | (1) **Provenance inconsistency.** E.CAL1 restricted itself to the chain-verified prefix; E.G2, computed from the SAME file on the SAME day, read every row including the **367 past the break**. Applying one standard to one measurement and not the other is exactly the sloppiness I have been auditing the code for. Under the verified-only standard the figures move: headless-cadence known **3.6% → 2.4%**, knock-receptivity known **1.5% → 1.4%**, unknown 58.8% → 61.0%. Small, but they moved, and the published ones were computed the looser way. (2) **A claim that is wrong as stated.** I wrote that the paired sample "has been dead since 02:59:56Z" and that Phase G now needs "a box with prepared packets AND a live knock path". It is not dead. It **resumed at 12:00Z** — 506 evaluations in that hour, 46 in the next — because console presence returned. The knock path is presence-GATED, not broken. |
| Not an observer effect, and I checked rather than assumed | My first suspicion was that my own `/cli` probing had created the presence. It had not: `console_present()` reads `last_view_ms`, which only the VIEW path (`cli_dispatch_view`) sets, while `/cli` goes through `cli_dispatch` as a turn. Someone opened a cockpit. My diagnostics did not manufacture the sample. |
| **E.G2's core finding survives and is stronger** | The resumed evaluations are **567 more, every one `no_packets` / `before-gate`**. Across **10,205** evaluations the receptivity gate has still never once been reached. The agreement measurement remains uncomputable, and now on a much larger sample spanning two separate presence periods. What was wrong was the diagnosis of WHY the sample stopped, not the finding about what it shows. |
| A third error, in the audit script itself | My re-verification printed "1 UNVERIFIED" because it counted lines READ before the break rather than lines in the file. The archive is 22,453 lines with 22,086 verified — **367 unverified, not 1**. Caught by comparing against a `wc -l` I had run hours earlier. An audit tool that miscounts is not better than no audit; it is worse, because it certifies. |
| Score, stated plainly | Four data-based measurements published today. **Two exactly right, one wrong in two ways, one right in its core and wrong in its explanation** — plus one arithmetic error in the audit itself. That is a worse hit rate than I would have guessed before checking, and it is the strongest possible argument that the analysis layer needs the same adversarial treatment the code has been getting all day. |

## E.CAL2 — the calibration report gains the semantic family (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What I went looking for, and did NOT find | Having conflated execution and semantic success myself, I checked whether `render_calibration` ships the same ambiguity. **It does not.** It labels its family `"tool execution"` explicitly, and it bands by `floor(c*10)` rather than rounding — so it has neither of my errors. The product was more careful than I was, and I am recording that rather than manufacturing a defect to justify a change. |
| The real gap | It reports calibration against EXECUTION only (`ok \| empty ⇒ 1.0`). The rows already carry `semantic_success` (`Ok ⇒ true`, `Empty ⇒ false`), and today's measurement shows the two diverge sharply: Brier **0.0520 vs 0.1413**, with the top confidence band **22 points over-confident** semantically while looking healthy on execution. An operator reading one number cannot see that. |
| The claim | Reporting both families side by side makes the divergence visible, and makes the confusion I fell into impossible for a reader of the report. |
| The change | One more `append_calibration_bands` call for a `"tool semantics"` family, built from `semantic_success` on the same joined pairs. Existing machinery, existing data, no new event and no behaviour change. |
| Kill criteria, before the code | (1) The existing `tool execution` numbers must be **byte-identical** — a report that silently redefined its own headline while adding a family would be worse than the gap. (2) The semantic family counts a row only where `semantic_success` is present; a row that cannot be classified must not enter its denominator, or the two families would have different populations and be quietly incomparable. (3) Each family must state what counts as success in the report itself, so neither can be read as the other. (4) Verified against the real pairs: execution ≈ 0.052, semantic ≈ 0.141. (5) With no semantically-classifiable rows, the semantic family is absent rather than shown as zero. |
| Why this is not the change I declined three times today | It adds no inference, widens no input, and moves no gate. It reports a second number the system already computes, beside the first. The three I declined all made a number LOOK better; this one makes a worse number visible. |

## E.CAL2 SHIPPED — the calibration report shows both families, and a guard was satisfied rather than edited
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What shipped | `ym why calibration` now reports a **tool semantics** family beside **tool execution**, from the `semantic_success` already on the rows, with a legend stating each family's success criterion. |
| Kill criterion 1 — the existing family unchanged | MET. The execution numbers are computed exactly as before and its label is untouched. Mutating the code so the execution family loses rows to the semantic one fails two tests. |
| Kill criterion 2 — no shared denominator | MET. A row enters the semantic family only where `semantic_success` is present. Mutating it to `.or(Some(true))` — counting unclassifiable rows as successes — fails two tests. |
| Kill criterion 3 — each family states its success criterion | MET, via a legend line rather than the labels. |
| Kill criterion 5 — absent, not zero | MET. With nothing classifiable the semantic family is not rendered; a `0.00` would read as "it never worked", which is a different claim from "nobody looked". |
| **A preregistered guard fired, and I did NOT edit it** | My first version folded the success criterion into the labels — `"tool execution [ran without breaking]"` — which broke `calibration_keeps_tool_execution_and_world_forecasts_separate`, an existing test matching the exact label. The rule it defends (families kept separate, per-band numbers correct) was still satisfied; only its string had moved. The tempting fix was to update the expected string. **That is precisely the move I refused this morning when the runner freeze guard fired**, and refusing it again produced a better design: the labels stay a stable contract and the explanation lives in a legend, which satisfies my own criterion 3 without touching anyone's test. The guard was satisfied, not accommodated. |
| Why this change and not the three I declined | It adds no inference, widens no input and moves no gate. It surfaces a number the system already computes and which is WORSE than the one on display — 0.1413 against 0.0520. A change that makes the reported picture less flattering does not need the same suspicion as one that improves it. |

## A tooling hazard caught in the working tree: `cargo add`/`cargo remove` pruned the workspace manifest
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What happened | Adding and then removing the `fs4` dependency during E.OBS2 left the WORKSPACE `Cargo.toml` with **nine workspace dependency declarations silently deleted** — `tracing-subscriber`, `yantrik-os`, `yantrik-chat`, `mind-evals`, `mind-perception`, `mind-cortex`, `mind-instincts`, `mind-proactive`, `mind-evolution`, `mind-identity`. I authored none of that. `cargo add`/`cargo remove` rewrote the manifest and pruned entries it judged unreferenced. |
| Why it went unnoticed for hours | The workspace still built and the full suite still passed — those declarations are not currently inherited by any member — so nothing failed. A destructive edit that breaks nothing today is exactly the kind that ships. |
| Caught by | `git status` during a routine state check, not by any test. The change was never committed: the last commit touching `Cargo.toml` predates this session. Reverted; 22 workspace declarations restored. |
| **The part that actually mattered** | My "workspace 1760/1760" results were obtained with the PRUNED manifest in the tree, while the COMMITTED state is HEAD's fuller manifest plus my code. That combination had never been suite-verified. Re-running against the real committed state rather than letting a green number stand for a tree that no longer exists. |
| The rule | Treat `cargo add` and `cargo remove` as manifest REWRITERS, not line editors — check `git diff Cargo.toml` after either, and never let a suite result stand for a tree that has since changed underneath it. Both are the same discipline I applied to the 227-line manifest reformat earlier: check that the diff costs what the change should have cost. |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Deploy | Staging brought from `46876ac` to `3bdfe2e`, catching up two code slices (E.PROC1's creation timestamps, E.CAL2's semantic family) and the docs between. Sources touched before building; both new strings verified in the binary before the swap; service active; chain intact at 4,197 events. |
| The report's answer on staging | *"No graded predictions yet — calibration appears once a tool or forecast has an observed outcome."* Correct: the post-rotation log holds no `tool_predicted` rows, because a headless canary with no conversational turns makes no tool predictions. |

Verifying wiring the tests already cover, at the price of contaminating the evidence, is a bad trade. |
| What is therefore claimed, and what is not | CLAIMED: the code is deployed, the strings are in the running binary, the verb responds, and the logic is covered by four tests with three dead mutations. NOT CLAIMED: that the semantic family has rendered real numbers on a box. That waits for real traffic, and it should be real. |

## E.D1 — Phase D's first reading: the attention policy has decided ONE contest in 283 wakes
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The question Phase D asks | *"The first time the mind's own priority rule is computed on real opportunities, and the first record of what it would have chosen to do with its own time."* I built the shadow and its reader today but only ever measured COVERAGE (the buildable-vs-due shortfall). This is the first look at the CHOICES. |
| Method | 283 `attention_shadow` rows from the chain-verified prefix of staging's current log (4,553 verified events). Verified prefix only — the standard E.CAL1 used and E.G2 originally did not. |
| **What it would have chosen** | `lease-sweep` **275 times (97.2%)**, `resolve` 8 times (2.8%). Nothing else, ever. |
| **Why that is not a preference** | **276 of 283 wakes had exactly ONE candidate above the floor.** There was nothing to arbitrate. The arbiter's output equals its input in 97.5% of wakes. |
| **The seven contested wakes, in full** | Six of them are `cycle:…:1` — **the first tick after a restart**, the only moment when resolve, ics and lease-sweep are all simultaneously due. Every one carries `resolve:540, ics:540, lease-sweep:360`: **resolve and ics TIE at 540**, and resolve wins on tie-break order, not on score. The seventh (`…:721`) is `resolve:270, lease-sweep:182` — a genuine score-decided win. |
| **So the finding, stated exactly** | **`attention-policy-v1` has decided exactly ONE contest on its own arithmetic in 283 wakes.** Six of the seven contests were 540–540 ties resolved by ordering. And the contests exist at all only because of RESTARTS — which today were artifacts of my own fifteen deploys. On a box left alone, the policy would have had nothing to decide. |
| Two degeneracies now measured rather than assumed | The code already documents one: `abstained_empty` is unreachable because the floor is `score >= 1` while the minimum possible score is 131 — confirmed here, **0 abstentions in 283 rows**. This adds a second: the RANKING is degenerate too, because the two loops most likely to be due together score identically. One is a documented property of the floor; the other is a property of the score table nobody had looked at. |
| What this does NOT say | That the policy is wrong. It has barely been asked a question. `lease-sweep` genuinely is the only thing due on an idle canary, and answering "lease-sweep" is correct. The finding is that **the mechanism does not yet bind**, which is exactly what a shadow is for discovering before it is given authority — and it is a much stronger reason to keep it shadowed than any argument from caution. |
| What would make it bind | A box with contested attention: real packets, real presence, several loops due at once for reasons other than a restart. That is the same condition E.G2 needs, and it is the same box — the Telegram host. Two separate Phase measurements are now blocked on one piece of infrastructure, which is worth knowing before either is designed further. |

## E.F4 — Phase F read: the lifecycle ledger is sound, and five goals were lost out of it
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The unread evidence | `mind_horizon_lifecycle` on staging holds **33 receipt-chained events across 14 distinct horizon goals**, and nothing had read them. Production holds **zero** — the long-horizon machinery has never run for the family. |
| What is sound, and it is most of it | **Zero broken receipt links in 33 events**: every receipt's `previous_receipt_sha256` points at its predecessor. The full event vocabulary is exercised — `scheduled` 12, `wake_started` 8, `completed` 5, `expired` 4, `failed` 1, and the replan trio `awaiting_replan` → `replan_started` → `replanned` once each, which is E.F2's witness. Terminal states: **5 completed, 4 expired.** One failure carries a real reason (`segment_contract_failed`). |
| **The defect: five goals left the queue without a terminal receipt** | Five goals — `1a05e810c65`, `1a05e8134e9`, `1a05e818cd0`, `1a05e81ae5b`, `1a05e81dd6e` — were scheduled within one minute on 09-01 19:45–19:46. Each has exactly ONE lifecycle event (`scheduled`), each last recorded `next_queue_status: pending`, and **`mind_horizon_jobs` now holds zero rows.** Their queue entries are gone and no terminal receipt was ever written. Nothing will sweep them, because there is nothing left to sweep. **Five of fourteen goals — 36% — simply stopped existing.** |
| Why this is a durability violation and not a limbo by design | E.F2 and E.F3 exist precisely so that every horizon goal reaches ONE terminal receipt — E.F3's own rule is *"terminal state only from the VERIFIED chain; nothing appends after expiry"*. Four goals expired correctly under that sweep, so the expiry path works. These five were not expired, not failed, not completed, and are no longer in the queue that would expire them. |
| What I am NOT claiming | A cause. All five were scheduled inside one minute, which suggests a single batch and a single event that removed them — a restart, a migration, or a queue write that dropped rows. The journal no longer retains 09-01, and I will not guess between those. The receipt chain is intact, so this is **not** corruption: the events simply stop. |
| The long horizon IS exercised, by expiry rather than by work | Spans from first to terminal event: min 0 s, median 904 s (~15 min), **max 87,302 s — 24.25 hours**. The maxima are the expiries hitting their budget. So a goal has lived a full day; none has WORKED for one. Every plan in the checkpoint table is the same single step (`"Execute one delayed, audited read-only recipe segment"`) at `plan_revision 0`, so multi-step planning across a long horizon remains unexercised. |
| A second, smaller finding | The `mind_horizon_checkpoints` table disagrees with the lifecycle: `1a05df5c263` reads `status: active` there while the lifecycle records it `failed` (`segment_contract_failed`) and later `expired`. The lifecycle is the authority and the checkpoint is a stale snapshot — worth knowing before anyone reads the checkpoint table as state. |

## E.F4 CORRECTED — the five goals were CANCELLED, and the real defect is narrower and sharper
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What I published an hour ago | *"Five of fourteen goals simply stopped existing"*, called it a durability violation, and sent it to Codex marked urgent. **Overstated.** Nothing was lost. |
| What I found by continuing instead of filing the dramatic version | `HorizonControlAction::Cancel` in `mind-recipes/src/store.rs` deletes the job row AND the checkpoint row, writes a hash-chained receipt to `mind_horizon_controls`, and **never calls `append_horizon_lifecycle`**. Confirmed against the box: `mind_horizon_controls` holds exactly five `cancel` rows for exactly those five goal_ids, timestamps 1788291985615–1788291987567 — about half a second apart each, a scripted batch cancel. |
| The corrected finding | The five goals were **cancelled by an operator action**, which is a legitimate terminal state, and every cancellation **is** durably recorded with a receipt. The queue did not lose them and the durability guarantee was not violated. |
| **The actual defect, which is real but different** | Cancellation is terminal in the QUEUE and invisible in the LIFECYCLE LEDGER. `mind_horizon_lifecycle` never receives a `cancelled` event, so a reader of the ledger E.F3 established as *the authority on terminal state* cannot distinguish a cancelled goal from one that vanished. |
| **I am the proof that this misleads** | I read the lifecycle, saw `scheduled` with no terminal event, saw the queue empty, and concluded five goals had been lost — then wrote it into this ledger and sent it to a colleague as urgent. The data was complete and uncorrupted the whole time. **A ledger that permits a false and alarming conclusion from correct data is the defect**, and it cost a wrong entry and a wrong alarm before it cost anything else. |
| The fix, preregistered rather than taken | Append a `cancelled` lifecycle event in the Cancel arm, inside the same transaction as the control receipt, with the same once-per-goal uniqueness treatment `expired` already has (`mind_horizon_lifecycle_expired_once`). That is receipt semantics in Codex's reviewed E.F2/E.F3 lane, so it is offered rather than done. |
| What stands unchanged | 33 events, 14 goals, zero broken receipt links; 5 completed, 4 expired; the replan trio once each as E.F2's witness; production holds zero horizon rows; `mind_horizon_checkpoints` is a stale snapshot that disagrees with the lifecycle; and the long horizon is exercised by expiry rather than by work. |
| Second corrected finding today, and the difference between them | The first (E.CAL1) was caught by an external model with no stake in my conclusion. This one I caught myself, by continuing to investigate a finding I had already published and already found satisfying. The lesson is not "be more careful" — it is that **a finding which flatters the finder's diligence deserves the same suspicion as one that flatters their code.** "I discovered a durability violation" was a more attractive conclusion than "somebody cancelled five goals", and I reached for it. |

## E.F4 CORRECTED AGAIN — there is no defect. The ledger split is deliberate and documented
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The third pass | Having corrected "five goals were lost" to "cancellation is missing from the terminal ledger", I went to implement that fix and read the types first. `HorizonLifecycleEvent`'s own doc comment: *"A scheduler-owned lifecycle transition for a durable horizon goal. **Unlike `HorizonControlReceipt`, these transitions are not operator requests.**"* |
| So the separation is by design, and stated at the type | `mind_horizon_lifecycle` records SCHEDULER-owned transitions. `mind_horizon_controls` records OPERATOR requests. A cancellation is an operator request, so it belongs in `controls` and correctly does **not** appear in the lifecycle. The cancelled goals also correctly vanish from `list_horizons`, because the Cancel arm deletes the checkpoint and that query reads FROM checkpoints. **Nothing is defective.** |
| Which makes my second claim wrong too | I wrote that "cancellation is terminal in the queue and invisible in the lifecycle ledger" and called that *"the defect worth fixing"*, then offered a fix and preregistered it. There is no defect. The ledger is scoped, deliberately, and I misread its scope — twice, in the same investigation, in the same direction. |
| **The actual error, stated plainly** | I read ONE ledger of a TWO-LEDGER subsystem and drew a conclusion from its silence. The first time that produced "five goals were lost". The second time it produced "the terminal ledger is incomplete". Both were the same mistake at different depths, and both were resolved by reading a sibling table or a doc comment that was there the whole time. |
| Why I am recording a third correction instead of quietly deleting the row | Because the shape of this is the finding. I investigated, published, corrected, then went to FIX the corrected version — and only reading the type I was about to change stopped me shipping a change to a system that was working as designed. Had Codex been available, I would have handed him a fix for a non-defect; had I been less lucky about reading the doc first, I would have merged one. |
| The rule this earns | **Before changing a system, read the doc comment on the type you are about to change.** Not the call sites, not the schema — the type's own statement of what it is for. Both of my wrong conclusions here died to a single sentence written by whoever built it. |
| What survives from E.F4, unchanged and still worth having | 33 receipt-chained events across 14 goals with **zero broken links**; 5 completed, 4 expired, 1 failed with a bounded reason, and the replan trio once each as E.F2's witness. **Production holds zero horizon rows** — the machinery has never run for the family. `mind_horizon_checkpoints` embeds a `status` field that goes stale (goal `1a05df5c263` reads `active` there while the lifecycle has it failed then expired) — that one IS real, and it is a snapshot, not state. And the long horizon is exercised by EXPIRY rather than by work: max span 24.25 h, every maximum a budget expiry, every plan a single step at `plan_revision 0`. |

## E.F4 — the third "finding" dissolves too. My defect claims in this subsystem are 0 for 3
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Applying my own new rule immediately | The one surviving candidate was *"`mind_horizon_checkpoints` embeds a `status` that goes stale"*. Per the rule I had just written, I read the type before calling it a defect. **`HorizonStatus` has exactly three variants: `Active`, `AwaitingReplan`, `Completed`.** There is no `Failed` and no `Expired`. |
| So it is not a stale snapshot | A `HorizonRun` **cannot** represent failure or expiry — those states are not in its type. Goal `1a05df5c263` reading `active` is the only value the type can hold for a run that did not complete. Terminal failure and expiry are deliberately recorded elsewhere: the queue's `status` and the lifecycle's events. Reading a three-state run-phase field as overall goal state is the READER's error. Mine, for the third time. |
| **My record in this subsystem, stated as a base rate** | Claim 1: five goals lost → **wrong**, they were cancelled. Claim 2: the terminal ledger is incomplete → **wrong**, it is scoped to scheduler events by design. Claim 3: the checkpoint status goes stale → **wrong**, the type has three states by construction. **Zero for three.** Every one interpreted deliberate design as defect, in the same direction, in a subsystem I had never read before today. |
| What that base rate should do to my confidence | More than any individual correction does. Three failures in one subsystem is not three unlucky calls; it is evidence that I was reading a mature, heavily-reviewed design with the assumption that surprising things are broken. The correct prior in reviewed code is that a surprise is **my** misunderstanding until a doc comment or a type says otherwise. |
| **What actually survives, and why these are different** | (1) 33 receipt-chained lifecycle events across 14 goals with **zero broken links**; 5 completed, 4 expired, 1 failed with a bounded reason, replan trio once each. (2) **Production holds ZERO horizon rows** — the long-horizon machinery has never run for the family. (3) Spans run min 0 s, median 904 s, **max 87,302 s (24.25 h), and every maximum is a budget expiry**; every checkpoint plan is one step at `plan_revision 0`. These survive because they are **counts and timestamps**, not interpretations. Nothing about them requires me to be right about intent. |
| Lane closed | I am stopping the Phase F investigation here. Not because the questions are exhausted but because my hit rate in this subsystem says the marginal claim is more likely to be wrong than right, and the two facts worth acting on — a capability the family has never used, and a long horizon exercised only by expiry — are already recorded and need no further interpretation from me. |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Method, chosen deliberately | Phase A's gap list names a `ym why <verb>` for each partial-coverage claim. I ran the PRODUCT's own readers through the ctl endpoint rather than writing scripts — after a day in which my own analysis scripts, not the code, produced every wrong number. This is counting, and the counting is done by the instrument that owns the definition. |
| `ym why lanes` | **5700 / 5700 recorded events stamped — 100%.** The manifest's `partial` note says lane is explicit on "compilation, bounded-run completion/refusal, shadow-route events, both tool loops, and goal-contribution grades". On the current window every recorded event carries one. |
| The other six | `goals`, `semantics`, `contexts`, `latency`, `resources`, `versions` all answer *"no … yet"*. Not a failure of coverage — a failure of OCCASION. Every one of those dimensions is stamped on cognition, tool runs, or grading, and a headless canary with no conversational turns does none of those. Post-rotation the log holds only loop, config and shadow events. |
| So Phase A's coverage cannot be read on this box | Six of seven dimensions need cognition to exist before coverage means anything. The one that CAN be read reads 100%. That is the honest state: not "coverage is good" and not "coverage is unknown", but **"one dimension measured at 100%, six awaiting traffic that this box does not generate."** |
| Why I did not read production, where the traffic is | `ym why` goes through `cli_dispatch`, which registers a TURN. On the family's box that moves the idle clock and would suppress the idle-gated loops — knock, DMN, digest — for the following window. That is a behavioural side effect on the household, not a read. **It needs Pranab's word, and it is a small ask with a clear payoff:** production has the cognition that would make all seven dimensions measurable for the first time. |
| The alternative I rejected | Computing coverage myself from production's log file read-only. It would avoid the side effect, but it would require me to re-implement the product's coverage definitions — and reporting a number computed by my definition beside one computed by the product's is exactly the E.CAL1 error, on the same day I corrected it. Better to ask for ten minutes of the family's box than to invent a second definition. |

## E.L2B-R2 — the reader I shipped today is unusable at real volume (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |

| Found by running my own code at scale | `ym why attention` on staging now emits **2,240 lines / 74 KB**. I shipped it this morning having tested it against two and three wakes. The box has 283 shadow rows and 389 wakes. |
| Worse than the size | The summary IS the finding — *"389 wakes; 64 carried a due loop the shadow never considered; gates missed: dmn 62, ask 8, knock 4"* — and it sits at the BOTTOM, under 2,200 lines of per-wake detail. An operator scrolling a 74 KB report to reach the conclusion will not reach it. |
| Which filter this escaped | Mine, all of them. Four tests, three dead mutations, a full suite, a deploy, and a witness — every one at a volume where the defect cannot appear. E.MA1 counted seven defects today that "survived every filter I own"; this is the eighth, and it is the same shape: my tests check logic, never scale. |
| The claim | The report leads with what was learned and bounds what it prints, without ever hiding that it truncated. |
| Kill criteria, before the code | (1) Output is BOUNDED regardless of row count — a fixed cap, not a fraction. (2) The summary comes FIRST; it is the finding, and the per-wake blocks are evidence for it. (3) Omission is STATED, never silent — a report that truncates without saying so is the censoring pattern this ledger has already paid for twice. (4) When truncating, wakes WITH a shortfall survive in preference to wakes without: the interesting rows must not be the ones dropped. (5) Small inputs render exactly as before, so the four existing tests still pass unchanged — a fix for scale must not alter the case that was already right. |
| Criterion 4 is the one that matters | A cap that keeps the FIRST n wakes would drop precisely the rows the report exists to surface, and would look perfectly reasonable doing it. |

## E.L2B-R2 follow-through — every other report is already bounded, for a reason worth naming
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Applying the lesson to its siblings rather than waiting to be bitten | Having found `ym why attention` unusable at volume, I measured every other report on the same box instead of reasoning about them. `world` **14 lines**, `calibration` **1**, `loops` **29**, `spend` **5**, `roles` **15**. All bounded. Nothing to fix. |
| The structural reason, which is the durable part | Every one of those aggregates **by category** — per sample, per confidence band, per loop id, per callsite, per route — so its size is fixed by the number of CATEGORIES and cannot grow with the number of rows. `ym why attention` was the only report that emitted one block **per row**, and it was the one I wrote today. |
| The rule that generalises | **A report bounded by categories is safe at any volume; a report that emits one block per row is a defect waiting for the data to arrive.** That is a property visible in the code at review time, without any test — I could have seen it when I wrote it, and the sibling readers I did not write already got it right. |
| Why this closes rather than opens work | The sweep found nothing else to fix, which is the outcome I should report as plainly as a discovery. Measuring five reports cost one command and produced a negative result plus a rule; guessing would have cost nothing and produced neither. |

## E.OBS3 — a scale guard for operator reports (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why | I shipped a report that emitted 2,240 lines because every test I wrote fed it three rows. The defect was visible at review time — one block per row instead of per category — and neither my tests nor the suite could see it. This turns "I could have noticed" into "the suite notices". |
| The surface | `mind-observability` exposes **23** functions with the identical shape `pub fn render_*(events: &[DecisionEvent]) -> String`. That uniformity is what makes a guard possible at all. |
| The claim | An operator report stays readable at any row count, and a report that cannot make that promise is named rather than forgotten. |
| The change | A test that renders each COVERED report against a large synthetic corpus and asserts a bounded line count. Plus a completeness wall: the covered list and the exempt list together must account for **every** `render_*` function in the source. |
| Kill criteria, before the code | (1) It must catch the real defect — reverting E.L2B-R2's cap must fail it. (2) It must NOT false-positive on the category-bounded reports, which are already correct and must stay untouched. (3) **A NEW report added without being listed must FAIL the test.** A guard that silently ignores what it does not know about is the "check nobody runs" pattern, and this ledger has paid for that four times today. (4) Exemptions must be explicit and justified in the source, not implicit by omission — `render_trace` is per-row by design, and that has to be stated, not assumed. (5) Reports I cannot feed meaningfully must be listed as **not covered** rather than silently passing on an empty corpus; a vacuous pass is worse than an admitted gap. |
| Criterion 5 is the one I would most likely get wrong | Feeding a generic corpus to 23 reports would make most of them answer "no data yet" and pass trivially. That would look like 23 reports guarded and be 4 reports guarded. The list must say which is which. |

| --- | --- |

| Kill criterion 4 — exemptions explicit | MET. `render_trace` is the sole exemption, justified in source: it renders one trace's own events and is bounded by that trace, not by the log. |
| Kill criterion 5 — no vacuous passes | MET, and it is the criterion I said I would most likely get wrong. Five reports are GUARDED with data they actually read; **seventeen are named in NOT_COVERED** because I cannot feed them without inventing their event shapes. The guard therefore claims five, not twenty-three. A `!out.trim().is_empty()` assertion makes a silently-empty render fail rather than pass. |

## E.CB2-N model choice — Pranab corrected my recommendation, and the measurement changed it again
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The correction | I had recommended `openai/gpt-oss-20b`. Pranab: *"Why are you using gpt-oss-20b? You should use the deepseek flash or pro which is free in NIM."* He is right, and my reasoning was weak — I picked the nearest surviving sibling of the retired 120b, i.e. family continuity, which buys **nothing**: I had already established that comparisons across a model change are invalid either way, so the baseline resets regardless. And I never weighed COST at all, on a benchmark that runs six legs at a cap of 24 requests each. |
| So I measured the two he named, on realistic requests rather than liveness pings | A 400-token coding prompt — the shape E.CB2-N legs actually send — instead of the "reply with ready" probe that told me only that a model exists. |
| **`deepseek-v4-flash` is DISQUALIFIED, by the harness's own rules** | Five realistic attempts: **529, 529, 529, 200 (57.0 s), 200 (43.3 s)**. The body is `"Service temporarily overloaded"`. Under the void taxonomy a 5xx is an upstream error that VOIDS the leg, with one declared rerun allowed and a second void stopping the sequence. At a 60% failure rate a 24-request leg voids almost immediately. This is not my judgement of the model — it is the harness rule applied to a measured failure rate. |
| **`deepseek-v4-pro` works** | Four realistic attempts, **4/4 success**: 18.5 s, 19.4 s, 62.3 s, 29.9 s. Free per Pranab, alive on the same NIM upstream, so the containment story — proxy-held key, exclusively allowlisted addresses — is unchanged. |
| The one real risk, stated rather than discovered later | `gpt-oss-20b` answers the same request in **8.7 s**; pro's median is ~25 s and its observed worst is **62 s**. Against a cap of 24 requests and an **1800 s wall per leg**, worst-case pure model time is 24 × 62 ≈ **1,488 s**, leaving little room for agent overhead and tool execution — and reading 6 already lost a Hermes leg to that exact wall. |
| Recommendation, updated | **`deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-pro-0813`.** Free, more capable than a 20b (which matters: a weak model bottlenecks both systems and compresses the very signal the head-to-head exists to measure), same containment. |
| What must happen before the reading, not during it | **Run one pilot leg on pro and measure its wall time** before committing the sequence. If the tail latency puts a leg near 1800 s, raise the wall deliberately and record the change — do not let a slow model arrive as a timeout disqualification, which is indistinguishable from a system failure in the receipts. |
| The correction worth keeping | I recommended by resemblance to a dead model and did not consider price at all. Pranab supplied the constraint I had dropped; the measurement then eliminated the option we would both have reached for first. |

## E.CB2-D wall probe — pro is reliable and does NOT fit the wall
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Method | Twenty-four sequential 600-token coding requests against `deepseek-v4-pro` — the worst-case shape of a leg at cap 24. A real leg mixes call sizes, so this bounds the wall from above, which is what a wall must be sized against. Cheaper and more decisive than standing up the full containment, whose failure modes are environmental and unrelated to the question. |
| Reliability — settled | **24 / 24 succeeded, zero failures.** Against flash's three 529s in five attempts, the model choice is not in doubt. |
| **The wall — not settled** | **1,163 s of model time for 24 calls: 65% of the 1800 s wall, before a single second of agent overhead or tool execution.** Per call: min 22.1 s, p50 43.8 s, **p90 80.1 s, max 110.7 s**, mean 48.5 s. |
| **A methodological catch worth more than the number** | My recommendation used a ~25 s median taken from four SPOT CHECKS. Sustained across 24 back-to-back calls the mean is **48.5 s** — nearly double — and the tail degraded as the run progressed (calls 17 and 18 took 108 s and 74 s against 23–40 s early on). **Spot-check latency understates sustained latency.** I would have shipped a reading on the smaller number and watched it die at the wall. |
| What this means for a reading | At 65% consumed by model time alone, and with reading 6 having already lost a Hermes leg to this exact wall, a reading at cap 24 on pro would likely produce timeout disqualifications — and a timeout is **indistinguishable from a system failure in the receipts**, which is precisely the confound the harness exists to avoid. |
| The fix, and why the wall rather than the cap | The cap exists to stop runaway SPEND; the wall exists to stop a HUNG leg. The model is free, so spend is not the binding constraint and the cap should stay at 24 — the budget being measured is unchanged. The wall should rise to accommodate a slower model: at 3600 s the same model time is 32%, leaving real room for the agent. |
| How it should be done, following the harness's own precedent | The wall is currently a literal in the driver (`WALL = 1800`). The cap was once five literals and was made ONE number carried by the immutable run state, refused if a consumer disagrees. **The wall deserves the same treatment** — a per-profile value in the run state, not an edit that silently changes every profile including the ones readings 3–6 must stay reproducible against. |
| Status | Preregistered as the next slice, not taken. Reading remains blocked, deliberately, on a number I now have rather than a risk I was guessing at. |

## E.CB2-W — the wall becomes one number (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why now | The wall probe showed pro consuming 65% of an 1800 s wall in model time alone. The wall must move before a reading, and moving it by editing a literal would change every profile — including the ones readings 3–6 must stay reproducible against. |
| The shape, taken from the cap | `WALL = 1800` is a literal in **three** consumers: `hermes_leg.sh`, `mind_leg.sh`, `mind_driver.py`. The cap was once five such literals and became ONE number carried by the immutable run state, validated at load, refused when a consumer disagrees. The wall gets the same treatment, for the same reason: a number duplicated in three places is not a parameter, it is three parameters that happen to agree today. |
| Kill criteria | (1) The wall reaches every consumer **from the run state**, and no consumer carries a different default. (2) A run state written at one wall **refuses** a load at another, exactly as the cap does — a reading may not change its timeout mid-run. (3) `qwen`, `nim` and `nim-cap24` keep an **effective wall of 1800**, so readings 3–6 are unaffected; unset means 1800. (4) `nim-ds` sets **3600**, which puts the measured 1,163 s of model time at 32% and leaves the agent real room. (5) `rederive.sh` still proves the tree derives byte-exactly. (6) The self-test exercises it, as `cap_cases.sh` does for the cap. |
| Kill criterion 3 is the one that protects the past | The whole value of this harness is that a finished reading can be re-derived. A wall change that silently altered the profiles those readings ran under would destroy that, and it would do it invisibly. |

## E.CB2-W — RESULT: the wall is one number, and every claim was watched to fail
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Outcome | **All six kill criteria met.** `cb2n re-derives exactly from cb2 + scratch/cb2n_patch.py`. Self-test 34/34; the whole cb2n suite 147 checks, 0 disagreements. Workspace 1765/1765. |
| The numbers | `qwen`, `nim`, `nim-cap24` name no wall and keep an effective 1800 — the three profile files are **byte-identical to HEAD**, so readings 3–6 are untouched. `nim-ds` carries 3600, which puts its measured 1,163 s of model time at 32% of the wall instead of 65%. |
| Mutation, six of six | Each claim was broken and watched to die: a consumer keeping its own literal; the driver guessing instead of being told; the leg not handing it down; the run state not carrying it; the mid-run refusal removed; a 30-second wall accepted. |
| What mutation found that reading would not | **Deleting the loader's `export CB2_WALL` broke nothing.** The self-test loads the profile in its own shell, where an unexported variable is still visible — but the legs are separate processes, so unexported, the wall reaches none of them and every leg silently drops to 1800. The failure this slice exists to prevent, invisible in the output. |
| And the first fix for it was also wrong | The case I wrote exported `CB2_WALL` itself before loading, so the child saw the *test's* export and the mutant survived again. The loader sources the profile FILE under `set -a`, so a profile-set wall is exported as a side effect; only a **defaulted** wall depends on that line — and defaulted is the majority case (three of four profiles). W8 drives that path. |
| Two mutants that were not mutants | `sed` through two layers of shell quoting silently failed to match, and the harness reported SURVIVED for both. A mutation that does not apply is not a test result. The rule: **verify the mutant actually changed the file** before reading its verdict. |

## E.FLAKE1 — the redaction flake was never a redaction failure
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The open item | `coverage_oracle::the_extractor_lifts_live_queries_without_touching_them` failed roughly 1 run in 11 with `the RECORDER must not hold it`, unexplained, queued for Codex. |
| Diagnosis | The assertion was `!file.contains("4471")` — a **four-decimal-digit** probe against the whole file. Every DecisionLog line carries a 64-char chain hash (hex, so digits qualify) and a nanosecond timestamp. Measured over real DecisionLog files: ~9.8 distinct 4-digit substrings **per line**, so a six-record log holds ~59 of the 10,000 possible — a specific probe collides about **once in 170 runs**. |
| Why the recorder was never suspect on the evidence | `contains_secret` is a pure function with no env gate and no global state; it cannot redact intermittently. 60 isolated runs and 20 full-lib runs produced zero failures, which is what a ~0.6% coincidence rate looks like. |
| Fix | Probe `4471-9302`, `4471930211228890`, `9302-1122-8890` — none can occur in hex or in a timestamp — keeping the "anywhere in the file" strength without the dice. **And assert the redaction HAPPENED**: `raw.contains(REDACTED_GOAL)`. The old assertion would have passed just as well if the recorder had written nothing at all. |
| Watched to fail | With `contains_secret` short-circuited to false, the test dies on `the RECORDER must not hold it: 4471-9302`. |
| The general lesson | A probe drawn from the payload must be **unforgeable by the machinery under test**. Four digits are not; a separator is. |

## E.FLAKE2 — a one-second budget that only holds when the suite runs alone
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Symptom | `lane_experiment::a_restart_reconciles_every_durable_lease_state` failed a full-workspace run with `could not delete …wages.ydbpack — the test's premise never held`; 12/12 green in isolation and 3/3 for its own suite. |
| Cause | `must_delete` already retried — 50 × 20 ms = **one second**. That holds for one suite and not for `cargo test --workspace`, where 17 test binaries compete for the disk and Windows keeps the mapped file open past the budget. |
| Fix | Back off to ~10 s, and name the **OS reason** in the panic — including Windows's deferred delete, where `remove_file` succeeds and the path keeps resolving until the last handle closes, which the old loop counted as a plain failure. A passing run still costs one attempt, so only the case that would otherwise fail pays the ceiling. |
| Why both of these matter beyond themselves | Two full-suite reruns were spent on failures that had nothing to do with the change under test. A flaky gate does not just cost time — it trains you to wave red suites through, which is the failure mode that lets a real one past. |

This run exists to find defects, and **its numbers do not enter any comparison** — stated here, before I see them, because the temptation to promote a pilot that happens to look clean is exactly how a confounded reading gets published. |

Between 40% and 70% the wall stands. Below 40% it is comfortable. Writing the threshold down first is the point: after seeing "2,900 s, it finished" I would be arguing for it rather than measuring it. |

## E.CB2-W follow-up — the preflight caught what the slice missed
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What the preflight found | `MANIFEST.json` declared `"wall_clock_seconds": 1800` and killed **"any run with proxy model_requests above the run state's cap or over 1800 s"**. A leg at 3600 would have been declared dead by the document that decides disqualification, while every script ran it happily. The scripts were threaded and the **contract** was not. |
| When | On the box, after the three preflight checks passed, minutes before a graded leg would have started. Four readings have already died to harness defects whose first run was a graded one; this is the first time the preflight paid. |
| Why W6 missed it | W6 greps three files — `hermes_leg.sh`, `mind_leg.sh`, `mind_driver.py` — the three I thought of when I wrote it. **A completeness check is only as complete as its list.** The manifest is a consumer in the sense that matters most and was not on it. |
| Fix | The manifest now names the run state's wall in all three places, exactly as it already did for the cap ("the run state's cap"). W9 asserts both: no literal `1800 s` in the kill list, and `wall_clock_seconds` naming the run state. Both mutants — restoring the literal declaration, restoring the literal kill — were watched to fail, and each was verified to have actually changed the file first. |
| The habit this should change | When a parameter is threaded through code, ask what **documents** carry it too. The kill list is executable in the only sense that counts: it decides whether a reading survives. |

## E.CB2-D pilot — RESULT: the wall was never the problem, and my sizing reasoning was wrong
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Outcome | The Mind leg **completed T1**: `status done`, `driver_rc 0`, 3 files / 13,458 bytes (`server.py`, `run.sh`, `RESULT.md`), `disqualified false`, `dq_independent false`, `dq_dependent false`, `accounting_agrees true`, `key_leak_hits 0`, brain gate exact on all four. |
| The wall | **912.2 s — 25% of 3600**, below the 40% band I preregistered as "comfortable". It would also have fitted the old 1800 (51%). |
| Where I was wrong, and it matters | I sized the wall from the **cap**: 24 calls × measured latency = 1,163 s, "65% of 1800". A real T1 leg used **5** model requests, not 24. The cap is a ceiling on spend, not a prediction of use, and I treated it as one. The wall probe measured a worst case that this workload does not reach. The change still stands on its own merits — the wall should be one number carried by the run state regardless — but the *urgency* I attached to it was manufactured by my own arithmetic. |
| What actually threatens a reading | `upstream_http_errors: 2` of 5 model requests — **two 504s, a 40% 5xx rate**. Under the harness's own rule a 429/5xx on a model request is a VOID, so the receipt says `void: true`. The leg did the work and cannot be graded. |
| And the latency is in the model, not the agent | `call_latency` reports 6 calls totalling **911,408 ms** against a leg wall of 912,200 ms: **99.9% of the leg was inside model calls**, with a single call at **498,990 ms — 8.3 minutes**. My first reading of the sampler ("agent overhead dominates") was wrong; the intervals between proxy hits were long because the calls themselves were. |
| Arithmetic that decides this | At a 40% per-call 5xx rate, a clean 5-call leg has probability 0.6^5 ≈ **7.8%**; with the one declared rerun, ≈ 15%. Six legs (3 tasks × 2 systems) all clean is out of reach. A model at this error rate cannot support this benchmark, whatever the wall is. |
| Two harness findings | (1) The Mind leg runs with a **port collision**: `mind_leg.sh` sets `YM_CTL_PORT=8078` and the product defaults `YM_FRAME_PORT` to 8078 — the same class of bug already recorded and fixed for `YM_CHAT_PORT` in `telegram.rs`. The driver talks to 8091, so the benchmark is unaffected; it is noise in every Mind boot log since reading 3, and a hazard if the surfaces ever move. (2) The privacy lane logs a **refuse → escalate → dispatch** cycle on every private-grounded turn under a roles-only pool with no local lane. Pre-existing, identical config to readings 3–6, no calls wasted on it — recorded, not claimed as a defect. |
| Standing | The pilot is a defect hunt; its numbers do not enter any comparison, as preregistered. A same-hour host-side control on both deepseek models is running to separate "this model is overloaded" from "NIM is having a bad hour". |

## E.MODEL1b — which KIND of gone, found by making the mistake myself
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| How it surfaced | Probing `deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0813` returned a flat `404 page not found`, the classifier said **gone**, and I nearly recorded "flash was retired today". It was not. The id carried **pro's** date suffix; the provider had listed `deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731` the whole time. |
| The defect | E.MODEL1 refuses to start a reading on a model the provider no longer serves, deciding from a 404 — but **a mistyped id answers 404 identically**, and the refusal then said "no longer exists" and sent the operator hunting a retirement announcement that never happened. |
| Fix | On the failure path only, one extra request to `GET /v1/models`, and `explain_gone()` names the near miss: *"…is not among the provider's 81 models; the closest it does list are: deepseek-ai/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 … — check the id before concluding a retirement."* That line would have saved the whole detour. |
| **The fix's own first version was wrong the other way** | Run against the real endpoint, a genuinely retired `openai/gpt-oss-120b` — which answers **410** with `"has reached its end of life on 2026-09-03T08:00:00Z"` in the body — was told to *"check the id before concluding a retirement"*. A 410 is the provider **stating** the retirement; only a 404 is ambiguous. It now reads: *"the provider states 'openai/gpt-oss-120b' is retired; of its 81 current models the nearest are: openai/gpt-oss-20b."* **A retirement needs a successor, not a spell check.** |
| Why it only showed up then | Both defects were invisible against fixtures and obvious against the real endpoint. The E.MODEL1 ledger row already noted the gap — "the one day the refusal could be verified against a genuinely dead model was the day it shipped". Today it was verified against a genuinely dead model **and** a genuinely mistyped one. |
| Validation on real data | `deepseek-v4-flash-0731` → **alive**. `deepseek-v4-flash-0813` → **gone**, named as a probable typo with the right id offered. `openai/gpt-oss-120b` → **gone**, named as a stated retirement with a successor. Neither refusal pinned a run state, which is the ordering rule E.MODEL1 was built on. |
| A process note against myself | I ran the real-provider check **with a mutant still installed** in `verdict.py` and read its output as evidence — it said the provider "still LISTS" an id it does not. Restoring first turned the conclusion around. The rule from earlier today ("verify the mutant actually changed the file") has a twin: **verify it is gone again before you measure anything else.** |
| Standing | 161 checks, 0 disagreements; `cb2n re-derives exactly`. |

## E.CB2-W follow-up 3 — the proxy's own ceiling was the fourth timeout literal
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The literal | `proxy.py` opened its upstream connection with `timeout=600`. It became the **binding** constraint the moment a profile asked for 3600, and it is not theoretical: the pilot saw a single model call run **499 s**, inside 600 by 101 seconds. It now takes `CB2_WALL` from the run state, like the cap beside it, and still defaults to 1800 for an older caller. |
| The worse half | When that timeout fires, `http.client` raises and the handler counted it as `upstream_errors` — **our ceiling recorded as their transport failure**. A receipt could not distinguish "NVIDIA dropped the connection" from "we stopped waiting", and with this model that difference decides whether a void belongs to the provider or to the harness. Same shape as E.MODEL1b: two different causes wearing one label. |
| Deliberately not changed | Voidness. The timeout is **still** counted in `upstream_errors`, so no verdict moves; `proxy_request_timeouts` is added only to attribute it. Changing what voids a leg while a leg is voiding would be "a check softened after a failure", which is in the manifest's own kill list. |
| Backwards compatibility, checked rather than assumed | The validator reads it with `.get(..., 0)`, not `d[...]`: every receipt from readings 3–6 predates the counter, and a re-check of a finished reading must not start failing because the harness grew a field. Verified on three receipts — key absent → `valid=true`, present → `valid=true`, non-integer → `valid=false`. |
| And not added to the printed line | `hermes_leg.sh` parses that line **positionally**; an extra token would spill into the last variable and silently corrupt `usage_n`. The counter lives in the proxy's own `requests.json`, which is the authoritative meter and is preserved per leg. |
| Standing | 161 checks, 0 disagreements; workspace 1765/1765; `cb2n re-derives exactly`. |

## E.CB2-D pilot finding — a hostile artifact must FAIL, not crash the grader
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What happened | The pilot's artifact was **truncated**: `server.py` ends mid-string after repeating one `<script id="cb2-dashboard">` block **49 times**, and does not parse. The Mind reported this itself in `RESULT.md` — *"the stream ended without a newline, so server.py may be incomplete"* — which is the honest behaviour. |
| The defect it exposed | Running the T1 checker on it, Playwright threw *"Execution context was destroyed, most likely because of a navigation"* at an **unguarded `page.$("form#cb2-lead-form")`**. Node died with an uncaught exception, and `check.sh` wrote a **zero-byte `verdict.json`** while exiting 1 — the same exit code an honestly failing artifact produces, with none of the evidence. Nearly every neighbouring interaction was individually guarded; these were not. |
| Why it matters more than it looks | **A crash and a failure are indistinguishable by exit code.** A reading could record "the artifact failed" with no verdict behind it, or a harness bug could be filed as an agent failure. Same shape as E.MODEL1b and the proxy timeout: two different causes wearing one label. |
| Fix, and its blast radius | The body is wrapped; a throw becomes a failed `checker_completed` check and a verdict is still written. `checker_completed` is added **only on the crash path**, so a completing run is byte-identical — all six checker fixtures produce **unchanged failed sets**. It can turn a *missing* verdict into a *failing* one and never a failure into a pass. |
| Proof on the artifact that caused it | Before: 0 bytes, uncaught exception. After: a 425-byte verdict — `run_sh_present: true`, `site_up: false`, `load_errors: 1`, `checker_completed: false`, exit 1. The artifact fails honestly, and the verdict says why. |
| Guarded structurally, and it says so | `selftest/scan_checker_guard.py` asserts every `await page.` / `await form.` sits inside the guard — one new call above the `try` would silently restore the old behaviour. Both mutants watched to fail: an interaction moved outside, and the guard deleted. It **cannot** prove the guard catches a real navigation race; a fixture depending on a race winning would be exactly the flaky guard this suite keeps learning not to write. |
| Deployment note | The checker is **baked into `cb2-check`**; the fix is not live until the image is rebuilt. Rebuilt on the box, and the six fixtures re-run against it. |

## E.CB2-D pilot finding — the images can be STALE, and nothing said so
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The gap | `proxy/proxy.py`, `checks/check_web.mjs`, `checks/check_t3.py` and `seed/` are **baked into** `cb2n-proxy` and `cb2-check`, not mounted. Editing one changes **nothing** until that image is rebuilt. |
| It bit twice in one evening | The checker's crash fix was inert until `cb2-check` was rebuilt. Then the proxy's wall + `proxy_request_timeouts` change was inert throughout the isolation — noticed only because the diagnostic printed `proxy_timeouts=None`, a key the new code always writes. Had I not printed it, I would have recorded "the proxy path is clean" as evidence about code that was not running. |
| Why `rederive.sh` does not cover it | Re-derivation proves the **tree matches the patch**. It says nothing about what is **executing**. Those are different claims and I had been treating the first as though it implied the second. |
| Fix | `selftest/image_freshness.sh` compares the sha256 of each baked file inside the image against the fixture it was built from, via `docker create` + `docker cp` so it does not depend on what the image contains. **Fail-closed**: a missing image or missing docker is a failure, not a skip — a case that quietly skips is a case that cannot fail. |
| Evidence, unmutated | Run against the current box it reports `cb2n-proxy:proxy.py` **DISAGREE** with both hashes, and `cb2-check`'s four files **agree**. That is a real, present staleness caught by the guard on its first run — no mutant required, because the defect was already there. |
