## CORRECTION — `timeout=600` bounds a socket operation, not a call
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What I wrote | In the E.CB2-W follow-up 3 row and commit `b2d8d5c`: the proxy's `timeout=600` "became the binding constraint" and "a call past 600 s becomes a 502 and a transport void". |
| Why that is wrong | `http.client`'s `timeout` is the **socket** timeout, applied per blocking operation. A streamed response that keeps delivering chunks resets it on every read, so a long call never trips it — only a **stall** longer than 600 s would. |
| The proof is in leg 2, not a docstring | A call ran **908,187 ms** through a proxy running `timeout=600`, and the receipt shows `upstream_transport_errors: 0`. Had the timeout bounded the call, it would have fired. It did not. |
| What still stands | Deriving the ceiling from the run state instead of a literal, and counting `proxy_request_timeouts` separately so our stall ceiling is not recorded as the upstream's transport failure. Both are right for the reason given — one number, and two causes must not wear one label. Only the **urgency** was wrong: the ceiling is a stall guard, and it was never as close to binding as I said. |

## E.CB2-D — five hypotheses walked, 45 clean probe calls, and the leg still fails
| Configuration (all on the leg's path unless noted) | Calls | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Host-side buffered, 600 max_tokens | 8 | all 200, p50 61 s |
| Host-side buffered, 3000 max_tokens | 6 | all 200, 134–229 s |
| Host-side **streaming** | 6 | all clean `[DONE]` |
| **Through the run's proxy from `cb2net`**, streaming | 6 | all clean, receipt zero errors |
| **Two concurrent** streams through the proxy (`YM_INFER_PERMITS=2`) | 6 | all clean, receipt zero errors |
| **Context-size ladder** through the proxy: 10k → 38k → 102k → 204k → **382k characters** | 5 | all clean |
| **Overlap** — one long generation held open, five short calls issued underneath it | 6 | all clean, receipt zero errors |
| Against which | — | leg 1: **2 of 5** 504s; leg 2: **3 of 4** 504s, `status failed`, `files_added 0` |
| Honest position | The failure is real, reproducible on the leg, and reproduced by **nothing else I can construct**. Concurrency, context size, streaming, the proxy relay and the container egress are each exonerated. My hypotheses are exhausted. |
| The clue I did have, and could barely read | Leg 2's `call_latency` gives `calls 4, total_ms 910,982, max_ms 908,187` — so the other three shared **2,795 ms**, about 930 ms each. Those 504s came back in about a second: **gateway rejections, not timeouts**. I had to derive that by subtraction from the *Mind's* accounting, because the proxy receipt counts outcomes and records nothing about them. |
| So: stop guessing, instrument | `by_status` now buckets **latency and request size per status code** in the proxy receipt. A handful of keys whatever the traffic — never one row per request, which is the shape this repo already refuses. One instrumented leg will say directly what five probes could not: how long each 504 took and how big the request was. |
| Two details that matter | Successes are timed **after the whole streamed body**; timing them at their headers would record time-to-first-byte and make every success look instant, destroying the comparison. Errors are timed at their headers, where they are complete. And `observe` **persists** — without it the last request's bucket never reaches the file, caught by a live cap test reporting `n=8` for nine requests. |
| Aside, recorded not chased | Under `nim-ds` the harness's own `captest_client.py` gets **nine 400s** where it expects eight 200s and a 429 — it sends `max_tokens: 4`, which this model rejects. `net/captest.sh` therefore cannot pass on this profile for two independent reasons (that, and cap 24 never refusing at nine requests). Not blocking the pilot; it would block a reading that runs the live cap proof. |

## E.CB2-D leg 3 (instrumented) — what one leg said that five probes could not
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Leg 3 | `status: done`, 3 files, 230-byte result, wall 373 s (**10% of 3600**), `proxy_accepted 4`, `upstream_http_errors 1`, `transport 0`, `proxy_request_timeouts 0`, `accounting_agrees true`, `disqualified false` — and **`void: true`**, like legs 1 and 2. |
| The buckets, first leg they existed for | `200` × 4 — `ms[min 152, max 149,269]`, `req_bytes[min 0, max 31,318]`. `502` × 1 — **`ms 75,034`, `req_bytes 6,170`**. (The `min 152 / 0 bytes` 200 is the metadata `GET /v1/models`, so the model POSTs are 3 × 200 + 1 × 502 = the 4 accepted.) |
| **CORRECTION — the "fast gateway rejection" reading was wrong** | I inferred from leg 2 that the failures "came back in about a second", by subtracting `max_ms` from `total_ms` in the **Mind's** `call_latency`. Measured directly, the failure took **75 seconds**. The subtraction was invalid: leg 3 shows `call_latency.calls = 6` against `proxy_accepted = 4`, so the Mind's "calls" do not map one-to-one onto HTTP requests and arithmetic across the two accountings proves nothing. **This is precisely why instrumenting beat guessing** — and it is the fourth time today a number derived under one frame was asserted about another. |
| What is now measured, not inferred | The upstream returns a **5xx after ~75 s** on a mid-sized (6 KB) request, while on the same leg a **31 KB** request succeeds and another runs **149 s** to a clean 200. So it is neither a fast rejection nor size-monotonic. Leg 3's was a **502**; legs 1 and 2 logged **504**. The Mind's own log agrees with the proxy exactly: one `http status: 502`. |
| The finding that actually decides the line | **Three legs, three voids.** 6 of 13 model POSTs across legs 1–3 returned 5xx. Under the harness's own rule any 429/5xx on a model request voids the leg, so on this model **no reading can be graded** — regardless of whether the legs succeed at the task (leg 1 and leg 3 did; leg 2 did not). The cause remains unisolated and I am not claiming one. |
| Not proposed | Any change to the void rule. "A check softened after a failure" is in the manifest's kill list, and three failures do not make it less so. |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |

## E.CB2-M — RESULT: it was never the model. NIM cuts a request at ~302 seconds.
| Leg | Model | Outcome |

| oss20 #1 | `openai/gpt-oss-20b` | `done`, 4 files, **void FALSE** — 3 POSTs, zero errors |
| oss20 #2 | `openai/gpt-oss-20b` | `done`, 4 files, **void true** — one **504 at 302,173 ms** on an 11,074-byte request |
| flash | `deepseek-v4-flash-0731` | `failed`, 0 files, **void true** — three **504s at 302,155 / 302,180 ms** on 6,172-byte requests |
| pilot 1–3 | `deepseek-v4-pro-0813` | all three **void true** |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **The measurement** | Four 504s across **two different models** land in the band **302,155–302,180 ms — a spread of 25 milliseconds**. That is not load and not chance: it is a fixed server-side deadline of about 302 seconds. Successes on the same legs are far below it (33 s, 115 s, 149 s, 223 s). |
| So the framing was wrong all day | This is not "deepseek is unreliable". Every NIM model tried hits the same edge, `gpt-oss-20b` included. The failure is a **structural incompatibility**: the Mind issues single generations that run past NIM's per-request deadline, and any 5xx voids the leg under the harness's rule. Choosing a different NIM model does not fix it — which is exactly why the preregistered criterion demanded **two consecutive** void-free legs. 20b passed one and failed the second. |
| It also resolves the accounting puzzle | Flash's receipt shows the Mind reporting `max_ms 908,110` for a logical call while the proxy's longest single request was 302,180 ms. The two accountings measure different things, so the subtraction I did on leg 2 — which produced the bogus "~930 ms fast rejection" — could never have been valid. Second instance of the same lesson today. |
| Why 45 probe calls missed it | Every probe finished under the edge; the longest was 320.8 s and **succeeded**, so the deadline is not a blanket wall-clock cap on all traffic. The Mind's requests are what reach past it. A probe I designed to mimic the leg was still not the leg — the fourth time today a measurement under one configuration failed to speak for another. |
| Not proposed | Any change to the void rule. |
| The decision this creates | It belongs to Pranab: the constraint he set was "free in NIM", and no free NIM model can currently produce a gradeable leg. Options are to shorten what the Mind asks for in one request (a product change with its own consequences), to use a provider without that deadline, or to accept that this line produces no reading. I have not chosen among them. |

## E.CB2-M — how HERMES handles the deadline (Pranab's question), and what it changes
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The question | Pranab: "how is hermes handling it?" — the right question, and it reversed the change I had proposed an hour earlier. |
| Reading 6's receipts, re-read for completion tokens **per request** | hermes T1 **16 requests / 5,908 tokens = 369 per request**; T2 **13 / 6,218 = 478**; T3 3 / 3,422 = 1,141. mind T1 **2 / 2,398 = 1,199**; T2 **2 / 3,223 = 1,612**; T3 2 / 1,426 = 713. |
| Why Hermes survives | It is an agentic tool loop: each turn is a short decision plus a tool call, so the deliverable arrives in pieces. Against a fixed 302 s deadline it has **3–4× the headroom per call** — not by design intent, as a side effect of being agentic. The Mind puts the whole deliverable in one generation at up to 16,000 tokens. |
| But it is NOT immune | `hermes_T2_void1` in reading 6 is a **voided Hermes leg** — 993 s, 76 s/request, killed by two upstream 429/5xx. In the qwen reading a Hermes T1 hung to the 1800 s wall. More headroom, not immunity. |
| **The reversal** | The Mind's few-big-calls design **was its measured advantage**: reading 6 recorded cost as "the one column not close" — 2 requests per Mind leg against 3–16, 35–73 s against 108–413 s. Going per-file always would fix a slow-provider problem by permanently discarding the dimension where the Mind clearly won. |
| The change that is actually right | **Derive the budget from the provider's deadline and observed throughput**, rather than a 16,000 constant: keep few-big-calls where the model is fast enough, split only where the provider forces it. On the retired 120b the whole Mind T1 was 34.8 s and nothing needed splitting. |
| Why the same brief now costs 13× | gpt-oss-20b emitted **10,842** completion tokens where 120b emitted **2,398** — 4.5× more verbose — at roughly a third of the throughput (≈69 tok/s vs ≈16–26). 4.5 × 3 ≈ 13, and 34.8 s × 13 ≈ 450 s, which is what the oss20 legs actually measured. Two compounding effects, neither of them the Mind's design. |
| Still unmeasured, being measured | Hermes on the slow models. Everything above about Hermes is from reading 6 on the retired 120b. |

## An operational fault of mine — the deploy wiped the Hermes archive
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What happened | The first Hermes leg refused instantly: `status: archive-mismatch, disqualified: true`, 0 requests. My redeploy used `find $D -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -name '*.tar.gz' -exec rm -rf {} +`, which protects only **top-level** files — and `docker/hermes-3ce1cf2.tar.gz` sits one level down, inside a directory that was removed wholesale. The archive is deliberately **not in the repo** (28 MB), so no redeploy could restore it. |
| Recovery | Restored from the frozen `/root/cb2/fixtures/docker/`, sha256 `30698554…aaac` — an **exact match to the pinned commit**, independently confirmed by my own earlier `fixtures.bak` copy. `cb2-hermes:latest` was untouched (it needs the archive only at build time). |
| What made it survivable | The leg **failed closed and said why**. `hermes_leg.sh` verifies the archive against the pinned hash before doing anything and writes a typed disqualification. A harness that had merely built from whatever was there would have produced a leg on the wrong source, and nothing would have said so. |
| The rule | An exclusion pattern written for top-level files does not protect the same pattern nested. Deploys must preserve `docker/` wholesale, since the one artefact that cannot be re-derived from the repo lives there. |

## E.CB2-M — MEASURED: Hermes on gpt-oss-20b, the same model the Mind cannot be graded on
| | Mind (oss20 #1 / #2) | **Hermes (oss20)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| wall | 420 s / 471 s | **92 s** |
| model requests | 3 / 4 | 4 |
| completion tokens per request | ~3,600 | **772** |
| **longest single model call** | **302,173 ms → 504** | **34,009 ms** |
| upstream 5xx | 0 / 1 | **0** |
| verdict | void false / **void true** | **void false, disqualified false** |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The answer | **Hermes handles it by never getting close.** 34 s against a 302 s deadline is 9× headroom. It built `index.html` + `server.py`, `rc 0`, `timed_out false`, `own_log_agrees true`, `model_ok true`. On the model where the Mind cannot produce a gradeable leg, Hermes produces one comfortably. |
| The mechanism, in one number | **772 completion tokens per request against the Mind's ~3,600.** It is not that Hermes is cheaper — it sends **20,317 prompt tokens** to the Mind's ~4,700, because a tool loop resends schemas and history every turn. It is differently shaped, and that shape is deadline-safe by construction rather than by intent. |
| So the asymmetry is real, not a harness artifact | This is the first leg-level evidence that the two systems differ in a way that *matters to whether a reading can happen at all*. It is not something to fix in the harness. |
| Incidental | 16 of Hermes's 19 non-model requests are **404s** — it probes `/api/tags`, `/v1/props`, `/props`, `/version`, `/api/v1/models`, hunting for an Ollama or llama.cpp server that NVIDIA does not serve. Free (not model requests, not errors, no cap cost) but ~2.5 s of wasted round-trips per leg. Recorded, not chased. |
| What it settles | The budget-from-deadline change stands, and per-file-always is dropped. Hermes shows the deadline is survivable without abandoning few-big-calls — the Mind simply needs its single call sized to the provider it is talking to, which on a fast model is no split at all. |

## E.CB2-B — sizing the build call to the provider (PREREGISTERED, and a correction to my own gate)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Diagnosis, settled | NIM cuts a request at **~302 s** (four 504s, two models, 25 ms spread). `build_recipe` authors every file in one `Think` at **`max_tokens: 16_000`** — 740–1,032 s at the measured 15.5–21.6 tok/s. Hermes clears the same deadline at **772 completion tokens/call, 34 s longest**, and produces a gradeable leg where the Mind does not. |
| **The gate I preregistered was wrong, and I am correcting it before running, not after** | E.CB2-M's criterion was "two consecutive void-free legs". That is **gameable by the exact failure this change risks**: producing *less* makes a leg void-free. I would have measured my way to a green light on a regression. |
| Corrected gate | Two consecutive legs that are **void-free** AND whose checker verdict is **not below reading 6's baseline** — T1 **11/11**, T2 **6/6**, T3 **9/10**. Both conditions, or the change is not accepted. |
| Why a smaller budget alone is NOT the fix | A call bounded to ~3,000 tokens finishes in ~194 s, but a file needing 5,000 arrives **truncated** — precisely pilot 1's `server.py`, cut mid-string after 49 repeated blocks. That trades a **loud** failure (504, voids the leg, impossible to miss) for a **quiet** one (a file that looks written and does not parse). A fix that changes which way it breaks is not a fix. |
| A hazard independent of NIM | The review step re-emits the **complete** set, and its `write_files` writes whatever parses. A review truncated mid-file **overwrites a complete file with a partial one**. That is a bug on any provider, and a smaller budget makes it *more* likely — so the review must be fixed in the same slice, not after. |
| The change | (1) Replace the `16_000` constant with a budget derived from the provider's deadline and observed throughput. (2) Bound files-per-call so a bounded budget yields COMPLETE files rather than truncated ones. (3) Make the review emit only what it CHANGES — its own prompt already states that a file missing from its output keeps its old contents, so the delta is already semantically safe and it removes the overwrite hazard. |
| Explicitly NOT doing | Per-file-always. Reading 6 measured the Mind's few-big-calls design as its advantage (2 requests against Hermes's 3–16; 35–73 s against 108–413 s), and Hermes shows the deadline is survivable without abandoning it. On a fast enough model the right split is **no split at all**. |
| What would make me stop | If a bounded budget cannot produce complete files without per-file authoring, the trade-off goes back to Pranab rather than being resolved by me — it would mean spending the Mind's measured cost advantage, which is his call and not a detail. |

## E.CB2-B step 1 — truncation becomes a VERDICT, which is what makes bounding the budget safe
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The gap the code had already named | `fileset::parse_file_stream` refuses to decide whether the last file is finished, and says exactly why: a missing trailing newline is equally consistent with a cut-off generation and a model that ended without one, so **"only the API's finish_reason could settle it, and this function does not have it."** A previous version dropped on the ambiguous signal and destroyed a complete `test_tracker.py`. |
| It was never absent | `LLMResponse.stop_reason` carries the API's finish_reason (`stop` / `length` / `eos` / `tool_calls`), and the OpenAI-compatible backend populates it. It was **discarded in one line** — the recipe's `Think` step stored `r.text` and dropped `r.stop_reason`, one move before the only consumer that needs it. **No cross-repo change was required**, which is what I had assumed. |
| The change | `Think` stores `{store_as}__stop_reason` beside the text; `build_recipe` passes each write its OWN step's reason; `publish_file_set` takes the verdict and drops the final file **only** when it is `"length"`; both `write_files` implementations report "was cut and NOT written" instead of "may be incomplete". |
| It cannot change an existing caller | Only the exact string `"length"` drops anything. An absent argument, an unresolved `{{…}}` placeholder, or any other stop reason all behave exactly as before — it **fails toward keeping files**, which is the direction the earlier regression taught. |
| Why this had to come first | Bounding the build's token budget makes truncation *more* common. Without a verdict, a smaller budget converts a **loud** failure (504, voids the leg) into a **quiet** one (a file that looks written and does not parse) — and on the review pass a partial file overwrites a complete one. |
| Four mutants, all watched to fail | `Think` drops the reason; `Think` records a constant `"stop"`; `publish_file_set` ignores the verdict; the recipe stops passing it to the review write. |
| **The first mutant SURVIVED, and that is the finding** | Deleting the `Think` hand-off broke nothing: the recipe interpolates `{{files__stop_reason}}`, a missing variable resolves to nothing, and truncation silently reverts to undetectable. Wiring declared but never proven to carry a **value** — the identical hole to E.CB2-W's missing `export`, found the same day by the same method. Closed with a test that drives a scripted backend reporting `length` and `stop` and asserts the variable arrives. |
| Standing | Workspace **1768/1768**. The budget change itself is next; this is its prerequisite. |

## E.CB2-B step 2 — the build budget is sized to the provider, not to a constant
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The constant | `build_recipe`'s four authoring/review steps each asked for **`max_tokens: 16_000`**, chosen when the only model in use finished it in well under a minute. At the measured 15–22 tok/s that is **740–1,032 s** against NIM's **~302 s** deadline: every build that used its budget was guaranteed to be cut, then retried three times at 302 s each. |
| The shape | `mind_inference::authoring_budget(requested)` **clamps, never replaces**. Callers keep saying what the work needs; the provider's declared deadline lowers it. `YM_PROVIDER_DEADLINE_S` unset → the request is returned **untouched**, so nothing changes for a provider that has declared nothing, and on a model fast enough the right split is **no split at all** — the shape reading 6 measured as the Mind's advantage. |
| The arithmetic, and why the floor | `deadline × 15 tok/s × 0.7`. **15 is the measured floor**, not the mean (15.5 / 16.2 / 21.6 across three models on real legs) — sizing to an average guarantees the slow half is cut, and being early costs a little headroom while being late costs the entire call. At 302 s that is **3,171 tokens ≈ 205 s at the floor**, inside the deadline with room for the round trip. |
| One number, and why not per-provider | The budget is chosen when a recipe is **built**, before the router has picked which link will serve the call, so a per-provider value could not be resolved where it is needed. `YM_PROVIDER_DEADLINE_S` is therefore the **tightest** limit any configured provider imposes. One conservative number is honest; a per-provider number resolved against the wrong provider would not be. |
| Not derived from observed failures | Deliberate. Deriving the deadline from the Mind's own error history makes behaviour depend on what has gone wrong before — hard to reason about, harder to reproduce, and it would drift a graded run's parameters underneath it. |
| Guards, all mutation-verified | The clamp ignoring the deadline; the clamp **raising** instead of lowering; a zero/nonsense deadline accepted as real; and **the recipe reverting to the hard-coded constant**. That last one is the lesson from earlier today applied pre-emptively: `authoring_budget` existing in `mind-inference` says nothing about whether `build_recipe` calls it, so the test asks the recipe. |
| A bad mutant, caught as such | The nonsense-deadline mutant did not apply the first time — `.filter(\|n\| *n > 0)` appears twice in the file — and a mutation that does not apply is not a test result. Re-run against a unique anchor, with the file diffed before and after to confirm it changed and was restored. |
| Standing | Workspace **1774/1774**. Step 3 (the review emitting only what it changes) is next, then the corrected gate. |

## E.CB2-B step 3 — the review emits a DELTA, and only the review may come back empty
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why it mattered | The review re-emitted the **complete** file set, which made it as large as the authoring step — so it hit the provider deadline for the same reason — and created the hazard that matters most: its `write_files` runs on whatever parses, so a review cut mid-file **overwrites a complete file with a partial one**. That is a bug on any provider, and a smaller budget makes it *more* likely, which is why it had to be in this slice rather than after it. |
| The semantics were already safe | Its own prompt says *"a file missing from your output is a file that keeps its old contents"*. Emitting only changed files was always permitted; the prompt simply asked for everything anyway. The rewrite keeps that rule verbatim and stops asking for the rest. |
| Consequence | The healthy case for a review is now **no output at all**. `allow_empty` makes that a success — *"the review changed nothing — the first set stands"* — instead of `the build produced no files`. |
| Only the review, and only a truly empty stream | The **first** write is the deliverable: an empty authoring result stays a real failure, asserted directly. And `allow_empty` excuses only a **blank** stream — prose without markers still errors, so "it ignored the format" stays visible, the same reason `ParsedSet` keeps the preamble as evidence rather than discarding it. |
| Four mutants, each verified to change the file before its verdict was read | The review reverting to the whole set; the review losing the omission-is-not-deletion rule; the **build** write being excused an empty result; the review write no longer allowing one. All caught. |
| Standing | Workspace **1775/1775**. All three code steps of E.CB2-B are in; the corrected gate is what remains. |

## E.CB2-B follow-up — the provider deadline joins the cap and the wall in the run state
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why | It decides how large a single generation the Mind asks for. A reading that changed it mid-run would be measuring two systems and calling them one — the same reason the cap and the wall are carried there. This was owed before any graded reading and is now paid. |
| `0` is a real answer | Unset means **no declared limit** and is carried as `0`, not defaulted to a number. `qwen` is an owned gateway and declares none; defaulting it to some value would silently clamp a profile nobody sized. |
| Guards | Carried in the run state; **refused** on a mid-run change, asserted on the message rather than the exit code (the loader returns 1 for half a dozen unrelated reasons); the same value reloads; nonsense refused rather than coerced. Four mutants, all watched to fail. |
| **The export hole, fourth occurrence — closed at class level** | A deleted `export` has now survived a mutation four times in one day: `CB2_WALL`, the recipe's `stop_reason` hand-off, the provider deadline, and it would have survived again here. The cause is always the same and always invisible: the loader sources the profile under `set -a`, so anything a profile **file** declares is exported as a side effect, and a case that declares its value in the profile proves nothing about the export line. Only a **loader-assigned** value depends on it. Two instance-shaped cases (W8, D7) were written and the hole reappeared with a new variable, so this closes the class. |
| Two ways the class guard was wrong before it was right | (1) It first watched **every** exported name and flagged `CB2_KEY_FILE`, which real profiles supply and the synthetic one does not — a false alarm, and a guard that cries wolf gets deleted. Narrowed to loader-assigned names. (2) It then derived its watch list **from the export line itself**, so removing a name un-watched it: the deleted export was caught only by accident, through the "watches at least four" assertion. **A guard that reads the line under test cannot catch a removal from it.** The watch list now comes from what the loader *assigns*. |
| Standing | cb2n suite **180 checks, 0 disagreements**; re-derives byte-exactly. |

## E.CB2-B follow-up 2 — every large budget is now clamped or an EXPLAINED exception
| Site | Budget | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `build_recipe` × 4 | 16,000 | **clamped** (shipped earlier) |
| `code.rs` forge-build | 7,500 | **clamped** — same defect in the venture lane: three complete files in one generation, ~500 s at the measured floor |
| `delegate.rs` critic × 3 | 15,000 | **EXEMPT, with the reason** |
| `lib.rs` dispatch | 8,000 | **EXEMPT, with the reason** |
| `mind-recipes` planner | 8,000 | outside the scanned files; headroom for a JSON plan, not a deliverable |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The finding that stopped a blanket fix | Only **one** of the six oversized budgets was the same defect. The critic's own comment is a direct warning against clamping it: *"a critique over a 12KB excerpt came back EMPTY at 2000… a judge that cannot afford to explain itself defaults to approving."* Truncating a judge into silent approval is **strictly worse** than the 504 it would prevent. Same for dispatch, where the budget carries a whole HTML page inside tool arguments and a small one yields unparseable JSON. |
| So they are visible instead of "fixed" | A registry: clamp, or list the site with a reason a reviewer can weigh. A budget added tomorrow either clamps or lands in front of someone. |
| The guard failed twice on its way to being right, both times usefully | It flagged `lib.rs:12028` because the literal is `8000` and my exemption said `8_000` — so exemptions are now keyed by **value**, since an exemption matching one spelling stops covering the site the day someone reformats it. And I had first left `lib.rs` out of the scanned files entirely, which would have hidden the dispatch budget — the exact "a list is only as complete as its author remembered" failure this registry exists to prevent. |
| **A mistake of mine worth recording** | I undid a mutation with `git checkout HEAD -- fileset_tests.rs` while that file held **uncommitted** work, and destroyed the registry guard I had just written. I had been backing up `code.rs` and `delegate.rs` with `cp` for exactly this reason and then reached for git on a third file out of habit. Rule: **mutate against a committed baseline, or restore from a copy — never `git checkout` a file carrying uncommitted work.** |
| Standing | Workspace green; the registry is the completeness wall for generation budgets. |

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| T1 | **2/11** | **11/11** | 3 / 16 | 171 s / 201 s |
| T2 | **6/6** | 4/6 | 3 / 5 | 101 s / 74 s |
| T3 | 9/10 | 9/10 | 3 / 15 | 71 s / 156 s |
| **total** | **17/27** | **24/27** | | |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Validity | All six legs **valid**: `void false`, `disqualified false`, `dq_independent false`, accounting agrees, model identity correct, zero key-leak hits, zero upstream 5xx across the whole reading. Nothing was rerun. The sequence ran exactly as preregistered. |
| The result | **Hermes wins by 7.** The entire gap is T1: the Mind's artifact was a 2,814-byte `server.py` with no `index.html`, and the server never started — `ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`. The Mind won T2 6/6 against 4/6 and tied T3 at 9/10. |
| My prediction, scored | I predicted the Mind would complete all three void-free — **correct**. I explicitly did not predict a win — **correct, and it lost**. Recording both halves, since the point of writing a prediction down is that it can be wrong. |
| What this does NOT settle | Whether the loss is variance or a regression from my own clamp. The two gate legs scored **11/11 twice on T1 with the same profile, the same clamp active, and the same deadline** — so the budget demonstrably suffices for a full T1 artifact. Three T1 samples now read 11/11, 11/11, 2/11. That spread is the finding, and it is not one I can resolve by staring at it. |
| The suspicion I must not wave away | The gate legs ran binary `87788793` (a400391); this reading ran `2632e857` (6350026). The only product change between them is the forge clamp in `code.rs`, a lane this benchmark does not use — so causation is implausible, but "implausible" is not "measured", and I have been wrong about exactly that shape of reasoning four times today. |
| A defect in my own instrumentation, found by using it | The crash guard adds `checker_completed` to the verdict, which inflates the denominator: the raw file reads `2/5` for a task with **11** checks. The tally above excludes it, but the verdict as written is misleading to anyone reading it directly. `checker_completed` should be reported beside the score, not inside it. |
| What the guard did earn | Without it, the Mind's T1 would have produced **no verdict at all** — the checker crashed on the navigation after the site failed to come up. Instead the reading has a scoreable, explainable failure. |
| Not doing | Rerunning T1 to get a better number. It was not void; the one declared rerun does not apply; and re-rolling a leg until it looks better is the exact thing the void rule exists to prevent. |
| Standing across readings | 5: Hermes 22–4. 6: Mind 26–25. 7: **Hermes 24–17**. Reading 6's own caution — "do NOT claim a win from 26-25, both systems are variable" — applies symmetrically, and reading 7 is the demonstration. |

## E.CB2-B2 — T1 deep dive: the loss was MY clamp, and my gate could not have caught it
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The artifact said it outright | Reading 7's `RESULT.md`: *"(1 files: run.sh) — **the generation hit its token limit, so server.py was cut and NOT written**"*. Not variance. The authoring generation hit the 3,171-token clamp, the truncation verdict correctly refused to ship a cut file, and the leg delivered `run.sh` alone. |
| Only the largest deliverable hit it | T1 `stop_reason: length` → **2/11**. T2 `stop` → 9 files → **6/6**. T3 `stop` → 6 files → **9/10**. The risk is a function of the largest **single file**, not the task's total: T2 used *more* files and T1 used *more* tokens overall (6,354 vs 5,561) — what mattered was one file that would not fit one generation. |
| The clamp sits exactly on T1's boundary | 3,171 per generation. gate1 passed at 5,982 total completion tokens, gate2 at 5,389, reading 7 **failed at 6,354**. Above the line sometimes, below it others. |
| Why decomposition decided it | gate1's 11/11 artifact was `server.py` (3,384 B) + `run.sh` + `data/` + `templates/` — multi-file, every generation fits. Reading 7's model wrote one monolithic `server.py` and ran out mid-handler. |
| **The finding about my method** | **Neither gate leg, nor either earlier oss20 leg, ever hit the token limit** — all four say "built" with no truncation note. My gate (two void-free legs AND no score regression) proved the clamp does not break the easy case. **Nothing in it exercised the case the clamp creates.** I had written the risk down in the preregistration — "a smaller budget alone trades a loud failure for a quiet one" — mitigated the quiet half with the truncation verdict, and shipped without the other half. |
| The general rule | **A gate must exercise the failure mode a change INTRODUCES, not only the one it removes.** This is the same shape as three other holes today: the liveness suite whose only inconclusive case was code 000; and four surviving `export` mutants whose cases all took the path that did not depend on the export. |
| Fix 1 — the completion pass | A third authoring call between the first write and the review: *"here is what landed, and it says if one was cut — write only what is missing, complete."* No conditional step is needed, because the writer's own message carries the fact and an empty answer is already a success under `allow_empty`. A complete set costs one cheap "nothing to add" call. |
| The cost ceiling moved, deliberately | From two model calls to three, with the reason recorded at the assertion. The ceiling exists to prevent an **open repair loop**; three fixed calls is still a ceiling. Measured cost of not having it: 2/11 versus 11/11, the entire margin of reading 7. |
| Fix 2 — **the same pattern in another lane, and it was mine** | The venture forge authors a file set the same way, parses the blocks **inline** rather than through `publish_file_set`, and had **no truncation verdict at all** — so it wrote a cut file silently. I made that strictly more likely an hour earlier by clamping its budget without giving it the protection. Now it consults `r.stop_reason`, drops only the final block, and says so. A fix applied only where the failure was observed is half a fix. |
| Tests restated as invariants, not positions | The recipe tests asserted "exactly two writes, exactly two thinks" and broke the moment a pass was added. They now assert what must be **true**: the first write is the deliverable and may not be empty; every later write improves and may be; every write is told its own generation's stop reason; no pass overtakes another; the call ceiling is fixed. |
| Standing | Workspace **1777/1777**; six mutants across both fixes, all watched to fail. |

## E.CB2-B2 validation — PREREGISTERED, with the failure mode FORCED rather than awaited
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why forced | My last gate never truncated once in four legs, so it validated nothing about the case the clamp creates. Waiting for a natural truncation is waiting for luck. `nim-oss20-tight` declares a **180 s** deadline — 1,890 tokens per generation instead of 3,171 — which guarantees T1's *set* will not fit one generation while each individual *file* still does. That is precisely the regime the completion pass exists for. |
| A real A/B, not a before-and-after story | Same profile, same task, same box, two binaries: **control** `87788793` (a400391 — the clamp, **no** completion pass) and **treatment** the build from `6469f5f`. `CB2_MIND_BINARY` selects, so nothing is swapped underneath. |
| **The run is INCONCLUSIVE unless a truncation is actually observed** | At least one leg must report `cut and NOT written`. If neither does, 180 s was not tight enough, the failure mode was again not exercised, and **the fix stays UNVALIDATED and I say so** — rather than letting clean legs stand in for it a second time. |
| Prediction, recorded to be wrong | Control ≈ **2/11** (truncated, main file dropped, nothing to recover it). Treatment **≥ 9/11** (truncated, then completed). If the treatment does not recover, the completion pass does not work and that is the finding. |
| What would make me stop | If the treatment truncates and *still* fails, I will not tune the deadline until it passes. The number is preregistered; moving it after seeing the result is fitting the test to the answer. |
| Not a reading profile | `nim-oss20-tight` deliberately handicaps the system. Nothing graded may run on it, and it is marked so in the file. |

## E.CB2-B2 validation — INCONCLUSIVE by its own criterion, and it still paid for itself
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Result | Control and treatment failed **identically**, twice: `the build produced no files`, 2/11 each, 1,902 completion tokens each. |
| **Inconclusive, per the preregistered rule** | The gate said: *"the run is INCONCLUSIVE unless a truncation is actually observed — at least one leg must report `cut and NOT written`."* Neither did. **Zero file markers** were emitted at 1,890 tokens: the model spent the budget on preamble and never reached a file. So the regime tested was "budget below the model's preamble", not "the set does not fit but each file does". **The completion pass remains UNVALIDATED and I am not claiming it works.** |
| Why 180 s was the wrong number | Chosen by arithmetic — one file ≈ 850 tokens, the set > 3,171 — which ignored what the model spends *before* the first marker. The constraint is the model's behaviour, not my division. |
| What it found anyway, which is the point of forcing failures | A real defect the clean-path gate could never have shown: when the authoring pass produces **only** a cut file, the first write failed hard (`ErrorAction::Fail`) and killed the chain **before** the completion pass that exists to finish it. **The recovery path was unreachable exactly when it was needed.** Now "everything was cut" returns a recoverable outcome and names what was lost, while "wrote prose" still fails — nothing to recover there, and it must not be retried forever. Both mutants watched to fail. |
| What I will NOT do | Tune the deadline until the treatment passes. The number was preregistered; moving it after seeing the outcome is fitting the test to the answer, and the whole reason this experiment exists is that I did the cheap version of that once already. |
| Next, declared before running | Validate at the **real 302 s deadline** — no tuned parameter at all — repeating T1 until a truncation is observed, up to **six legs**. Reading 7 truncated on its first T1 at that setting and the gate legs did not, so roughly one in three; six legs is about a 90% chance of reaching the regime. **If six legs produce no truncation, I report the fix as unvalidated and say the failure is too rare to force at the real setting** rather than inventing a number that makes it appear. |

## E.CB2-B2 — the regime was reached, and the completion pass worked but shipped a fenced file
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Validation at the REAL 302 s deadline, no tuned parameter | leg 1 **11/11** (4 files, no truncation) · leg 2 **11/11** (4 files, no truncation) · **leg 3 TRUNCATED** → the regime the last experiment failed to reach. Roughly one T1 in three, as reading 7 suggested. |
| The completion pass **ran and worked** | 4 model requests instead of 3, 8,179 completion tokens instead of 6,354, and it wrote the missing file under **the right name** — `main.py`, matching what `run.sh` invokes. The recovery machinery is sound. |
| It still scored 2/11, for a different reason | The recovered `main.py` begins with a **markdown fence**. It was written verbatim, did not parse, the site never came up. **The content was correct; the wrapper killed it.** |
| The lesson was already in the codebase | `publish_page` says it outright: *"A model asked for 'only the HTML' still wraps it in a ```html fence about half the time. Refusing that would fail the chain on a formatting habit, so unwrap it here — the alternative is a prompt that has to win every time."* `publish_page` unwraps. The file-set lane never did, and the prompt lost. **Third time today a fix existed in one lane and was missing from its twin.** |
| Fix | `unfence()` strips ONE wrapping fence, and only when the first non-empty line opens one *and* the last is a bare closing fence — so a Markdown file that merely contains fenced blocks keeps every one. |
| **A mutant found my fix was half-applied** | There are three `FileEntry` construction sites; I patched one. The **final** file in a stream is built on a different path — so the last file was never unfenced, which is *exactly the motivating case*: a completion pass emitting one file makes that file the final one. **My fix would not have fixed the bug that motivated it.** Caught only because a surviving mutant forced me to probe what the code actually did instead of what I traced it doing. |
| Four mutants, all now caught | Both unfence calls removed; the closing-fence requirement dropped; the opening-fence requirement dropped; a one-line fence treated as a wrapper. Each verified to change the file before its verdict was read. |
| A shell trap that made three "SURVIVED" verdicts meaningless | `sed -i "$m"` with backticks inside **double quotes** performs command substitution, so the pattern was mangled and the file never changed. The rule I already had — *verify the mutant changed the file* — is the only reason this was caught; the mutation harness now hashes the file before and after. |
| Standing | Workspace **1779/1779**. |

## E.CB2-B2 — GATE MET: a leg TRUNCATED and RECOVERED to 11/11
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The leg | Truncated (`templates/index.html` cut and refused by the first write), then **recovered to 11/11** — the preregistered bar was ≥ 9/11. 4 model requests, 6,978 completion tokens, 3 files, 150.8 s, `void false`. |
| The whole chain, verified link by link | Authoring generation **cut** → truncation detected from `stop_reason` and the partial file **refused** → the writer **names what was lost** → the completion pass **rewrites it** → `unfence` leaves it parseable → `run.sh` points at a `server.py` that starts `#!/usr/bin/env python3` and parses → **every check passes**. |
| What this cost | One extra model call on the legs that need it (4 instead of 3). Legs that do not truncate pay one cheap "nothing to add" call. Against Hermes's 15–16 requests on T1, the Mind is still at 3–4. |
| Honest limits | **n = 1** for a truncating leg that recovers. The gate asked for one and got it; that is the claim and no more. The ~1-in-3 truncation rate on T1 means a six-leg reading should expect one or two of these, so the next reading is itself the wider sample. |
| The three defects, all now closed | (1) the clamp cuts the authoring generation — mitigated by recovery rather than by loosening the clamp; (2) an all-cut pass killed the chain before recovery could run; (3) the recovered file arrived wrapped in a markdown fence. Each was hidden by the one before it, and each was only reachable by forcing the failure rather than waiting for it. |
| The method that found all three | Force the failure mode a change introduces. Two clean legs proved nothing; the first forced run found defect 2; the real-deadline repetition found defect 3; a surviving mutant found my fix for defect 3 was applied to only one of three call sites — **the fix would not have fixed the bug that motivated it**. |

## E.LOOP-T1 — TWIN-LANE SHADOWING: three guards are not in force on the live page path
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| How it was found | Pranab: *"this is basically loop engineering… let's dig deeper."* So instead of waiting for the next failure, I diffed the **twin lanes** — capabilities that exist in more than one dispatch — which is the mechanically findable form of the defect class that has now bitten three times today. |
| The routing, verified rather than assumed | `run_tool` consults the plugin registry **first** and `return`s on a hit, so a registered capability **shadows** the built-in `match`. The `dashboards` spec declares `["make_dashboard", "publish_page"]` and is `enabled: true` by default → **`publish_page` runs the capability version.** `write_files` is *not* in that list, so it correctly reaches the guarded built-in. |
| What the shadowed (dead) implementation has that the live one lacks | (1) **fence unwrapping** — `extract_document`, with the comment "the alternative is a prompt that has to win every time"; (2) the **document + truncation gate** — refusing a page cut mid-generation, which its own comment calls preventing *"the worst outcome available: a live URL, an announcement that it is ready, and a page that is a hero followed by nothing"*; (3) **E.PAGE1** — `required_filename` outranking the page's `<title>`. |
| Why (3) matters beyond tidiness | E.PAGE1 exists because "a brief asking for `index.html` got a slug of its `<title>` instead". Reading 6 attributed the Mind's twelve-point gap to "plumbing rather than model capability — one file instead of many, a router rebadging code work as a page, and **a filename**." That fix is not in force on the path an agent actually calls. |
| Why reading 6 still saw a refusal | Not from this tool. The page **recipe** carries its own repair guard using the same `is_publishable_document`, which the built-in's comment names ("ONE gate, shared with the page recipe's repair guard"). The recipe path is guarded; a **direct tool call is not**. |
| Nothing pins the routing | No test asserts which of the two implementations answers `publish_page`. The page-lane tests exercise the recipe against a stub tool host, so they cannot see it. |
| The fix, and why this shape | **One source of truth**: the capability defers so the single guarded implementation runs, rather than the guards being copied into a second place to drift again. The codebase already uses this reasoning for `contains_secret` — "the SAME function guarding memory writes (one source of truth)". |
| Kill criteria | A test must pin that `publish_page` reaches the guarded implementation, and each of the three guards must be shown to apply on the live path. Mutants: re-add the capability arm; drop each guard. |

## E.LOOP-T1 — RESULT: one shadowing case, fixed at the class level
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The census | 96 plugin-declared tools, 473 built-in dispatch arms, 9 capability arms. Intersecting all three — declared **and** answered by a capability **and** implemented by the built-in — yields exactly **one**: `publish_page`. |
| Why only one | `write_files` is answered by a capability but **not plugin-declared**, so routing never reaches it and the guarded built-in runs. `make_dashboard` is declared and answered, but the built-in has no arm — the capability is its only implementation. The scan distinguishes these three situations, which is what makes the single hit meaningful rather than alarming. |
| Fix | The capability **defers** (`"publish_page" => return None`) so the one guarded implementation runs. Guards were not copied into a second place to drift apart again — the same reasoning the codebase already applies to `contains_secret` ("one source of truth"). The plugin spec still owns the tool for enablement and for the model-facing description; only the **behaviour** moved to one place. |
| The guard is the class, not the case | The test re-derives the intersection from the three sources every run. A future capability arm for a plugin-declared tool the built-in also implements must **defer** or be listed with a reason — silence is what let this one through. It also asserts the scan can still SEE (≥5 capability arms, ≥50 built-in arms, `publish_page` still declared), so it cannot pass vacuously if a parse breaks. |
| Mutation | Restoring the shadowing arm is caught. |
| What is now in force on the live page path | Fence unwrapping; refusal of a document cut mid-generation; and E.PAGE1's `required_filename` precedence. **All three were previously live in unreachable code.** |
| Honest scope | This changes which implementation answers `publish_page`. It is a behaviour change on the agent path, gated by the workspace suite (1780/1780) and by the page-lane recipe tests, but **not yet exercised by a leg**. It should be visible in the next reading rather than asserted now. |

## E.CB2-B3 — the completion pass is skipped when nothing was cut
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why | Most builds are not truncated. Spending a model call on every one trades reading 7's failure for a permanent tax on the Mind's cheapest column — 2 requests against Hermes's 3–16 is what reading 6 measured as its advantage. |
| **A correction I owe** | I said the recipe engine had "only `Tool`/`Think`/`ThinkCited` — no loop", and used that to justify making the completion pass unconditional. It has **twelve** step kinds including `JumpIf`, and the **page lane already guards its repair the same way**, stating the argument I should have found: *"the extra call is spent only where the publish would have failed, which is the whole cost argument."* My variant scan had been truncated and I did not check it. |
| The guard | `JumpIf { Not(VarContains { var: "project_url", substring: "was cut" }) } → the review step`. It keys on the **writer's own message**, which says "was cut and NOT written" exactly when a generation was truncated. A clean build now jumps straight to the review and is byte-identical to before this slice. |
| Cost restored | Clean build: **2 model calls** (author + review), as before E.CB2-B2. Truncated build: 3. The recovery is paid for only where it is needed. |
| Mutants, all caught | The guard removed entirely; the jump **overshooting** the review (which would silently drop the quality round); the condition inverted; the guard reading the wrong variable. |
| **A refinement of my own mutation rule** | The removal mutant first reported SURVIVED — because my mutation added an attribute rather than deleting the step. It changed the file, so it passed the "did it apply" check, while **not being the mutation I had named**. Verifying the file changed is not enough: the change must be the one described, and the harness now asserts the construct is genuinely gone. |

## E.CB2-P — PLAN-THEN-AUTHOR, sized to MEASURED limits (Pranab's proposal, preregistered)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The proposal | Pranab: *"the first call will be planning and create the recipe, then execute step by step… if models know, or by provider we know, what configs produce the most optimal results, that would be dynamically adjusted."* |
| The half the evidence supports | **Decomposition decided every T1 outcome measured today.** Multi-file layouts (`server.py` + `run.sh` + `data/` + `templates/`) scored 11/11; single monolithic files were cut and scored 2/11. The model chose that decomposition **implicitly and blind** — it is never told the budget it must fit. A planning step makes the choice explicit and checkable **before** any content is generated. |
| The half I am pushing back on | **A model's self-report about its own limits is remembered, not measured.** This codebase already carries the lesson: `myself`/`my_config` exists because, asked what LLMs it was using, the mind "confidently invented a five-backend failover chain and a list of mounted packs that do not exist", and the fix states the rule — *"Self-configuration is STATE, and state is measured, never remembered."* Asking a model for its optimal `max_tokens` yields a plausible number with nothing behind it. |
| What we DO know, because it was measured | NIM's **~302 s** per-request deadline (four 504s, two models, a 25 ms band); throughput **15–22 tok/s**, sized to the floor; a fixed **preamble cost** (at 1,890 tokens the model emitted zero file markers); a **~1-in-3** T1 truncation rate. All from our own telemetry — `by_status` buckets, `stop_reason`, usage counts — none from the model. |
| The design | (1) A **plan** step emitting a file list with rough sizes, **told the per-generation budget**. (2) The plan is **checked** against that budget; a file estimated over it is sent back to be split, or the run reports that the brief cannot be built within the provider's limit. (3) Author in **budget-sized GROUPS**, not strictly per file. (4) Budget derived from the run state's provider deadline × the measured throughput floor — never from self-report. |
| Why groups, not per file | Strict per-file authoring costs 1 + N calls: for T1 that is 5 against today's 2, spending the exact cost advantage reading 6 measured (2 requests against Hermes's 3–16). Grouping to fill a budget gives the same fits-by-construction guarantee at ≈ 1 + ceil(total ÷ budget) ≈ 3. |
| Gate — and it must exercise what this change INTRODUCES | Today's recurring lesson. A plan-then-author design fails in a **new** way: **the plan is wrong** — an underestimated file still overruns, or the planner lists files the author then ignores. So the gate is not "legs pass": it must include a leg where a planned file **exceeds** its estimate, and show that the outcome is a *reported* failure or a split, never a silently truncated deliverable. |
| Kill criterion | If plan-then-author cannot beat the current arrangement on **both** score and call count across the measured T1 variance, it does not ship — the completion pass already recovers truncation at 2 calls on clean builds. |

## E.CB2-P step 1 — the author is TOLD its measured budget (preregistered measurement)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The change | The authoring prompt now states the affordable token count and what to do with it: *"several complete files beat one large one — split a big program by responsibility rather than writing one file you cannot finish."* No extra model call. |
| Measured, never asked | The number is the run state's provider deadline × the observed throughput floor. With **no** declared limit, **no number is stated** — inventing one would be exactly the self-report this design refuses, and a mutant that asserts a budget regardless is caught. |
| Baseline, from legs already run at the 302 s deadline | **3 token-limit truncations in 8 T1 legs** (clean: gate1, gate2, v1, v2, e2e1; cut: reading 7, v3, e2e2). |
| What I will run | 8 T1 legs with the budget-aware prompt, same profile, same binary lineage. |
| **Stated before the result** | 8 legs is a small sample. A drop from 3/8 to 0/8 is **suggestive, not conclusive** (Fisher p ≈ 0.08), and I will report it as such rather than as proof. What would be conclusive is the truncation rate over a longer run, which the next readings supply for free. |
| Kill criterion | If truncations do not fall, the prompt is not doing the work and the answer is the **plan step** — an explicit file list checked against the budget — not a louder instruction. If scores fall, it ships nothing. |

## E.CB2-P — the budget note stopped the truncations and revealed what was underneath
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Truncation | **0 in the first 4 legs**, against a 3-in-8 baseline, and every leg decomposed the way the note asked — `run.sh` + `server.py` + `templates/` + `data/`. The blind-decomposition problem is answered. |
| But the scores did not follow | Legs 1–2 scored 11/11; legs 3 and 4 scored **7/11 and 2/11 with NO truncation**. Fixing one failure mode exposed the next, which is the honest shape of this kind of work. |
| **Leg 4, diagnosed by RUNNING it** | The artifact is complete, well-formed and parses. It dies at import: `from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, TCPServer` → **`TCPServer` is in `socketserver`**. `site_up` fails, `ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`, 2/11. **The model review step read this file and approved it.** One execution finds it in under a second. |
| Leg 3 for contrast | Starts cleanly and serves; fails four checks for unrelated reasons. So the two low scores have **different causes**, and only one descends from the truncation family. |
| What this settles | ARCH8 listed "verify by executing" third. It is **first**. Truncation is now largely handled, and what remains are **runtime** failures a model reviewer cannot see by reading — the review step's own comment already said so: *"a model checking its own work is weaker than executing it."* This is that sentence, measured, on leg 4 of a live run. |
| The caution that does not go away | Executing generated code is a security decision. It was tried inside the benchmark container and abandoned for good reasons, and nothing here changes that. The question is whether a **box that already trusts the mind** should run its own build before announcing it — which is a different question, and one nobody has asked. |
| Honest accounting of the change | The budget note is a **partial** win: it removes truncation without improving the score distribution, because the next failure was waiting underneath. I will not claim it as a score improvement. |

| | baseline | with the budget note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| truncated | **3/8** | **1/8** — and that one **recovered to 11/11** |
| scores | 11,11,11,11,2,11,11,2 | 11,11,7,2,11,11,11,8 |
| mean | **8.75/11** | **9.00/11** |

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| **The statistic, as preregistered** | Fisher exact two-tailed on the truncation table: **p = 0.57**. The drop from 3/8 to 1/8 is **not statistically distinguishable from noise** at this n. I said before running that 8 legs could only be suggestive, and it is less than that. |
| What IS solid, and is not a rate | **Mechanistic**: every one of the 8 legs decomposed the way the note asked — `run.sh` + `server.py` + `templates/` + `data/` — where the baseline produced monoliths. The instruction demonstrably changes the model's decomposition; whether that translates to fewer cuts needs more legs than a change of this size deserves. |
| The mean did not move | 8.75 → 9.00. **The ceiling moved rather than lifted**: failures shifted from truncation to runtime defects, which is exactly what the preregistration predicted and refused to claim as an improvement. |
| The remaining ceiling, named | Leg 4 — 2/11, complete and parseable, dead at import (`TCPServer` imported from `http.server`). Leg 3 — 7/11, starts and serves, fails four checks. Leg 8 — 8/11. **None of these is a truncation descendant, and none is visible to a model reading its own files.** |
| Verdict on the change | **Keep it**: it costs nothing (no extra call), it demonstrably changes decomposition, the one truncation that occurred recovered fully, and it removes a failure mode whose recovery costs a model call. **But it is not a score improvement and is not recorded as one.** |
| What this measurement actually bought | The clearest possible statement of where the next value is. With truncation handled, the distribution is capped by defects that only execution can find. That is now the top of the ARCH8 list on evidence, not on argument. |

## E.CB2-P step 2 (plan-then-author) — KILLED by its own preregistered criterion
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The criterion, written before the measurement | *"If plan-then-author cannot beat the current arrangement on **both** score and call count, it does not ship."* |
| What the measurement showed | The **cheap** version achieved what the expensive one was for. All 8 legs decomposed by responsibility — `run.sh` + `server.py` + `templates/` + `data/` — from a prompt sentence costing **zero extra calls**. A plan step would spend a model call to produce a decomposition the author now produces for free. |
| So it fails both halves | It cannot beat the current call count (it adds one), and it cannot beat the score, because the score is no longer limited by decomposition — it is limited by **runtime defects a plan cannot see**. Leg 4's plan was fine; its `import` was wrong. |
| Recorded rather than quietly dropped | Pranab proposed plan-then-execute and the instinct was right — decomposition *was* the problem. The cheapest expression of that instinct solved it, so the expensive one is not owed. If a future task shows decomposition failing where a prompt cannot fix it, this becomes live again and the preregistration stands. |

## E.LOOP-S — the SCHEDULING loops audited for today's defect classes: NO defect found
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Why look | Six defects in the **work** loops in one day (clamp, unreachable recovery, fence, half-applied fix, twin-lane shadowing, budget-blind decomposition). The obvious next question is whether the **scheduling** loops carry the same classes. |
| What was checked | Every `wake_tick` call site in `loops.rs` (18 of them), against the class "a loop that is **silent when it does not act**" — where absence of a row cannot be told from absence of instrumentation. |
| The hypothesis, and it was wrong | I expected `knock` to record nothing when held for no presence, on the strength of a memory that a debugging session had used "absence of rows" as its diagnostic signal. **It records `HeldReason::NoPresence`**, as do `digest` and `ask` — and a test already asserts all three flags exist and that the reason appears exactly five times. The memory described an upstream idle-gate condition, not this one. |
| Verdict | **No defect found.** The scheduling loops are better instrumented than the work loops, which is unsurprising: L1, L1b and L1d were dedicated slices on exactly this, and the work loops never had one. |
| Why record a negative result | It says where **not** to look, and it is the difference between "audited and clean" and "not audited". Reporting only the hunts that find something is how a census becomes a highlight reel. I was once 0-for-3 on defect claims in one subsystem by not checking first. |
| Where the remaining value is | Not here. It is the **execution** gap — a decision I have deliberately not made alone, since running generated code is a security question before an engineering one. |

## E.LOOP-I — a runtime-defect check that needs NO execution: sized before building
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The insight | To learn that `from http.server import TCPServer` is wrong, only **`http.server`** — a standard-library module — has to be imported. The artifact is **parsed, never executed**. That puts a real subset of runtime defects inside reach **without** answering whether generated code may be run, which is a security decision and not mine to take. |
| Sized on real artifacts before building anything | Run over 11 T1 artifacts produced today: **2 flagged, 0 false positives.** The two flagged are the two worst scores in the set — p4 (**2/11**, the `TCPServer` import that the model review approved) and v3 (**2/11**, an unparseable file). All six 11/11 legs are clean, as are the 7/11, 8/11 and 9/11 ones. |
| A false positive found and fixed during the sizing | The first version flagged `from http import server` on a leg whose server **started fine** — a submodule import is valid Python even though `hasattr(http, "server")` is false until it is imported. It now resolves the submodule before accusing anyone. **A checker that cries wolf gets turned off**, which is the same reasoning that narrowed the literal scanner earlier today. |
| What it would be worth | p4 is the only leg in the current run it catches; repairing that one moves the 8-leg mean from **9.0 → ~10.1**. It cannot catch p3, p8 or r7, whose defects are behavioural rather than structural — those still need execution. |
| Where it would go | Not a new step: feed the findings **into the existing review round** as concrete lines ("these imports do not resolve"), so the repair is aimed instead of guessed. The review already re-emits only what it changes. |
| **The decision I am flagging rather than taking** | The check is Python-specific and needs `python3` on the box to introspect the stdlib. That is a **runtime dependency on the mind**, far milder than executing generated code but still a design choice, and it degrades to a skip where python3 is absent. I am not adding a dependency to the mind's runtime unilaterally at the end of a long session. |
| Honest limit | This is a **subset**. It catches "the file cannot possibly run"; it cannot catch "the file runs and does the wrong thing", which is what p3 and p8 are. Execution remains the only answer to those, and that question stays with Pranab and Codex. |

## E.LOOP-T1b — the dead duplicate removed, and the guard widened to catch duplicates not only shadows
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| What was left | `capabilities.rs` carried a `write_files` arm that **no `PluginSpec` declares**, so `handler_for_tool` never routes to it and it has never run. It nonetheless held a **second copy** of the writer's logic — the truncation verdict, `allow_empty`, the all-cut recovery — all of which I kept in step **by hand** earlier today without noticing it was dead. |
| Why a dead copy is not harmless | It is the copy the next person fixes instead of the live one, and it becomes a **real shadow** the moment someone adds the tool to a spec. Its twin, `publish_page`, was live and three guards behind — same file, same shape, and only the routing differed. |
| Fix | It defers, like `publish_page`. One guarded implementation, no second copy to drift. |
| The guard was too narrow and now is not | It only flagged arms whose tool was **plugin-declared** — so it could not have seen this one, because the hazard exists *before* the routing does. It now flags any capability arm duplicating a built-in, declared or not; `declared` survives only to sharpen the message. |
| Mutants | Both deferrals removed independently, each caught, and each mutation asserted to have actually removed the deferral it names. |
| Standing | Workspace **1782/1782**. |

## E.PAGE1 — the rule is now testable, and the shadow had made it unverifiable as well as unreachable
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The situation | E.PAGE1 says a filename the TASK required outranks the page's `<title>` — it exists because a brief asking for `index.html` got a slug of its title, and reading 6 named that as part of the Mind's gap. The rule was **correct, unreachable** (a capability shadowed it — E.LOOP-T1) **and unverifiable** (it lived inline in a match arm), all at once. |
| Fix | Extracted as `page_filename(required, html, name)` — a pure function that can be asked. The precedence is pinned: a requirement wins; with none, the title; then the caller's name; then `"page"`. An **empty** requirement is not a requirement and falls through rather than producing `""`. |
| Mutants caught | The title outranking the requirement again (the original bug); an empty requirement counting as one; the arm hardcoding a name beside the rule; the arm no longer reading `required_filename`. |
| **A weak assertion, found by mutating it** | The first wiring check asked whether the arm *contains* `page_filename(` — and a mutant that called it and **threw the result away** passed. Tightened to require the arm to **bind the name from** the rule. |
| Stated rather than glossed | This is a **source assertion and cannot prove behaviour**; a determined refactor defeats it. It catches the realistic regression — someone reintroducing a hardcoded name beside the rule — and saying what a check cannot do is part of the check. |
| Fifth instance today of one class | A value declared and never proven to arrive: `CB2_WALL`'s export, the `Think` stop-reason hand-off, `CB2_PROVIDER_DEADLINE_S`, `authoring_budget` in the recipe, and now the filename rule in the publisher. Every one was found by mutation, none by reading. |
| Standing | Workspace **1783/1783**. |

## E.LOOP-F — the forge has four unbounded retries, and its own guard cannot fire (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The finding | Four stages report *"will retry next tick"* and leave the stage unchanged: brainstorm synthesis unparsable, brainstorm failed, spec unparsable, build emitted no parseable files. **None increments anything.** The venture state is `{id, idea, stage, iter, max_iter, log, updated_ms}` — there is no per-stage attempt counter. |
| Why the existing guard cannot catch it | `forge_due()` treats a venture as due when `now - updated_ms > 900_000`. But `updated_ms` is refreshed **after the match, on every tick**, including every failure path — so a failing venture always looks freshly updated and simply becomes due again 15 minutes later. **The guard's firing condition is destroyed by the very failure it would otherwise bound.** Same shape as the recovery path that was unreachable exactly when needed. |
| The only stop is a human | `forge_cmd("kill")` is an **owner command**. A venture whose spec never parses retries every 15 minutes, one model call at a time, until a person notices. A loop that requires human intervention to stop is not bounded — which is ARCH7's whole thesis and ARCH8's own rule: *"bound every loop, and make the bound visible."* |
| The precedent is already in the file | `max_iter: 2` bounds the rate→iterate loop and exits **honestly**: *"shipped AS-IS at 6/10 after exhausting 2 iterations — honest ceiling, artifacts kept for review."* The parse-failure paths deserve the same treatment, not a different invention. |
| The change | A per-stage attempt counter, reset whenever the stage **advances** so slow progress is never punished, and a terminal stop after a small bound that **says which stage gave up and why**. Terminal is `killed`, because `st != "shipped" && st != "killed"` is the non-terminal test in three places and a new stage name would silently keep the venture due. |
| Kill criteria | A venture failing the same stage N times must stop; it must say which stage and why; a venture that advances must reset its count. Mutants: the counter removed; the counter never reset on advance; the bound not applied. |
| Honest scope | This is **spend and noise**, not correctness — the retries are slow (4 calls/hour) and the artifacts are untouched. It is worth fixing because "the owner can kill it" is the pattern this codebase criticises elsewhere, not because anything is on fire. |

### E.LOOP-F — RESULT: shipped, and the fix's own first version was wrong
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Shipped | A venture carries `stage_tries`/`max_stage_tries` (3). A tick ending on the stage it entered counts; a tick that advances clears the count. At the bound the venture goes terminal and the report names the stage and the attempt count, following `max_iter`'s honest-ceiling precedent. |
| The bound cannot punish progress | Checked rather than assumed: every stage arm advances on its success path (brainstorm→research→spec→build→test→rate→iterate→ship/kill/build), so a same-stage tick is *always* a failure. The build↔iterate cycle is bounded separately by `max_iter`, and each transition in it clears the count. |
| **The first version of the fix was wrong** | The strong-builder path advances build→test and **returns early**, skipping the tick's bookkeeping entirely — so a venture that failed to build twice and then succeeded would arrive at `test` carrying two failed attempts and die on its first hiccup. The give-up would have killed exactly the ventures that had just started working. Found by auditing whether the bound could punish progress, not by a test. |
| The fix for the fix | Not a patch to that one call site — the next early return would reintroduce it. The count now **names the stage it counts**, and a count recorded against a stage the venture has left is ignored rather than applied. Self-correcting for every early-returning path, present and future. |
| Mutation | 4 mutants on the bound, all killed: counter never grows; bound never applied; advancing does not reset; give-up does not name the stage. Plus 1 on the stage-keying: applying a count regardless of which stage earned it — killed. |
| One survivor, and what it meant | Deleting the `stage_tries_for` write from the *advance* branch survived every test. Traced rather than papered over: the advance branch already zeroes the count, so `prior` is 0 whether or not the label is current — an **equivalent mutant**. The line was redundant, not untested, so it was deleted rather than given a test that pretended it mattered. |
| Honest scope | Spend and noise, not correctness, as preregistered. The finding that earns its keep is the second one: a bound whose reset is unreachable on one path is worse than no bound, because it kills healthy work instead of merely wasting calls. |
| Suite | 1786/1786 workspace tests green. |

## E.LOOP-G — one transient judge error blinds foresight on a subject FOREVER (PREREGISTERED)
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| The finding | `resolve_predictions` judges a prediction when `status == "open"` and `resolve_by_ms <= now`. When the judge model errors it does `continue` — *"leave it open; try again next pass"* — touching neither field. The prediction is therefore **permanently due** and spends a model call every pass, with no cadence gate at all (the forge at least retried only every 15 minutes). |
| Why it is correctness, not spend | `store_prediction` refuses to stack a second open prediction on a subject that already has one (`already_open`). **Only one place in the file ever sets a status off `open`** — the judge's success path. So a single transient model error leaves a prediction that can never close, on a subject that can therefore never be forecast again. One network hiccup silently and permanently blinds foresight on that subject, and nothing reports it. |
| Nothing else can rescue it | `preds` is never pruned or capped — it only grows. The `len() > 1000` cap nearby is on `judgment_ledger`, a different structure. There is no expiry, no give-up, and no operator command equivalent to the forge's `kill`. |
| The class | Third instance today of *a guard whose firing condition is destroyed by the very failure it exists to catch*: the retry's own precondition (still open, still due) is exactly what the failure preserves. |
| The change | Count judge failures on the prediction; after a small bound, close it as **`unjudged`** — a terminal status that is neither a hit nor a miss, so calibration is untouched. Verified safe first: every reader of a prediction's status either tests `== "open"` (a new status correctly drops out of the open views in `briefing.rs` and `fitness.rs`) or matches `hit`/`miss` explicitly (`foresight.rs` scoring ignores it). |
| Kill criteria | A prediction whose judge keeps failing must stop being retried; it must stop blocking new predictions on its subject; it must NOT be scored as a hit or a miss; and it must say why. Mutants: the counter removed; the bound not applied; the status left `open`; the give-up scored as a verdict. |
| Honest scope | The blindness is silent and unbounded, which makes this more serious than E.LOOP-F — but it is still a degradation of a secondary faculty, not a wrong answer to a user. |

### E.LOOP-G — RESULT: shipped, and the prereg named the wrong path
| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Shipped | Both no-verdict paths go through one `note_unresolved`, which counts failures and at the bound closes the prediction `unjudged` — terminal, but deliberately not a verdict, so no calibration evidence is written from a judgment that never happened. |
| **The prereg named the wrong path** | I preregistered the judge-error `continue` as the finding. The first test — written against a judge that is simply down — **failed against my own fix**, because a fresh store has no held understanding and the pass never reaches the judge at all: it exits at `if reality.trim().is_empty() { continue; }`, a second unbounded path I had not seen. The likelier one in practice, too: any subject the mind cannot gather evidence about can never resolve. Watching the test fail is the only reason the fix is not still half-done. |
| Scope corrected downward too | The prereg implied a general pattern; the loop's third `continue` (lagging trip/event ledgers) turned out to be genuinely bounded — a two-week grace, after which it resolves to a machine `miss`. Two unbounded paths, not three. Checked before the claim went into a comment. |
| Safety of the new state | Verified before adding it, not after: every reader of a prediction's status either tests `== "open"` (so `unjudged` correctly drops out of the open views in `briefing.rs:420` and `fitness.rs:202`) or matches `hit`/`miss` explicitly (`foresight.rs` scoring ignores it). The forge taught this — a new stage name there would have kept ventures due forever. |
| Mutation | 5 mutants, all killed: counter never grows; bound never applied; either path failing to count; and closing as `miss` instead of `unjudged` — the last one guards the honesty property specifically, that an ungraded prediction is never scored. |
| Suite | 1788/1788 workspace tests green. |

### The class, after three instances in one session
`E.CB2-B` (a recovery path unreachable exactly when needed), `E.LOOP-F` (a staleness guard whose clock the failure itself resets), and `E.LOOP-G` (a retry whose precondition is what failing preserves) are one defect: **the guard's firing condition is destroyed by the very failure it exists to catch.** The tell is a comment reassuring the reader that something will be retried, next to code with nothing that counts. Two follow-on rules, both earned the hard way today: a bound is only sound if its *reset* is reachable on every path that advances (the forge's strong builder returned early and would have made the give-up kill healthy ventures), and the failure a fix introduces must be exercised by the fix's own test (which is how E.LOOP-G's real path was found, and how reading 7's loss was not).
